Chapter 71: Listening Overview & Format

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Describe the full IELTS Listening test structure, timing, and scoring rules for Academic and General Training.
  • Predict question types and difficulty patterns across all four sections.
  • Apply a pre-listening, during-listening, and post-transfer routine that protects accuracy.
  • Manage the 30-minute listening window plus 10-minute transfer time without losing marks to procedure errors.
  • Diagnose your personal error profile (spelling, pace, distractors, accents) and assign targeted drills.
  • Use prediction, signpost tracking, and note-taking micro-skills appropriate to each section.
  • Integrate Listening practice with vocabulary and spelling systems from Parts 2–3 of this book.

Theory / Explanation

71.1 What IELTS Listening Measures

IELTS Listening assesses your ability to understand spoken English in everyday and academic contexts. You are not tested on background knowledge of a topic; you are tested on whether you can:

  1. Follow main ideas in conversations and monologues.
  2. Catch specific factual detail (names, numbers, dates, places).
  3. Recognise attitudes, opinions, and purpose (especially Sections 3–4).
  4. Track discourse organisation — how a speaker moves from point to point.
  5. Handle paraphrase — the answer rarely matches the audio word-for-word.

The same Listening test is used for Academic and General Training candidates. Your Listening score contributes equally to both versions.

71.2 Test Structure at a Glance

Feature Detail
Sections 4
Questions 40
Approx. duration 30 minutes (+ 10 minutes transfer on paper; see below)
Recording Each section heard once only
Voices Mix of monologues and conversations; various English accents
Question types Form/note/table completion, multiple choice, matching, map/plan/diagram, sentence/summary completion, short answer
Scoring 1 mark per correct answer; no penalty for wrong guesses

Section difficulty curve:

Section Context Typical speakers Difficulty
1 Social/everyday Two people Lower
2 Social/monologue One person Medium
3 Educational/training Two to four people Medium–high
4 Academic lecture One person Highest

Why the curve matters: Many candidates treat Section 1 as “easy” and over-focus on Section 4. Band 7+ requires near-perfect Section 1–2 plus strong Section 3–4 — you cannot recover five lost marks in Section 1 through Section 4 heroics.

71.3 Paper vs Computer Delivery

Paper-based test (PBT): - You write answers on the question booklet during listening. - After the recording ends, you receive 10 minutes to transfer answers to the answer sheet. - Spelling and grammar on the answer sheet must be correct.

Computer-delivered test (CDT): - You type answers during listening; there is no separate 10-minute transfer at the end of Listening (transfer time may appear between modules in the full exam). - Typing speed and accuracy matter; practice typing names and numbers quickly.

Strategic implication: PBT candidates must rehearse legible handwriting under time pressure. CDT candidates must rehearse keyboard entry without mis-clicks.

71.4 How Raw Scores Convert to Bands

Raw scores (out of 40) map to band scores via official conversion tables that vary slightly by test form. Approximate guides:

Raw /40 Typical band
39–40 9.0
37–38 8.5
35–36 8.0
32–34 7.5
30–31 7.0
26–29 6.5
23–25 6.0

Why “approximately”: A form with harder Section 4 may allow 33/40 for Band 7.5. Treat mock conversions as trends, not guarantees.

71.5 The Listening Timeline (Minute by Minute)

Understanding the invisible clock reduces panic.

Before Section 1: - Instructions explain the test. - Example question played — use this to confirm sound level and question layout.

Between sections: - Short pause to read upcoming questions (typically 30–60 seconds depending on item count). - This is active study time, not rest.

During each section: - Audio plays continuously; you cannot pause or rewind. - Questions generally follow audio order (with rare exceptions in matching).

After Section 4: - PBT: 10-minute transfer. - CDT: check typed entries immediately.

Why timeline awareness helps: Candidates who “wait for the conversation to start” waste the most valuable seconds — the preview window.

71.6 Core Micro-Skills

Prediction

Before audio begins, read questions and guess: - Word class (noun, number, adjective) - Topic field (price, date, location, reason) - Synonyms the speaker might use

Example: Question says “cost of membership”. Audio may say “annual fee” or “subscription charge”.

Signpost tracking

Speakers signal structure:

  • “First of all…” / “Moving on to…” / “The main problem was…”
  • Contrast: “However…” / “On the other hand…”
  • Correction: “Actually, I mean…” / “Sorry, not Tuesday — Wednesday.”

Why corrections trap candidates: The first number mentioned is often a distractor; the corrected value is the answer.

Note-taking vs answer-writing

In fast sections, jot minimal cues (e.g., Wed, £45, lib ref desk) then expand during transfer. Avoid writing full sentences during Section 4 unless you can touch-type quickly.

Spelling discipline

Misspelled correct answers score zero. British and American spelling are usually both accepted if listed on the official key — when unsure, use the spelling in the question paper if provided.

71.7 Question-Type Map (Preview)

Detailed chapters follow; overview here:

Type Chapters Frequency
Form / note / table completion 72 Very high
Map / plan / diagram labelling 73 Medium
Multiple choice 74 High
Matching 75 Medium–high
Sentence / summary completion 76 High
Short answer 77 Medium

Cross-cutting skills: Accents, paraphrase, distractors — Chapter 78.

71.8 Accent Exposure Strategy

IELTS uses British, Australian, North American, and New Zealand English among others. You are not marked on accent production — only comprehension.

Training plan: - Week 1–2: identify your weakest accent (often Australian or regional British). - Week 3–4: deliberate exposure — podcasts, news clips, lecture excerpts. - Week 5+: mixed-accent mock sections under timed conditions.

Why accent training is not optional at Band 8+: Section 1 may feature Australian English while Section 4 uses British academic intonation; fatigue increases mishearing risk.

71.9 Common Failure Patterns

Pattern Symptom Fix
Spelling loss Knows word, loses mark Personal spelling list + dictation
Distractor capture Writes first heard option Wait for correction / full clause
Preview neglect Enters section cold Strict 30-second question skim rule
Section 4 freeze Misses Q31–35, recovers late Skip-flag-return protocol
Transfer error Right booklet, wrong sheet Double-check question numbers
Over-writing Exceeds word limit Count words before writing

71.10 Integration with Other Modules

Listening feeds: - Speaking — rhythm, chunking, discourse markers. - Writing — spelling of academic vocabulary (Chapter 69 AWL). - Reading — paraphrase recognition transfers directly.

Weekly integration drill: After each Listening mock, extract 10 new collocations into your vocabulary notebook (Chapter 44).

71.11 Equipment and Test-Day Listening

  • Confirm headphones fit and volume during the example.
  • Raise hand immediately for audio issues — you cannot replay.
  • Ignore other candidates’ pacing; trust your question numbers.
  • PBT: bring sharp pencil; eraser clean.
  • CDT: practice on similar keyboard if possible.

71.12 Building a Listening Study Cycle

Phase A — Accuracy (untimed): - Single section replay (non-official practice only) to analyse paraphrase. - Transcript shadowing for weak accents.

Phase B — Speed (timed): - Full test weekly; no pauses. - Section 4 isolation drills twice weekly.

Phase C — Exam simulation: - Full LRW morning mock including transfer. - Post-mortem: error log by type (Chapter 6).

Examples

Example 1: Section 1 Preview Reading

Questions (extract): - Customer name: ___________ - Membership type: ___________ - Start date: ___________

Prediction notes (written in margin): - Name = proper noun, spelling letter-by-letter likely - Membership = gold/silver/basic OR annual/monthly - Date = day + month; watch ordinals (3rd vs 30th)

Example 2: Signpost in Section 3

Audio: “We initially planned the survey for March, but recruitment delays pushed it back to April.”

Question: *Survey month: ___________

Trap: March (first mention). Answer: April (corrected timeline).

Example 3: Word Limit

Question: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

Audio: “The workshop is in the main lecture hall.”

Wrong: main lecture hall (3 words). Right: lecture hall OR main hall — choose the pair that preserves meaning and fits limit.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Raw Score to Band Goal

Target: Band 7.0 (typically 30–31/40).

Mock result: S1 9/10, S2 8/10, S3 7/10, S4 5/10 → 29/40 = Band 6.5.

Diagnosis: Section 4 pace + note density, not overall “listening ability.”

Plan: Two Section 4-only tests per week; AWL vocabulary for lecture topics (science, urban planning); maintain S1–2 perfection drills.

Worked Example 2: Transfer Error Prevention (PBT)

Candidate writes answers in booklet Q11–20 during Section 2. During transfer, shifts all answers one line down from Q12 onward.

Prevention rule: Transfer section by section, verbally confirming “Section 2, question 11” before writing each block.

Worked Example 3: Skip-Flag-Return

In Section 4, candidate misses Q33 (complex paraphrase). Instead of rewinding mentally (impossible), they: 1. Flag Q33 in booklet. 2. Capture Q34–36 immediately. 3. If Q37 paraphrase echoes Q33 vocabulary, attempt fill-in.

Why it works: Audio order means later context sometimes clarifies earlier gaps — but only if you stay forward-moving.

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — Format Knowledge (Questions 1–15)

  1. How many sections are in IELTS Listening?
  2. How many times is each section played?
  3. Which section is usually an academic monologue?
  4. Name three question types in Listening.
  5. Is there a penalty for wrong answers?
  6. How long is the listening recording approximately?
  7. PBT: how many minutes for transfer?
  8. Which section typically has two speakers in a social context?
  9. GT vs Academic — same Listening test?
  10. What happens if spelling is wrong but word is correct orally?
  11. Name two English accent varieties used in IELTS.
  12. What is a “distractor” in Listening?
  13. Do questions usually follow audio order?
  14. What word-limit instruction means maximum three words?
  15. Section 2 is usually monologue or conversation?

Exercise Set B — Mini Transcript Analysis

Transcript (Section 1 style — original):

Receptionist: Good morning, Riverside Sports Centre.
Caller: Hi, I’d like to enquire about joining the swimming programme.
Receptionist: Certainly. Are you interested in the adult lane swimming or the family splash sessions?
Caller: Adult lanes, please. I work near the river, so the lunchtime slots suit me.
Receptionist: We have midday sessions on Tuesdays and Thursdays, from twelve thirty to one fifteen.
Caller: Thursdays work better. What does it cost?
Receptionist: A single visit is nine pounds fifty, but the monthly pass is thirty-two pounds — much better value if you come twice a week.
Caller: I’ll take the monthly pass. My name is Elena Voronova — V-O-R-O-N-O-V-A.
Receptionist: And a contact number?
Caller: Zero seven nine four, double six, one oh eight three.
Receptionist: Perfect. The pass activates from the first of next month — that’s September.

Questions: 16. Type of swimming programme: ___________ 17. Day of session: ___________ 18. Cost of monthly pass: £___________ 19. Customer surname: ___________ 20. Phone number: ___________ 21. Pass start month: ___________

Exercise Set C — Section 4 Extract (Questions 22–28)

Transcript (abbreviated lecture — original):

Today we’ll examine how urban planners use green corridors — strips of vegetation connecting parks — to support biodiversity. Unlike isolated pocket parks, corridors allow species to migrate safely. A 2019 study in Melbourne tracked possum movement along planted verges beside a tram line. Researchers found crossing rates increased by forty percent within eighteen months. However, corridors fail when canopy gaps exceed fifteen metres; small birds refuse to fly across wide open space. Maintenance costs are often underestimated: irrigation alone can consume twelve percent of a municipal parks budget. Planners now prioritise native drought-resistant species to reduce watering. Public engagement matters too — community planting days improved vandalism rates in two Sheffield estates.

Questions (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER): 22. Vegetation strips connecting parks are called green ___________ 23. Study city: ___________ 24. Percentage increase in crossing rates: ___________ 25. Maximum gap birds tolerate: ___________ metres 26. Irrigation may use ___________ percent of parks budget 27. Plants chosen to reduce watering: native ___________ species 28. Public help reduced ___________ in Sheffield

Q Question stem Your prediction (word class / field)

(Prediction samples in Solutions.)

Solutions (with WHY)

Set A

  1. Four — standard since test inception.
  2. Once — no replay; preview time compensates.
  3. Section 4 — academic lecture format.
  4. Any three: form completion, multiple choice, matching, map labelling, sentence completion, short answer.
  5. No penalty — always guess if unsure.
  6. ~30 minutes — plus transfer on PBT.
  7. 10 minutes — PBT only.
  8. Section 1 — social dialogue.
  9. Yes — identical test.
  10. Zero mark — spelling counts; WHY candidates lose “easy” marks.
  11. British, Australian, American (any two).
  12. Plausible wrong option mentioned to test careful listening.
  13. Usually yes — order principle aids navigation.
  14. NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS — count includes articles unless exception stated.
  15. Monologue — one speaker, social context (e.g., tour guide).

Set B

  1. adult lane swimming — caller rejects family sessions.
  • Wrong: “family splash” — distractor from receptionist’s offer.
  1. Thursday(s) — caller chooses Thursday over Tuesday.
  • Wrong: Tuesday — mentioned but rejected.
  1. 32 / thirty-two — monthly pass price; single visit £9.50 is distractor.
  2. Voronova — spelled letter-by-letter; must match exactly.
  3. 0794661083 — UK mobile format; double six = 66.
  4. September — “first of next month” from conversation frame.

Set C

  1. corridors — defined in opening sentence.
  2. Melbourne — study location explicit.
  3. 40% / forty percent — numeric detail; common trap: 18 months (time not rate).
  4. 15 / fifteen — “exceed fifteen metres” = maximum tolerated gap.
  5. 12 / twelve — irrigation budget share.
  6. drought-resistant — paraphrase “reduce watering.”
  7. vandalism — “improved vandalism rates” = reduced vandalism.

Set D (sample predictions)

  1. Number | 30. Noun phrase (reason) | 31. Book/title | 32. Time | 33. Yes/No | 34. Number/currency | 35. Place noun

WHY prediction matters: Pre-activates vocabulary so paraphrase is recognised faster under audio pressure.

Review

  • Listening = 4 sections, 40 questions, one play only, ~30 minutes.
  • Difficulty rises; Sections 1–2 are scoring foundations.
  • Master preview, paraphrase, spelling, word limits, distractor awareness.
  • PBT transfer time needs procedure rehearsal.
  • Accent variety is deliberate — train mixed exposure.
  • Error log by type, not “I am bad at Listening.”

Quiz

  1. Raw score for approximately Band 8.0?
  2. Which section has educational discussion among multiple speakers?
  3. CDT: separate 10-minute Listening transfer?
  4. What is the order principle?
  5. Name one signpost word for correction.
  6. Maximum marks if spelling wrong?
  7. Section 2 context type?
  8. First step when entering new section?
  9. Green corridors example tested which skill?
  10. Skip-flag-return is used when?

Assignment

  1. Take one official-style full Listening test under exam conditions. Score by section; log errors in four categories: spelling, distractor, pace, accent.

  2. Write a personal Listening routine (before/during/after) of 150–200 words.

  3. Collect 20 AWL items from one Section 4 transcript; note how each was paraphrased in questions.

  4. Record yourself reading aloud 10 numbers, dates, and proper nouns — simulate letter-by-letter spelling drills.

Revision Notes

LISTENING OVERVIEW

4 sections × 10 Qs = 40; heard ONCE
S1 social dialogue → S4 academic lecture
Preview every gap BEFORE audio
Paraphrase > exact match
Spelling & word limits = marks
Distractors + corrections common
PBT: 10-min transfer by section
Error types: spell / pace / trap / accent

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Use the example question at the start to set volume — not after Section 1 begins.

Exam Strategy: Never leave a blank: no negative marking — intelligent guesses after elimination beat empty boxes.

Exam Strategy: If you miss an answer, move on immediately — staying stuck costs the next two questions.

Exam Strategy: Section 1 deserves 100% focus — these marks are the most accessible in the entire test.

Challenge Questions

  1. Design a four-week Listening plan for a candidate stuck at 27/40 (Band 6.5) who needs 32/40 (Band 7.5). Specify daily minutes and section emphasis.

  2. Compare PBT and CDT Listening risks in a table of five rows — procedure, spelling, review, anxiety, equipment.

  3. Explain why “transcript-only study” without timed audio fails to raise band scores.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 listeners treat question preview as a micro-reading test — they underline limit words (ONLY, NOT, NO MORE THAN) and predict grammar before the first syllable plays.

Band 9 Secret: High-band scorers maintain a section score ledger across mocks; they refuse to proceed until Sections 1–2 average 19/20 or higher.

Band 9 Secret: Elite performers verbalise corrections in practice (“March—no, April”) until the habit becomes automatic under exam noise.

Band 9 Weekly Listening Log (original template)

Mock S1 S2 S3 S4 Total Top error Drill
M1 10 9 8 6 33 S4 pace AWL lecture bank
M2 10 10 8 7 35 Spelling Dictation 15 min/day

Discipline: Band 9 is often procedure perfection in easy sections plus controlled recovery in hard ones — not mythical “perfect ears.”

Next: Chapter 72 — Form, Note & Table Completion

Chapter 72: Form, Note & Table Completion

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Recognise form, note, and table completion formats across all four Listening sections.
  • Apply word-limit rules precisely, including articles, numbers, and hyphenated compounds.
  • Capture names, addresses, phone numbers, dates, prices, and spellings with exam-ready accuracy.
  • Use row/column navigation in tables to stay synchronised with audio order.
  • Predict answer grammar from gap position and surrounding syntax.
  • Avoid distractors in numeric sequences, corrected details, and listed options.
  • Complete high-frequency Section 1–2 forms at near-perfect accuracy consistently.

Theory / Explanation

72.1 What Are Completion Tasks?

Form, note, and table completion items present a partially filled document. You write missing words or numbers heard in the recording. The document may resemble:

  • Forms: membership applications, booking sheets, registration cards.
  • Notes: lecture notes, meeting minutes, interview summaries.
  • Tables: schedules, comparison charts, survey results.

Despite different layouts, the cognitive task is identical: map spoken information to a labelled gap while respecting constraints.

72.2 Why Completion Dominates Section 1

Section 1 almost always opens with a social dialogue completing a form. Examiners test:

Skill Example
Spelling Surnames, street names
Numbers Prices, phone, postcodes
Dates/times Appointments, opening hours
Classification Membership type, room category
Listening for correction “No, the 14th, not the 4th”

Band impact: Ten Section 1 questions reward precision, not inference. Losing four marks here often drops an entire band half-step.

72.3 Word-Limit Rules (Non-Negotiable)

Instructions appear in CAPS above each question group:

Instruction Meaning
ONE WORD ONLY Single word; numbers as digits usually OK
NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS 1–2 words
NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER Words + numbers combined; count carefully
NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER Very common in Sections 1–2

Rules: - Hyphenated compounds may count as one word (well-known, mid-range). - Numbers expressed as digits (45) or words (forty-five) unless specified. - Articles (a, the) count as words unless question already includes them. - Exceeding the limit → zero mark, even if content correct.

72.4 Grammar Prediction from Gap Position

Gap context Expected answer
The ___ is broken. Noun
It was extremely ___. Adjective/adverb
They decided to ___. Verb (base/infinitive)
Meet at ___ on Monday. Place/time
Cost: £___ Number
Contact: ___@email.com Email fragment

Why grammar helps: If you hear an adjective but gap needs noun, you may have misaligned question numbers — immediate red flag.

72.5 Forms: Field-by-Field Strategy

Step 1 — Scan field labels (30 seconds): underline keywords (surname, deposit, preferred).

Step 2 — Predict content type per field.

Step 3 — During audio: - Write in pencil lightly; confirm spelling when speaker repeats. - For letters, use block capitals on answer sheet if unsure of cursive clarity.

Step 4 — Corrections: When speaker self-corrects, cross out gently, write final value.

72.6 Tables: Row and Column Tracking

Tables add visual complexity. Audio still follows question order left-to-right, top-to-bottom (usually).

Technique: 1. Identify headers (days, prices, features). 2. Place finger on first gap cell before audio. 3. Move cell-by-cell; never jump ahead visually.

Trap: Speaker discusses Row C while you stare at Row B — misalignment cascade.

72.7 Notes: Abbreviation During Listening

Notes completion (Sections 2–4) allows shorthand in booklet during listening, but answer sheet needs full acceptable form within word limit.

Shorthand Transfer as
gov government (if one word limit fails — use longer only if allowed)
approx approximately (check limit!)
temp temperature

Caution: Transfer exactly what fits the limit; trim intelligently.

72.8 Numbers, Dates, and Money

Numbers

  • teen vs ty: 13 vs 30 — stress pattern differs; practice minimal pairs.
  • Double/triple: “double six” = 66.
  • Thousands: 1,500 may be “fifteen hundred” or “one thousand five hundred.”

Dates

British order often day-month-year in speech: the third of November. Watch ordinal vs cardinal: May 15th not May 50.

Money

Currency may precede or follow: £45 / 45 pounds. Decoys: deposit vs total vs monthly fee — label match essential.

72.9 Spelling Patterns in IELTS

High-frequency spelling traps:

Category Examples
Double letters accommodation, committee, beginning
-ance/-ence attendance, licence (noun UK)
Proper nouns Kettering, Woolwich, Fitzgerald
Job titles receptionist, coordinator

System: Maintain personal “Listening Spelling Hit List” from every mock.

72.10 Distractors Specific to Completion

  1. Option lists: Speaker mentions A, B, C; answer is B — others are traps.
  2. Partial match: Question asks for reason; speaker gives reason embedded in long clause — extract core noun phrase within limit.
  3. Homophones: site vs sight, stationary vs stationery.
  4. Corrected info: First value wrong; second right.

72.11 Section Distribution

Section Completion style
1 Full form common
2 Notes or table (monologue)
3 Notes in discussion context
4 Lecture notes or summary gaps

Difficulty rises through vocabulary abstraction, not necessarily different instructions.

72.12 Transfer Discipline (PBT)

  • Complete one section block before moving to next on answer sheet.
  • Say question number aloud silently: “Eighteen…”
  • Check plural endings heard at word end (requirements not requirement).

Examples

Example 1: Form Gap with Article Trap

Question: Equipment needed: ___________ (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)

Audio: “You’ll need a helmet and gloves, but we provide the harness.”

Wrong: a helmet (two words but question may expect equipment not provided — read full dialogue).

If question asks what student must bring → helmet OR helmet gloves depending on full context.

Example 2: Table Completion

Day Instructor Level
Mon Sarah beginner
Wed ___ intermediate
Sat Marco ___

Audio: “Wednesday classes are taken over by James this term… Saturday remains advanced with Marco.”

Answers: James, advanced.

Example 3: Note Completion with Paraphrase

Note: Main cause of delay: ___________

Audio: “The project stalled chiefly because funding approval arrived late.”

Answer: funding approval (two words) or late funding — choose fit within limit matching question wording style.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Phone Number

Audio: “My number is oh one two three, four double eight, nine oh one.”

Breakdown: - oh = 0 - double eight = 88 - nine oh one = 901

Answer: 0123 488 901 (format as heard; spaces optional unless specified).

WHY wrong answers fail: 0123 489 801 swaps digits; missing “double” loses a digit.

Worked Example 2: Corrected Date

Audio: “Let’s book the fifteenth of June… actually, make that the eighteenth — the fifteenth is fully booked.”

Question: Booking date: ___________

Answer: 18 June / June 18 / 18th June (accept test conventions).

WHY: Fifteenth is explicit distractor before correction.

Worked Example 3: Word Limit Trim

Audio: “The library’s extended study zone is on the second floor.”

Limit: ONE WORD ONLY

Wrong: second floor (two words)

Right: second if question is *Floor: ___* OR re-read question — if gap is *Location: ___* with two-word limit → second floor.

Lesson: Gap label determines extraction.

Practice 1

Field Answer WHY

Address Willow Street name only in gap
Postcode BN4 7QP UK format read aloud
Phone 01273944210 Zero=0, double four=44
Max items 8 / eight Explicit limit

Incorrect alternatives: “student” (offered not chosen); “14” if gap asks road name only.

Gap Answer WHY

Instructor Omar Named explicitly

Practice 3

Gap Answer WHY

Equipment binocular Singular pair needing fix

Practice 4

  1. waggle dance — defined term
  2. sun / the sun — direction reference
  3. duration / length — paraphrase “longer waggle runs”
  4. polarised — cloudy-day mechanism

WHY wrong fails: “vertical” describes orientation not direction cue; “software” from different topic.

Practice 5 (sample answers)

  • Bring: laptop (tablets rejected)

Review

  • Form/note/table = same skill: gap filling with limits.
  • Preview labels, predict grammar, track order.
  • Spelling and numbers decide Section 1 bands.
  • Tables need cell-by-cell tracking.
  • Corrections override first mention.
  • Transfer section-by-section on PBT.

Quiz

  1. ONE WORD ONLY — can “post office” fit?
  2. “Double three” equals what digit pair?
  3. Table audio order usually follows what visual path?
  4. Article “the” counts when?
  5. Section 1 typically uses which completion format?
  6. Hyphenated word word-count rule?
  7. Why write block capitals for names?
  8. Deposit vs total fee — what prevents error?
  9. Notes completion commonest section pair?
  10. Exceed word limit — mark awarded?

Assignment

  1. Complete five original form transcripts (write your own answers, swap with partner).

  2. Build spelling list of 30 words missed in completion tasks; dictation test daily.

  3. Design a table with 8 gaps; record 90-second audio; self-mark.

  4. Analyse one Section 1 from any practice test: classify each error as spelling, distractor, limit, or alignment.

Revision Notes

FORM / NOTE / TABLE COMPLETION

Scan labels → predict type → listen in order
Word limits sacred; count articles
Numbers: teen/ty, double/triple
Dates: watch corrections
Tables: cell-by-cell finger track
Spelling = Section 1 gold
Cross out & replace on correction

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: When the speaker spells a word, write each letter immediately — do not wait for the end.

Exam Strategy: For prices, write the currency label in the question if already printed; don’t duplicate unless gap requires it.

Exam Strategy: If two answers seem possible, choose the one last confirmed by the speaker.

Challenge

Create a 10-gap hotel booking form with embedded distractors (wrong dates, rejected room types). Exchange with a study partner. Target: 10/10 in one play.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 candidates pre-write probable field formats in margins (e.g., ___ Rd, BN_ ___) so handwriting stays compact during fast dictation.

Band 9 Secret: They never transfer ambiguous digits — if “15 or 50,” they flag and resolve from context before leaving the section.

Band 9 Secret: Section 1 completion is treated as a spelling exam with background noise — zero tolerance mindset.

Next: Chapter 73 — Map, Plan & Diagram Labelling

Chapter 73: Map, Plan & Diagram Labelling

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Orient yourself quickly on maps, floor plans, site plans, and process diagrams before audio begins.
  • Follow directional language (left, right, opposite, beyond, adjacent) under time pressure.
  • Match labelled options from a box to diagram locations without wasting time rewriting words.
  • Track multi-step routes and sequential process stages in audio order.
  • Distinguish map labelling (Sections 1–2) from academic diagram tasks (Sections 2–4).
  • Avoid classic traps: mirror confusion, starting-point shifts, and recycled option letters.
  • Label unfamiliar spaces using landmark anchoring and compass-style mental models.

Theory / Explanation

73.1 Task Types in This Family

IELTS Listening uses visual-spatial tasks in several forms:

Format Visual Typical section Answer style
Map labelling Town/campus/park map 1–2 Word from list OR short phrase
Plan labelling Building floor plan 2 Letter or word
Diagram labelling Process/equipment diagram 2–4 Word from box
Flow chart stages Sequential boxes 4 Gap fill

All require linking spoken description to spatial or sequential position.

73.2 Why Maps Appear in Section 2

Section 2 often features a monologue tour — museum guide, campus orientation, festival layout. Speaker walks listener through space. Questions test:

  • Directional comprehension
  • Landmark reference (past the fountain, behind the café)
  • Renaming / temporary changes (what used to be the gift shop is now…)

73.3 Pre-Listening Orientation Protocol (60 Seconds)

Step 1 — Locate YOU ARE HERE or implicit entrance (often bottom-centre).

Step 2 — Identify north** if shown; if not, assign mental north upward on page.

Step 3 — Mark fixed landmarks** already labelled (car park, river, main gate).

Step 4 — Read option list** (A–H) — note word class (building types, facilities).

Step 5 — Predict route start** from first question instruction.

Why 60 seconds matters: Audio begins walking immediately; unprepared candidates chase the speaker visually.

73.4 Directional Language Lexicon

Expression Meaning
On your left/right Relative to speaker’s facing direction
Opposite / facing Across a path or road
Adjacent / next to Sharing a boundary
At the corner of Intersection of two paths/streets
Beyond / past Farther along same route
In the middle of Central position
At the far end Maximum distance on axis
Diagonally opposite Across and offset
Fork / branch Path splits
Roundabout / circle Circular junction

Critical: Speaker’s left may differ from your map orientation if they face toward you. Follow movement direction on the map step by step.

73.5 Letter-from-Box vs Write-the-Word

Two answer modes:

Mode A — Choose letter: Map shows gaps 11–14; list A–H at bottom. Write letter only on answer sheet unless instructed otherwise.

Mode B — Write word: No letters; write exact word from list (spelling must match list).

Exam tip: Never write both letter and word unless required — wastes time and risks ambiguity.

73.6 Process and Equipment Diagrams

Section 4 may describe scientific apparatus or natural cycles:

  • Water treatment stages
  • Life cycle of insect
  • Parts of hearing mechanism

Strategy: 1. Identify entry point (input/raw material). 2. Follow ** arrows** if present. 3. Note parallel paths (split flows confuse).

Audio describes stages in sequence — usually matches question order.

73.7 Distractors in Spatial Tasks

  1. Mentioned but not answer: Speaker passes café en route to answer (library).
  2. Temporary relocation: “The clinic has moved to…”
  3. Double naming: “Old gymnasium, now called Sports Hall B”
  4. Option reuse prohibition: Each letter used once in many tasks — elimination helps.
  5. Dead-end paths: Speaker describes wrong turn then corrects.

73.8 Note-Taking on Maps

Light pencil marks during audio: - Arrow path along route - Cross out eliminated options - Circle final labels

Erase clutter before transfer if PBT.

73.9 Integration with Vocabulary

Map tasks favour facility nouns:

Domain Lexis
Campus lecture theatre, refectory, accommodation block
Town pedestrian zone, bypass, roundabout
Nature wetland, boardwalk, viewing platform
Museum gallery, atrium, temporary exhibition space

Study Chapter 63 (Transportation) and Chapter 57 (Tourism) for collocations.

73.10 Accessibility and Scale

Some maps lack scale bars. Use relative distance language:

  • “Just a short walk” ≈ adjacent
  • “At the far side of the field” ≈ opposite edge

Why: Absolute metres rarely appear; relational phrases dominate.

73.11 Common Errors and Fixes

Error Fix
Mirror left/right Trace speaker path with finger
Lost start point Reset at labelled landmark each question group
Wrong option reused Track used letters in margin
Missed “used to be” Circle tense shift verbs in preview

73.12 Practice Progression

  1. Static maps: label from description without walking audio (teacher reads).
  2. Guided tours: podcast city walks with map PDFs.
  3. Timed IELTS sections: strict one-play.
  4. Blind draw: listen, sketch route, compare — builds mental mapping.

Examples

Example 1: Relative Position

Audio: “The gift shop is opposite the main entrance, on the other side of the courtyard.”

If entrance at south, shop at north across courtyard — not adjacent east/west.

Example 2: Process Diagram

Stages: Collection → Screening → Sedimentation → Filtration → Disinfection

Audio skips explicit “screening” but mentions “removing large debris” — maps to screening** box.

Example 3: Correction

Audio: “Turn left at the rose garden — sorry, I mean right — toward the lake.”

Answer path uses right turn.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Campus Map (Letters A–F)

Options: A Library, B Gym, C Pharmacy, D Bus stop, E Pond, F Accommodation

Audio excerpt: “Starting from the bus stop, walk straight past the library on your right. The gym is the large building facing the pond, not the one near accommodation.”

Question 11: Building facing pond → B (Gym)

WHY not F: “Near accommodation” describes a different building (distractor).

Worked Example 2: Festival Plan

Gaps: First aid, Food court, Stage 2

Audio: “Beyond the main stage, follow the path that curves left. Food stalls cluster at the bend. First aid is back near the entrance, beside the information kiosk.”

Mapping: - Food court → at bend (left curve) - First aid → entrance/kiosk - Stage 2 → inferred main stage already labelled; Stage 2 opposite field per earlier context

Worked Example 3: Diagram — Bee Anatomy (Section 4 style)

Audio: “Pollen collects on the hind legs in structures called corbiculae, often visible as yellow pellets.”

Gap label on leg diagram → hind legs (must match word box if provided).

Practice Exercises

Practice 1 — Riverside Park Map (Section 2)

Speaker tour transcript (original):

Welcome to Riverside Park. Enter through the south gate. Immediately on your left is the visitor centre. Walk north along the main path; the playground is on the east side, beside the café. Continue to the footbridge crossing the river. On the far northern bank, you’ll find the bird hide. The car park remains outside the south gate, across Mill Road. Cyclists should note the bike rack sits between the visitor centre and the playground.

Map gaps (label from list): - South gate area (off-map): Car park = - Left of path on entry: - East side mid-park: - Crosses river: - North bank: - Between visitor centre and playground:

Word box: visitor centre, playground, footbridge, bird hide, car park, bike rack

Practice 2 — Museum Floor Plan

Transcript (original):

Level one: Temporary exhibitions occupy the atrium — that’s the open space just inside the entrance. Permanent sculpture is west wing, upstairs via the grand staircase. The café moved last month to the east wing ground floor, replacing the bookshop. Restrooms remain adjacent to the cloakroom, north of the atrium.

Questions: 1. Open space at entrance: ___________ 2. Sculpture location: ___________ 3. Café now in: ___________ 4. Restrooms location: ___________

Practice 3 — Water Treatment Diagram (Section 4)

Transcript (original):

Raw water enters the intake screen. Fine particles settle in tanks after coagulation chemicals are added. Clear water passes through sand filters before chlorine is injected. Finally, water enters the reservoir for distribution.

Stages (in order): intake → ___ → settling tanks → ___ → ___ → reservoir

Word box: sand filters, chlorine, pumping station (distractor), coagulation (may be implied)

Practice 4 — University Orientation (Multiple choice map)

Transcript (original):

The science faculty building sits diagonally opposite the student union, across the plaza. The medical library is behind the hospital block, not beside the pharmacy school as old maps show. Buses stop on West Lane, not East Lane since the roadworks.

Practice 5 — Diagram Labelling Practice

Label parts of a volcano cross-section from lecture:

Magma rises through the central vent. Gas and ash erupt from the crater at the summit. Secondary openings called side vents may form on flanks. Molten rock stored underground lies in the magma chamber deep below.

Solutions (with WHY)

Practice 1

Gap Answer WHY
Car park car park Outside south gate across road
Left on entry visitor centre Immediate left from south
East mid playground Beside café east side
River footbridge Crosses river
North bank bird hide Far northern bank
Between VC & playground bike rack Explicit between

Trap: café mentioned but not in gap list for those labels.

Practice 2

  1. atrium — open entrance space
  2. west wing (upstairs) — permanent sculpture
  3. east wing — café moved; bookshop distractor
  4. north of atrium / cloakroom — adjacent restrooms

WHY wrong: bookshop is former café location.

Practice 3

Order: intake → (coagulation implied before tanks) → settling tanks → sand filters → chlorine → reservoir

Pumping station not mentioned — box distractor.

Practice 4 (sample MCQ answers)

  • Science faculty: diagonally opposite student union
  • Medical library: behind hospital block
  • Bus stop: West Lane

Practice 5

  • vent (central)
  • crater (summit)
  • side vents (flanks)
  • magma chamber (deep)

Review

  • Orient first — entrance, north, landmarks.
  • Trace route with finger during audio.
  • Directional language is precise; corrections happen.
  • Diagrams follow process order.
  • Option boxes: each letter once (usually).
  • Facility vocabulary from topic chapters supports prediction.

Quiz

  1. What symbol often marks starting point?
  2. “Diagonally opposite” means?
  3. Section 2 map tasks usually monologue or dialogue?
  4. Write letter or word when box says A–H?
  5. “Used to be” signals what?
  6. Process diagrams follow what order?
  7. Name three directional phrases.
  8. Why mark eliminated options?
  9. Speaker’s left vs map left — resolve how?
  10. Section 4 diagrams often describe what fields?

Assignment

  1. Print any campus map; record 2-minute orientation audio with 6 labels.

  2. Complete three official-style map tasks; log left/right errors separately.

  3. Draw a volcano or water cycle diagram; write 120-word labelling script.

  4. List 25 facility nouns by category (education, health, recreation).

Revision Notes

MAP / PLAN / DIAGRAM

60-sec orient: entrance, north, landmarks
Finger-trace speaker path
Left/right = speaker movement direction
Box labels: track used letters
"Used to be" / "now called" = update label
Process: follow arrows & sequence
Corrections override first direction

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: If lost, wait for the next landmark — speakers re-anchor (“now we’re back at the fountain”).

Exam Strategy: For box lists, write the letter on the answer sheet if instructions specify letters only.

Exam Strategy: Diagram Section 4: skim all gap labels before audio — know if gaps are parts, stages, or chemicals.

Challenge

Listen to a real museum or campus virtual tour online. Sketch the route from memory. Compare to official floor plan. Repeat until accuracy reaches 90%.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 mappers assign temporary nicknames in pencil (VC, PH) to unlabelled gaps before audio — faster than re-reading full words.

Band 9 Secret: They eliminate box options aggressively when a facility is mentioned but already placed — narrows remaining choices logically.

Band 9 Secret: For process diagrams, they number arrows 1–6 in preview so audio triggers slot into pre-marked slots without re-scanning the whole image.

Extended Practice Set F — Campus Map (Section 2)

Word box A–G: A Pharmacy, B Bookshop, C Lecture Theatre, D Gym, E Pond, F Bus stop, G Accommodation

Transcript (original):

Enter campus from the bus stop on East Road. Directly ahead is the lecture theatre — the circular glass building. Walk clockwise around the pond; the gym sits on the north side, opposite accommodation blocks. The bookshop is between the pharmacy and the lecture theatre — sorry, the pharmacy is actually east of the bookshop, nearer the bus stop. Medical services use the pharmacy building after hours.

Gaps:
11. Entrance from: ___
12. Circular building: ___
13. North of pond: ___
14. Opposite gym: ___
15. East of bookshop: ___

Solutions: 11-F bus stop | 12-C lecture theatre | 13-D gym | 14-G accommodation | 15-A pharmacy — WHY: correction relocates pharmacy east of bookshop (D3 distractor if you matched pre-correction).

Appendix 73.A — Directional Phrase Flash Cards

Front Back
Bear left at the fork Take left branch at split path
Diagonally opposite Across and offset
At the foot of Bottom of slope/stairs
Adjacent to Next door sharing wall
Beyond the bridge Farther after crossing

Review 10 cards daily until automatic — map tasks fail when directional vocabulary is passive recognition only.

Extended Practice Set G — Industrial Site Plan

Transcript (original):

Trucks enter via the north gate, proceed to the weighbridge, then unload at bay three. Office staff park near the main entrance south side. Hazard storage is east of the production hall, fenced separately. Assembly occurs in the central hall — tours never enter. Emergency assembly point is the car park beyond the south entrance. Visitors collect badges at reception before proceeding to the viewing gallery above assembly.

Label gaps: north gate route → weighbridge → ___ → hazard storage location → emergency point → ___

Solutions: bay three | east of production hall | car park (south) | viewing gallery — WHY tours never enter assembly: distractor if you label assembly as visitor destination.

Extended Exercises Set H (21–30)

  1. “At the far end of the corridor” means?
  2. Plan without compass — assign mental north how?
  3. Each letter once — unused letters normal?
  4. Speaker faces you — their left is your?
  5. Process diagram without arrows — listen for?
  6. “Temporary marquee” signals?
  7. Map Q11-14 box A-H — minimum unused?
  8. Diagram Section 4 common topic types (name 3)?
  9. Finger tracing prevents what error?
  10. “Opposite the refectory” requires knowing?

Solutions: 21-max distance along corridor | 22-top of page | 23-yes typically 2-3 unused | 24-right | 25-sequence markers first/next/finally | 26-relocatable landmark | 27-3 unused | 28-life cycle, water treatment, body parts | 29-left/right mirror | 30-refectory location on plan

Chapter 74: Multiple Choice

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Identify single-answer vs multiple-answer multiple choice formats in IELTS Listening.
  • Eliminate distractors using paraphrase recognition and tone/intention cues.
  • Manage longer option stems in Sections 3–4 without reading during critical audio moments.
  • Apply preview strategies that front-load keyword comparison maps (option A/B/C vs predicted synonyms).
  • Handle “choose TWO letters” tasks with checkbox logic and mutual exclusivity.
  • Recognise when speakers agree, disagree, or partially accept options among discussants.
  • Maintain accuracy when options are long, similar, or ordered differently from audio.

Theory / Explanation

74.1 MCQ Formats in IELTS Listening

Format Instruction example Answer sheet
Single choice Choose the correct letter A, B, or C One letter
Multiple answer Choose TWO letters A–E Two letters
Picture options Rare; usually letter labels under images Letter

Sections: MCQ appears in all sections but lengthens in Sections 3–4 — options become full clauses, not single words.

74.2 Cognitive Demands

Multiple choice tests:

  1. Global understanding — main idea, purpose, attitude.
  2. Detail discrimination — similar options differ by one criterion.
  3. Paraphrase tolerance — correct option rewords audio; wrong options may use exact words from audio (keyword traps).

Key principle: The correct answer matches meaning, not surface wording.

74.3 The Preview Window Strategy

Before audio:

Step 1 — Read question stem (the actual question line).

Step 2 — Underline focus word** (why, main, except, most, initially).

Step 3 — Skim options; note difference dimension**:

Options Difference axis
A cost / B location / C time Topic dimension
A too small / B too expensive / C too far Reason type
A agreed / B disagreed / C not mentioned Opinion status

**Step 4 — Predict likely paraphrase field.

Do NOT memorise full option text — build comparison skeleton.

74.4 Single-Answer Process During Audio

  1. Listen for question moment — when stem topic addressed.
  2. Eliminate options contradicted explicitly.
  3. If two remain, identify narrower vs broader — IELTS prefers precise match.
  4. Mark tentative letter in booklet; confirm if speaker revises.

Time rule: Decide before next question group begins — no replay.

74.5 Multiple-Answer (Choose TWO/THREE)

Constraints: - Exactly two (or three) correct; selecting one less or one more = wrong scoring for item set. - Each letter scored together — partial knowledge helps if one of two locked.

Strategy: - Treat as two single-answer questions sharing one audio passage. - When first answer confirmed, mentally mute that option unless audio reopens it. - Watch for list structure: “Two factors are X and Y” — direct gift.

74.6 Section 3 Discussion Patterns

Academic dialogues feature:

Pattern MCQ target
Agreement Both select same option
Disagreement Question asks what they disagree on
Tentative might, perhaps — weaker than definite
Student vs tutor correction Final tutor view often authoritative

Tone cues: Rising intonation = uncertainty; emphatic stress = preferred answer.

74.7 Section 4 Lecture MCQ

Monologue MCQ tests:

  • Main purpose of research
  • Cause/effect relationships
  • Researcher conclusion vs intermediate finding

Trap: Option states true fact from lecture but does not answer question stem (e.g., question asks reason, option gives description).

74.8 Distractor Taxonomy

Type Mechanism
Exact-word trap Uses audio phrase in wrong option
Partial truth Correct in one clause, false in another
Extreme language always, never — rarely correct in IELTS
Out-of-order mention Mentions before context shifts
Not mentioned Plausible but absent
Opposite Negation missed

74.9 Reading vs Listening Time

Never read all options during dense audio. Preview before; during audio, glance only if needed.

Band 7+ candidates preview options twice when time allows: initial section preview + between-question pause.

74.10 Elimination Shortcuts

  • Mutually exclusive pairs: If A says “only X” and B says “only Y,” both rarely correct together unless multi-answer.
  • Qualifiers: Options with some, often, mainly survive better than absolutes.
  • Speaker alignment: In student-tutor dialogues, final confirmed statement outweighs student’s first guess.

74.11 Guessing Protocol

If forced to guess: 1. Eliminate exact-word traps and extremes. 2. Choose paraphrase over verbatim. 3. For attitude questions, avoid neutral if speaker clearly positive/negative.

74.12 Recording Answers

Write capital letter clearly. For two-answer items, order usually irrelevant — verify practice test key convention.

CDT: click precisely; mis-clicks costly.

Examples

Example 1: Paraphrase Match

Question: What problem does the speaker identify?

Audio: “Commuters waste hours stuck in congestion every morning.”

Option Analysis
A Parking shortages Not mentioned
B Traffic jams Paraphrase of congestion ✓
C High fuel prices Not mentioned

Example 2: Partial Truth Trap

Audio: “The sample size was small, though the methodology was sound.”

Question: Limitation of the study?

Wrong: B Methodology flawed (contradicted).
Right: A Small sample (first clause).

Example 3: Choose TWO

Audio: “We’ll need volunteers and funding before we can expand the programme; publicity would help later but isn’t urgent.”

Choose TWO needs: volunteers + funding (not publicity — deprioritised).

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Section 3 — Disagreement

Question: What do the students disagree about?

Audio summary: Maya argues online surveys reach more people; Jonas insists face-to-face yields richer data. They agree costs are similar.

Option Verdict
A Survey method Disagreement locus ✓
B Cost Agreement — eliminate
C Sample age Not discussed

Answer: A

Worked Example 2: Section 4 — Purpose

Question: The lecture mainly aims to…

Audio: Entire lecture describes bee decline causes; last minute mentions policy briefly.

Option Verdict
A Explain causes of bee decline Matches bulk ✓
B Propose new legislation Minor end note
C Compare honey types Irrelevant

Answer: A — mainly keyword decisive.

Worked Example 3: Keyword Trap

Audio: “Tourism hasn’t destroyed the village entirely.”

Option C: Tourism has completely destroyed the village.

Eliminate C — completely destroyed contradicts hasn’t destroyed entirely even though “tourism” and “destroyed” appear.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1 — Section 2 (Single choice)

Transcript (original):

Good morning. The heritage walk begins at the clock tower. Please note: today’s route skips the canal section because of flooding. We’ll add the mill visit instead, which is wheelchair accessible — unlike the canal path. Dogs are not permitted on the mill tour. Refreshments available at the end, not at the start.

Questions: 1. Why is the canal section closed?
A Ice
B Flooding
C Repairs

  1. What has been added to replace the canal?
    A Museum
    B Mill visit
    C Garden tour

  2. Which restriction applies?
    A No dogs on mill tour
    B No wheelchairs
    C No refreshments

Practice 2 — Section 3 (Choose TWO)

Transcript (original):

Tutor: What challenges did you face in the experiment?
Leo: Equipment calibration took forever, and we struggled to recruit enough participants. The ethics form was fine — approved quickly. Weather affected outdoor trials slightly, but we compensated statistically.

Choose TWO challenges A–D:
A Equipment
B Ethics approval
C Participant numbers
D Weather

Practice 3 — Section 4 (Single choice)

Transcript (original):

Urban heat islands occur when cities replace vegetation with concrete and asphalt, raising temperatures several degrees above surrounding countryside. Green roofs mitigate this by retaining moisture and providing shade. A Chicago study found roof gardens reduced building cooling costs by fifteen percent, though installation costs remain a barrier for older buildings.

Questions: 1. Main cause of urban heat islands?
A Lack of wind
B Loss of vegetation
C Industrial pollution

  1. Chicago study finding?
    A Reduced cooling costs
    B Eliminated installation costs
    C Increased rainfall

  2. Limitation mentioned?
    A Green roofs illegal
    B High installation cost for old buildings
    C No effect on temperature

Practice 4 — Attitude Question

Transcript (original):

I’m enthusiastic about electric buses in principle, but the city’s charging infrastructure is nowhere near ready. Until that improves, I’d call the current rollout premature.

Speaker’s view on current rollout?
A Fully supportive
B Premature
C Opposed to electric buses entirely

Practice 5 — Long Option Set (Section 4)

Question: What does the researcher recommend?

Audio: “Policy should prioritise early childhood nutrition programmes rather than subsidising processed food.”

A Subsidise processed food
B Focus on early childhood nutrition
C Reduce all food subsidies

Solutions (with WHY)

Practice 1

  1. B — flooding explicit; repairs/ice distractors
  2. B — mill replaces canal
  3. A — dogs not permitted; wheelchairs ARE allowed

Practice 2

A + C — calibration + participant recruitment stressed
WHY not B: ethics approved quickly (not challenge)
WHY not D: weather mentioned but compensated — weaker; only TWO needed

Practice 3

  1. B — vegetation replaced by concrete
  2. A — 15% cooling cost reduction
  3. B — installation cost barrier for older buildings

Practice 4

B Premature — enthusiastic in principle but rollout too early
WHY not C: not opposed to electric buses entirely

Practice 5

B — matches recommendation; A opposite; C not stated

Review

  • MCQ rewards meaning match, not keyword match.
  • Preview difference axis among options.
  • Sections 3–4: track agreement, correction, main focus.
  • Multi-answer: exactly N letters; use elimination.
  • Beware partial truth and stem mismatch.
  • Decide and move — no replay.

Quiz

  1. Choose TWO means how many letters on sheet?
  2. Exact-word trap — define.
  3. “Mainly” in stem forces what reading skill?
  4. Section 3 MCQ often tests what interaction?
  5. Extreme words in options — usually correct?
  6. Preview priority: stem or option A first?
  7. Tutor correction — whose view likely final?
  8. Paraphrase vs verbatim — which preferred?
  9. Partial truth trap example?
  10. Miss MCQ — guess or leave blank?

Assignment

  1. Collect 20 MCQ items; label each distractor type from taxonomy (74.8).

  2. Write a 90-second Section 3 dialogue with 3 MCQ including one Choose TWO.

  3. Practice “option skeleton” preview: reduce each option to 3 words before listening.

  4. Record error log: keyword trap vs stem mismatch vs pace.

Revision Notes

MULTIPLE CHOICE

Preview stem + difference axis
Correct = paraphrase match
Exact audio words in wrong option = trap
Partial truth / opposite / not mentioned
Choose TWO: lock one, hunt second
Section 3: who wins disagreement?
Section 4: bulk of lecture = "main" answer
Guess after elimination

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Underline EXCEPT, NOT, MAINLY in question stems — they change the target answer.

Exam Strategy: If options are long sentences, letter-mark in booklet during preview (A= cost, B= time…) for glance reference.

Exam Strategy: In Choose TWO, confirm both are explicitly supported — not implied once vaguely.

Challenge

Take a Section 4 lecture MCQ set. Before listening, write what each option would sound like if paraphrased. Then listen — score paraphrase predictions.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 listeners reject options in real time — mental “eliminated” list prevents re-considering keyword traps under stress.

Band 9 Secret: For “main aim” questions, they note time spent — where the lecturer returns repeatedly beats one passing remark.

Band 9 Secret: They never let MCQ reading steal attention from Section 4 detail — preview is front-loaded precisely to avoid mid-lecture option scanning.

Extended Practice Set F — Section 4 MCQ Cluster

Transcript (original lecture excerpt):

Renewable microgrids supply isolated communities without national grid access. Solar panels paired with battery storage smooth overnight demand. A Kenyan pilot reduced diesel imports by sixty percent within two years. Critics argue maintenance skills locally are insufficient; proponents cite training programmes embedded in rollout. Policy must address tariff structures so communities retain savings rather than redirecting profits to external operators. The lecturer’s primary recommendation is community ownership models, not technology subsidies alone.

Questions: 11. Main benefit documented in pilot?
A Eliminated all diesel
B Reduced diesel imports 60%
C Doubled solar capacity

  1. Critics’ concern?
    A Cost of panels
    B Local maintenance capacity
    C Weather variability

  2. Primary recommendation?
    A More subsidies
    B Community ownership
    C Import tariffs

  3. Choose TWO factors essential for long-term success (A–E):
    A Battery storage
    B Eliminate all fossil fuels immediately
    C Training programmes
    D Higher diesel taxes abroad
    E Ban external operators

Solutions: 11-B (not eliminated all — partial truth trap A) | 12-B | 13-B | 14-A+C — WHY not B: extreme immediate elimination not stated; WHY not E: ban not recommended though profits concern mentioned.

Appendix 74.A — MCQ Preview Skeleton Template

Stem focus word: ___________
A = ___________ (3 words)
B = ___________ (3 words)
C = ___________ (3 words)
Difference axis: ___________
Predict paraphrase field: ___________

Complete skeleton in 20 seconds before every MCQ group — converts reading time from audio-stealing to audio-supporting.

Extended Practice Set G — Attitude and Purpose MCQ

Transcript (original — Section 3):

Tutor: Worth publishing?
Lin: Optimistic — the methodology is sound even if sample small.
Raj: Skeptical — we’d need replication before claiming generalisation.
Tutor: Balanced view — submit to student journal first, then expand.

Questions: 11. Raj’s stance? A Optimistic B Skeptical C Neutral
12. Tutor recommendation? A Abandon B Student journal first C Immediate international journal
13. Lin prioritises? A Sample size B Methodology C Replication

WHY: Raj explicitly “skeptical”; tutor “student journal first”; Lin “methodology is sound” despite sample — paraphrase match not keyword optimistic alone for Q13.

Extended Exercises Set H (31–40)

  1. Choose THREE letters — how many on answer sheet?
  2. Option with “always” — usually?
  3. Stem says MAINLY — listen for?
  4. Two options paraphrase same idea — issue?
  5. MCQ during Section 4 — when preview?
  6. Letter-only instruction — write word?
  7. Partial truth trap example in one line?
  8. Elimination when 5 options 2 answers?
  9. Tone: emphatic stress suggests?
  10. Guess after eliminating one — wise?

Solutions: 31-three letters | 32-eliminate/suspect | 33-bulk lecture time | 34-ambiguous key — rare | 35-before section starts | 36-no | 37-true clause + false clause | 38-narrow to 3 then listen | 39-likely key point | 40-yes if two eliminated

Appendix 74.B — Section-by-Section MCQ Expectations

Section MCQ focus Option length Typical trap
1 Rare Short N/A
2 Purpose, rules Medium Time/place distractors
3 Agreement, opinion Long clauses Keyword echo
4 Main idea, inference Long clauses True but not “main”

Study implication: Sections 3–4 MCQ require reading speed in preview — practice reducing 15-word options to 3-word skeletons (Chapter 74 appendix 74.A) until automatic.

Appendix 74.C — Sample MCQ Writing Task (Assignment Extension)

Write one Section 4 MCQ with: - Stem containing primarily - One D1 echo trap - One D5 scope trap - Correct option paraphrased twice removed from audio wording

Exchange with partner; explain WHY each distractor fails — designing items accelerates recognition during real tests.

Next: Chapter 75 — Matching

Chapter 75: Matching

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish matching people/opinions, features, dates, and categories across Listening sections.
  • Apply “each letter may be used once only” rules without duplication errors.
  • Track multiple speakers in Section 3 matching tasks using voice and role cues.
  • Handle matching when option order differs from audio order (non-linear matching).
  • Use elimination grids to narrow remaining options efficiently.
  • Match long option lists (A–F, A–H) under time pressure without losing audio sync.
  • Recognise when speakers change positions mid-discussion and update matches accordingly.

Theory / Explanation

75.1 What Is Matching in Listening?

Matching tasks require you to pair items from two lists:

List 1 List 2
Questions 21–25 (people, places, events) Options A–H (opinions, features, dates)

You write the correct letter (usually) on the answer sheet. Variations include matching course modules to descriptions, museum exhibits to themes, or research stages to actions.

75.2 Core Rule: Used Once?

Instructions state:

  • “Each letter may be used once only.” — standard; elimination powerful.
  • “You may use any letter more than once.” — rare; read carefully.

Most IELTS matching = once only. Cross off assigned letters in preview margin.

75.3 Linear vs Non-Linear Order

Linear: Audio discusses Item 1, then Item 2 — matches question order.

Non-linear: Audio jumps — e.g., Speaker A discussed, then C, then B. Questions still numbered 21–25 in fixed order — you match as evidence appears.

Strategy: Maintain grid:

Person A B C D E
Maya ?
Jonas

Fill when confident; leave blank until speaker returns.

75.4 Section 3: People and Opinions

Classic format: three students + tutor discuss project; match each person to opinion or contribution.

Speaker identification cues:

Cue Function
Name at turn start “Maya, what do you think?”
Voice change Distinct pitch/pace
Role language “As your tutor, I’d say…”
Agreement “I agree with Jonas” links opinion

Practice: Podcasts with named hosts build speaker tracking.

75.5 Matching Features to Categories

Example: Match wildlife species (questions) to habitats (options A–F).

Audio may describe species in random order. Each species mentioned once; habitat option used once.

Anchor on unique detail: “The sandpiper nests only on shingle banks” → match shingle option.

75.6 Date and Event Matching

Timeline matching tests:

  • Chronology words: initially, subsequently, finally
  • Date traps: two events same month — listen for day or sequence

Write letter of event description, not the date itself, unless question asks for date completion separately.

75.7 Long Option Lists (A–H)

With 8 options and 5 questions, 3 distractors never used — useful sanity check at end.

If 6 letters used for 5 questions under “once only” — error detected; review.

75.8 Paraphrase in Matching

Options rarely copy audio:

Audio Option
“worried about funding” B financial constraints
“keen to expand sample” D increase participants

Build concept bridges in preview.

75.9 Combined Matching + Other Types

A section may blend matching with MCQ or completion. Read instruction boundaries — where matching ends, completion begins.

75.10 Common Errors

Error Fix
Duplicate letter Cross-off rule
Wrong speaker Name tally each turn
Early commit Wait for correction
Distractor mention Match main clause
Skim options too late Preview all A–H before audio

75.11 CDT and PBT Matching

PBT: write letter clearly in box.
CDT: some interfaces drag-drop; practice official familiarisation test.

75.12 Progression Drill

  1. Static: Match quotes to speakers on paper (reading) — build grid habit.
  2. Audio drama: BBC radio clips with 3 characters — note who said what.
  3. IELTS timed: full section one-play.

Examples

Example 1: Opinion Matching

Options:
A Needs more data
B Too expensive
C Ethically problematic
D Perfect as is

Maya: “I’m not comfortable with how we collected consent.” → C

Jonas: “The price of sensors exceeds our grant.” → B

Example 2: Non-Linear

Questions order: Project A, B, C
Audio order: B, C, A

Fill B when heard; don’t force A before its mention.

Example 3: Used Once Check

5 questions, options A–G. After matching, letters D, F, G unused — consistent with 7 options, 5 answers.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Three Students

Match concern to person:

Option Concern
A Sample size
B Time limit
C Equipment failure
D Location access

Audio: - Priya: “We only had twelve respondents.” → A - Sam: “The spectrometer broke twice.” → C - Priya later: “Also, the site warden delayed our entry.” → D for Priya’s second concern? Question structure matters — if one concern per person only, first Priya answer locks A; warden issue may be separate question.

Lesson: Read whether one match per person or multiple items per person.

Worked Example 2: Exhibit Matching

Exhibits 11–14: Pottery, Textiles, Coins, Manuscripts
Themes A–F: Trade routes, Domestic life, Royal court, Religious ritual, Warfare, Agriculture

Audio: “The coin hoard mainly illustrates long-distance trade, whereas the pottery fragments reflect everyday household activity.”

Matches: Coins→Trade (A), Pottery→Domestic (B).

Worked Example 3: Elimination

Five questions, options A–F. After four matches, one question remains with two plausible unused letters — re-listen mentally to audio memory; if tied, choose option with stronger paraphrase match, not keyword.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1 — Section 3 Project Discussion

Match each person to their primary recommendation (A–E). Each letter once.

Options:
A Extend deadline
B Change methodology
C Reduce scope
D Seek external funding
E Publish early

Transcript (original):

Tutor: Recommendations?
Elena: We’re running out of time — I’d ask for an extension.
Marcus: I think we should narrow the research question — too broad now.
Elena: Funding could help us hire an assistant — actually external grant might work.
Tutor: Marcus, still prefer scope reduction?
Marcus: Yes, cut the secondary survey.
Tutor: I’ll publish preliminary findings on the department blog.
Elena: Good — early visibility helps recruitment.

Questions:
1. Elena (primary)
2. Marcus
3. Tutor

Note: If one recommendation each, Elena’s PRIMARY is extension A; funding mention secondary.

Practice 2 — Festival Events

Match event to day (A–F).

Options: A Friday, B Saturday am, C Saturday pm, D Sunday am, E Sunday pm, F Monday

Transcript (original):

The folk concert opens the festival Friday evening. Craft workshops run Saturday morning only. The fireworks display is Saturday night. Food fair continues all Sunday. Parade closes the event Monday midday.

Practice 3 — Research Methods

Match study to limitation heard (A–D).

A Small sample
B Cultural bias
C Outdated data
D Measurement error

Transcript (original):

Study one on teen sleep used only forty participants. Study two on diet compared 1990s records to today. Study three on posture relied on self-report questionnaires. Study four on noise used ** miscalibrated microphones** initially.

Practice 4 — Hotel Facilities (A–H)

Match room type to feature described.

Transcript (original):

Deluxe rooms face the harbour and include breakfast. Standard rooms overlook the car park but have kettle facilities. Suites add a sofa bed and evening turn-down service. Family rooms provide ** bunk beds** and playstation console.

Practice 5 — Non-linear Speaker Match

Speakers: Anna, Ben, Cara
Topics: A Transport, B Accommodation, C Budget, D Marketing

Transcript order: Ben (budget), Cara (marketing), Anna (transport), Cara (budget comment — agree), Ben (accommodation)

Questions fixed order: Anna, Ben, Cara — match main topic focus.

Solutions (with WHY)

Practice 1

  1. Elena → A (extension primary first)
  2. Marcus → C (reduce scope)
  3. Tutor → E (publish early)

WHY not D for Elena: grant mentioned but primary recommendation time extension first.

Practice 2

Event Day
Folk concert A Friday
Craft workshops B Saturday am
Fireworks C Saturday pm
Food fair D/E Sunday (specify all day — often D or full Sunday letter)
Parade F Monday

Practice 3

Study Limitation
Teen sleep A
Diet C
Posture B (self-report bias)
Noise D

Practice 4 (sample)

Room Features
Deluxe harbour + breakfast
Standard car park + kettle
Suite sofa bed + turn-down
Family bunk beds + console

Practice 5

  • Anna → A Transport
  • Ben → C Budget first focus; accommodation also — if ONE topic, budget introduced first
  • Cara → D Marketing

Debate resolution: Question usually asks main responsibility — track opening assignment.

Review

  • Matching = grid + cross-off letters.
  • Order may not follow questions — patience.
  • Section 3: identify speakers reliably.
  • Paraphrase bridges lists.
  • Verify once-only rule at end.
  • Unused options often expected — sanity check.

Quiz

  1. “Once only” implies what technique?
  2. Non-linear matching means?
  3. Section 3 matching often involves?
  4. Write letter or full option text?
  5. Three distractors in 5Q/8-option task?
  6. Speaker tracking cue (name two).
  7. Chronology matching listens for?
  8. Grid helps prevent what error?
  9. More than once allowed — where checked?
  10. Paraphrase “financial constraints” might match?

Assignment

  1. Build 5×6 matching grid from any Section 3 transcript; fill during replay.

  2. Write original 4-speaker dialogue with 4 matching items; peer-test.

  3. Log speaker confusion errors separately in error journal.

  4. Practice BBC “In Our Time” — note who supports each claim.

Revision Notes

MATCHING

Preview BOTH lists; cross-off used letters
Grid: question vs option letters
Audio order may jump
Section 3: names + voice roles
Paraphrase, not keyword
Once-only → elimination
Unused options = normal
Confirm per-person vs per-item rules

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Write tiny cross next to used letters the moment you commit — prevents duplicate assignment under stress.

Exam Strategy: If two speakers agree, both may map to similar options — read whether questions ask for shared or individual views.

Exam Strategy: Don’t match on one word — wait for full opinion clause.

Challenge

Listen to a 3-person podcast segment. Without pausing, note which speaker made each of six claims. Score 6/6 before attempting IELTS matching again.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 matchers assign provisional letters in pencil and adjust only on explicit correction — avoids erasure panic.

Band 9 Secret: They preview distractor options knowing three will never appear — accelerates late-section elimination.

Band 9 Secret: Speaker maps include role tags (T=tutor) before audio — one glance resolves turn-taking ambiguity.

Extended Practice Set F — Course Module Matching

Match module (11–15) to description (A–G). Each letter once.

Modules: Ethics, Statistics, Field Methods, Literature Review, Presentation Skills

Options:
A Requires outdoor clothing
B Covers plagiarism rules
C Includes software workshop
D Assessed by seminar talk
E Focuses on citation databases
F Mandatory for all first-years
G Involves hypothesis testing

Transcript (original):

Ethics covers plagiarism rules and consent — mandatory for all first-years. Statistics involves hypothesis testing and a software workshop. Field Methods needs outdoor clothing for wetland visits. Literature Review trains citation databases. Presentation Skills culminates in a seminar talk assessment.

Solutions: Ethics→B+F (if one: F mandatory primary) | Statistics→C+G | Field→A | Literature→E | Presentation→D — WHY Statistics not E: databases belong to Literature module only (scope trap).

Appendix 75.A — Matching Grid Template

       A  B  C  D  E  F  G
Q11
Q12
Q13
Q14
Q15
Used: __ __ __ __ __
Unused (expected): __ __

Print and reuse — visual grid prevents duplicate-letter errors responsible for ~30% of matching losses at Band 6.5.

Extended Theory — Voice Identification Drills

When names are infrequent, track:

Speaker Pitch Speed Role vocabulary
Student A higher fast “I think”, “maybe”
Student B lower slow “data shows”
Tutor measured deliberate “you should”, “the criteria”

Practice with BBC drama clips: pause every 30 seconds — note who spoke last line. Why this matters: Section 3 matching without reliable speaker ID forces guesswork on opinion questions.

Extended Practice Set G — Historical Events Timeline

Match event (11–14) to century (A–F).

A 15th century | B 16th century | C 17th century | D 18th century | E 19th century | F 20th century

Transcript (original):

The printing press reached England in the late fifteenth century. Industrial textile mills expanded rapidly in the early nineteenth. The scientific revolution peaked in the seventeenth. Railway networks dominated Victorian Britain — nineteenth century again, but later than textiles’ initial phase. Digital archives emerged in the twentieth.

Solutions: printing-A | textiles-E (early 19th) | scientific revolution-C | railways-E (later 19th — if one letter once, distinguish by question: “railway dominance” vs “textile mills” may both be E — exam would separate sub-periods or use different option sets) | digital-F — Note: Real IELTS avoids ambiguous double-E; pedagogical point: time qualifier (“early”/“late”) disambiguates.

Extended Exercises Set H (31–40)

  1. Non-linear matching definition?
  2. 5 questions 8 options — distractors count?
  3. Cross-off when?
  4. Speaker agreement — same letter twice?
  5. Match feature to category — anchor on?
  6. Date matching — write letter or date?
  7. Grid prevents?
  8. “Each may be used once” misread risk?
  9. Section 3 turn-taking cue?
  10. Provisional letter pencil rule?

Solutions: 31-audio order ≠ question order | 32-3 | 33-on commit | 34-read if shared or individual | 35-unique detail | 36-letter unless completion | 37-duplicate letters | 38-using letter twice wrongly | 39-name at start | 40-yes adjust on correction

Appendix 75.B — Speaker Tracking Log Template

Time Speaker Key verb Option link
0:15 Maya proposed
0:42 Jonas disagreed
1:03 Tutor confirmed

Use during Section 3 practice until speaker identification reaches 95% accuracy without transcript — prerequisite for reliable matching at Band 8+.

Appendix 75.C — Matching vs Classification

Matching: pair two lists of equal conceptual level (person ↔︎ opinion).
Classification: assign items to categories (species ↔︎ habitat).

Same grid technique applies; classification often has more options than questions — elimination identical.
