Chapter 76: Sentence & Summary Completion

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Complete sentence gaps with grammatically correct words drawn from the recording.
  • Handle summary paragraphs with and without optional word boxes.
  • Apply word limits while preserving grammatical fit (singular/plural, verb form).
  • Use surrounding sentence syntax to predict missing word class before listening.
  • Track paraphrased summaries in Section 4 where gaps condense entire clauses.
  • Distinguish sentence completion from note completion regarding grammar requirements.
  • Avoid inserting words that fit meaning but break grammar or exceed limits.

Theory / Explanation

76.1 Task Variants

Variant Description Common section
Sentence completion Single sentences with one gap each 2–4
Summary completion Connected paragraph with multiple gaps 3–4
Summary with word box Choose from provided list (may include distractors) 4

All require exact words from recording unless word box supplies fixed spelling.

76.2 Grammar-Sensitive Gap Filling

Unlike some note completion, sentence completion gaps must produce grammatical sentences when filled.

Preview technique: Cover the gap mentally; read before + after:

Frame Gap type
The ___ was measured in metres. Noun
Researchers were surprised by the ___. Noun phrase head
This process occurs more ___ in winter. Adverb
The chemical can ___ water quality. Verb (base)

Why grammar matters: IELTS sometimes accepts only singular if article is a; plural if many.

76.3 Word Limits and Inflection

Instructions: typically ONE WORD ONLY or TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER.

  • Plural -s counts as part of word — requirements is one word.
  • Numbers as digits or words per practice.
  • Do not add articles unless gap is after verb and limit allows: “became a leader” — if limit ONE WORD → leader not a leader unless a printed in question.

76.4 Summary Completion Flow

Summary paraphrases lecture out of order occasionally — but gaps usually follow audio order within the summary block.

Strategy: 1. Read entire summary for topic skeleton. 2. Identify co-reference (this process, the study) linking sentences. 3. Listen for synonym chains connecting gap to audio.

76.5 Word Box Tasks

Box contains more words than gaps — unused words are distractors.

Process: - Mark words that cannot fit grammar of any gap immediately. - Assign high-confidence matches during first pass. - Use elimination for remaining.

Spelling: Copy exactly from box — never alter box word form unless instruction allows transformation (rare in Listening — usually exact box word).

76.6 Paraphrase Density in Section 4

Example:

Audio: “Photosynthesis enables plants to convert light energy into chemical form.”

Summary gap: Plants transform light into ___ energy.

Answer: chemical (ONE WORD) — extracts from paraphrase.

76.7 Synonym Prediction Table

Question summary word Possible audio words
reduce lower, decrease, cut
important significant, crucial, key
fast rapid, quickly (grammar!)
problem challenge, difficulty, issue
show demonstrate, indicate, reveal

Build personal table from AWL (Chapter 69).

76.8 Trap Patterns

  1. Same root, wrong form: economy heard but gap needs economic.
  2. Near synonym not accepted: Rare — key follows official answer; practice materials teach acceptable paraphrase tolerance.
  3. Over-writing: Adding adjective when limit one word.
  4. Off-topic word from later paragraph — misaligned question number.

76.9 Handwriting and Articles on Answer Sheet

Illegible letters cost marks. If unsure between affect/effect, context + grammar decide.

76.10 Integration with Reading Skills

Summary completion resembles Reading gap fill but one play only. Reading scan returns; Listening demands real-time capture.

Transfer skills: grammar prediction, word class, collocation awareness.

76.11 Section 3 Sentence Completion

Dialogue may complete sentences about project decisions — still grammatical fit required.

Voices alternate; answer often in final agreed statement.

76.12 Review Before Transfer

Read completed sentences whisper-quiet: - Does each sentence sound English? - Any plural disagreement? - Word limit respected each gap?

Examples

Example 1: ONE WORD ONLY

Sentence: The main pollutant came from ___________ waste.

Audio: “Industrial discharge was identified as the primary source.”

Answer: industrial — industrial waste complete; discharge changes meaning.

Example 2: Summary Box

Box: chemical, chemically, chemistry, chemist

Gap: Plants convert light into ___ energy.

Answer: chemical — adjective modifies energy; not chemically (adverb).

Example 3: Two-Word Limit

Sentence: Traffic noise affects sleep ___________.

Audio: “…affects sleep quality patterns.”

Answer: quality patterns (two words) OR if ONE WORD limit → quality.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Grammar Lock

Sentence: The experiment was conducted in a controlled ___________.

Audio: “…in a controlled environment chamber.”

Limit: ONE WORD → environment (not chamber alone if sentence needs environment; full phrase environment chamber = two words if allowed).

Decision tree: Read limit → extract minimal words preserving meaning.

Worked Example 2: Section 4 Summary

Summary: Urban trees reduce the ___ island effect in cities.

Audio: “…mitigate the heat island effect…”

Answer: heat — heat island effect is fixed collocation; gap already has island effect.

Worked Example 3: Distractor in Box

Box: funding, fund, funded, fundamental

Gap: The project lacked sufficient ___________.

Answer: funding — noun fits after sufficient; fund verb/noun ambiguity wrong slot.

Practice Exercises

Practice 1 — Sentences (Section 2)

Transcript (original):

The community garden opened in 2018 on former railway land. Volunteers grow organic vegetables sold at the weekend market. The council provides free compost, but tools must be donated privately.

Sentences (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS): 1. The garden occupies former ___________ land.
2. Produce is sold at the ___________ market.
3. The council supplies ___________ free.
4. Tools come from ___________ donations.

Practice 2 — Summary (Section 4)

Transcript (original):

Migratory birds navigate using a combination of magnetic fields and landmark recognition. Young birds learn routes from experienced adults during their first journey. Climate change shifts feeding grounds, forcing some species to alter timing of migration. Conservationists recommend protecting stopover habitats along flyways.

Summary gaps (ONE WORD ONLY): - Birds use magnetic fields and ___________ recognition.
- Juveniles learn from ___________ adults.
- Climate change moves ___________ grounds.
- Experts urge protection of ___________ habitats.

Practice 3 — Word Box

Box: vertical, vertically, visibility, visible, vision

Audio: “Bees orient using the angle of the sun relative to the vertical plane.”

Gap: Angle measured against the ___________ plane.

Practice 4 — Section 3

Transcript (original):

Tutor: Main finding?
Student: Participant motivation dropped when rewards were removed.
Tutor: Implication?
Student: External incentives may undermine intrinsic interest.

Sentence: Removing rewards reduced participant ___________.

Practice 5 — Long Summary (Section 4)

Transcript (original):

Plastic microfibres shed from synthetic clothing enter waterways through laundry discharge. Filters capture only a fraction of fibres; most pass into sewage systems. Researchers advocate front-loading washing machines and lower spin speeds to reduce shedding. Policy proposals include mandatory filter fittings on new machines sold after 2027.

Summary: Microfibres from clothing enter water via laundry. Current filters trap only a (1) of fibres. Scientists suggest front-loading machines and reduced (2) speeds. Some policymakers want (3) filters on new appliances.

Solutions (with WHY)

Practice 1

  1. railway — former railway land
  2. weekend — weekend market (two words if limit allows: weekend market)
  3. compost — council provides free compost
  4. private — donated privately → private donations / privately (private if “donations” in question stem)

Check limits: If TWO WORDS: Q2 = weekend market, Q4 = private donations

Practice 2

  1. landmark — stated directly
  2. experienced — modifies adults
  3. feeding — feeding grounds collocation
  4. stopover — stopover habitats

WHY wrong: feeding vs feeding grounds — ONE WORD gap forces feeding if “grounds” outside gap.

Practice 3

vertical — adjective before plane; vertically ungrammatical

Practice 4

motivation — dropped when rewards removed

Practice 5

  1. fraction
  2. spin — lower spin speeds
  3. mandatory — mandatory filter fittings → ONE WORD mandatory if gap before filters

Review

  • Sentences must be grammatical when complete.
  • Predict word class from frame.
  • Summaries paraphrase — hunt synonym chains.
  • Word box: spelling exact; eliminate grammar misfits.
  • Limits sacred; inflection counts.
  • Section 4 summaries = dense paraphrase training ground.

Quiz

  1. Sentence completion vs note completion — key grammar difference?
  2. ONE WORD — can “the government” fit one gap?
  3. Word box extra words purpose?
  4. “Heat island effect” gap needs which word?
  5. Plural -s counts how?
  6. Summary gaps usually follow?
  7. Preview cover-gap technique?
  8. industrial vs industry — decide how?
  9. Section 3 sentence answers often in?
  10. Over limit penalty?

Assignment

  1. Write 150-word summary of any lecture with 8 gaps; exchange with partner.

  2. Convert 10 Reading sentences into Listening-style audio scripts with paraphrase.

  3. Grammar-only drill: given gap frames, predict word class without audio.

  4. Error log: grammar misfit vs paraphrase miss vs spelling.

Revision Notes

SENTENCE & SUMMARY COMPLETION

Grammar fit mandatory
Cover gap → predict class
Paraphrase ≠ different meaning
Word box: exact spelling
ONE/TWO word limits strict
Summary: skim skeleton first
Section 4 = synonym density
Read aloud check before transfer

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: If audio gives three-word phrase but limit ONE, extract the head noun that carries core meaning.

Exam Strategy: Word box tasks: assign sure matches first — reduces combo guess at end.

Exam Strategy: Watch singular/plural verb agreement either side of gap — The results are → plural noun likely.

Challenge

Take a 200-word academic paragraph from a textbook. Paraphrase into summary with 6 gaps. Record audio lecture. One-play test yourself.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 candidates silently read completed sentences during transfer — catches grammar slips completion-only listeners miss.

Band 9 Secret: They maintain collocation pairs (heat island, stopover habitat) in vocabulary logs — summaries test chunks not isolated words.

Band 9 Secret: For word boxes, they reject wrong part of speech in under 2 seconds — never consider chemically for adjective slot.

Extended Practice Set F — Section 4 Summary (250 words)

Transcript (original lecture — Ocean Acidification):

When oceans absorb carbon dioxide, they become more acidic, threatening shell-forming organisms. Pteropods — tiny sea snails — show dissolving shells in waters below pH 7.8. Coral reefs simultaneously face bleaching from temperature spikes, creating a dual stressor environment. Fisheries depending on calcium carbonate structures may collapse within decades without emission cuts. Mitigation aligns with broader climate targets; local protection alone cannot restore pH. Monitoring buoys now track acidity in real time across fourteen Pacific sites. Public awareness campaigns link dietary seafood choices to sustainable harvest, though consumer behaviour change remains gradual. Researchers urge integrated policy addressing emissions and runoff pollution together.

Summary (ONE WORD ONLY unless noted): 11. CO₂ absorption increases ocean ___________
12. Shell damage seen in ___________
13. Critical pH threshold: ___________
14. Corals face bleaching plus ___________ stress
15. Structures contain ___________ carbonate
16. Local protection cannot fix ___________
17. Buoys measure in ___________ time
18. Policy must combine emissions and ___________ pollution

Solutions: 11-acidity | 12-pteropods | 13-7.8 | 14-acidification OR temperature (context: dual stressor = acidification if “acidic” theme) — accept acidification as second stress beside bleaching | 15-calcium | 16-pH | 17-real | 18-runoff — WHY “temperature” wrong for 14 if ONE WORD: lecture frames acidification as parallel stressor to bleaching; acidification captures CO₂ pathway.

Appendix 76.A — Grammar Prediction Drill (No Audio)

Predict word class only:

Sentence frame Class
The experiment revealed significant ___ noun
Participants felt increasingly ___ adjective
The process occurs rapidly in ___ noun (place)
Researchers sought to quantify ___ noun
Results were largely ___ adjective

Why drill without audio: Isolates grammar skill from listening speed — fixes misfit answers that “sound right” in isolation.

Extended Theory — Summary vs Sentence Order

Occasionally summary paragraphs reorder lecture sequence for rhetorical cohesion. Gaps still usually follow audio chronology within the summary block — but if disoriented:

  1. Anchor on proper nouns (Melbourne, Pteropod) — locate audio moment.
  2. Reset alignment rather than forcing sequential guess.

Band 8+ habit: Note margin timestamp ticks: ✓ Q11 ✓ Q12 ? Q13 when uncertain — clarifies realignment point on transcript review.

Extended Practice Set G — Word Box Summary (Section 4)

Box (A–J): A visible B visibility C visibly D commercial E commerce F commercialised G ecology H ecological I economist J economic

Summary: Satellite imaging improved forest ___ monitoring. ___ factors now drive conservation funding. Researchers warn against ___ exploitation of protected zones.

Audio (original):

Visibility from orbit enables ecological monitoring at scale. Economic factors increasingly fund parks. Avoid commercial exploitation of reserves.

Answers: 1-visibility (B) | 2-economic (J) | 3-commercial (D) — WHY not F commercialised: limit and grammar; WHY not A visible: need noun after forest → visibility/ ecological pattern — gap 1 visibility, gap 2 economic, gap 3 commercial.

Extended Exercises Set H (41–50)

  1. Sentence completion must satisfy?
  2. Summary box word “economic” — gap needs?
  3. ONE WORD — “the effects” acceptable?
  4. Plural heard — gap after “many”?
  5. Nominalisation example verb→noun?
  6. Read completed sentence aloud when?
  7. Word box 10 words 6 gaps — unused?
  8. Section 4 summary paraphrase density?
  9. Article in gap “a ___“?
  10. Wrong grammar right meaning — mark?

Solutions: 41-grammar of full sentence | 42-adjective economic or noun economy context | 43-“the” counts if not in gap | 44-plural noun likely | 45-implement→implementation | 46-at transfer | 47-4 unused normal | 48-very high | 49-include a if limit allows | 50-zero

Appendix 76.B — Collocation Gaps in Summaries

Section 4 often tests fixed phrases:

Partial gap Complete collocation
carbon ___ footprint / emissions
food ___ chain / security
climate ___ change
random ___ sample
statistical ___ significance

When preview shows adjective + gap + noun, predict collocation middle — audio may supply only the missing component (significance after statistical).

Appendix 76.C — Transfer Checklist for Completion

Before closing booklet (PBT):

30 seconds per section — prevents completion-specific transfer errors distinct from spelling mistakes.

Next: Chapter 77 — Short-Answer Questions

Chapter 77: Short-Answer Questions

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Answer direct short-answer questions that require brief factual responses from the recording.
  • Apply word limits (typically NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER) with precision.
  • Distinguish short-answer from sentence completion when questions are full interrogatives.
  • Locate answers efficiently using question word cues (who, what, when, where, why, how).
  • Handle multi-part questions where one audio segment supplies several answers in sequence.
  • Avoid copying unnecessary surrounding words that exceed limits.
  • Integrate short-answer skills with note-taking for fast Section 2–4 retrieval.

Theory / Explanation

77.1 What Are Short-Answer Questions?

Short-answer (SAQ) items ask direct questions:

  • What time does the shop close?
  • Who conducted the research?
  • How many species were recorded?

You write a brief answer — not a full sentence — respecting stated word limits.

Frequency: Less common than completion or MCQ but appear in Sections 2–4, sometimes grouped 3–5 questions.

77.2 Question Word Routing

Question word Answer type Listen for
Who Person/organisation Proper nouns, roles
What Thing/concept Nouns/noun phrases
When Time/date Numbers, months, periods
Where Place Locations, directions
Why Reason because, due to, so that
How many/much Quantity Numbers
How Method/manner Process verbs, by + -ing

Preview: Circle question word; predict answer category before audio.

77.3 Word Limits in SAQ

Typical: NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER

Question Audio Acceptable
What material? “Made of recycled glass” recycled glass (2)
How old? “About twelve centuries” 12 centuries / 1200 years — check context
Who? “Dr Patel from Leeds” Dr Patel / Patel — if THREE WORDS max

Articles: the, a count unless question structure includes them separately.

77.4 SAQ vs Sentence Completion

Feature SAQ Sentence completion
Form Question sentence Statement with gap
Grammar check Answer standalone Must fit sentence frame
Preview focus Question word Syntax around gap

Same listening skill; different verification method.

77.5 Answer Extraction Rules

  1. Minimal sufficient answer — don’t add padding.
  2. Exact spelling for proper nouns.
  3. Number format — digits usually fine.
  4. Hyphenated compounds = one word.

Wrong: Question asks Where → answering with full clause “in the library on campus” when library suffices and limit tight.

77.6 Section 2 Short Answers

Monologue contexts: museum info, tour, facility rules.

Answers often straightforward detail — closing time, price, eligibility.

Trap: Speaker mentions multiple times; question asks specific event (evening lecture vs general hours).

77.7 Section 3–4 Short Answers

Higher paraphrase:

Q: What problem did the initial survey reveal?
Audio: “Respondents struggled to understand the terminology.”
A: terminology / confusing terminology (within limit)

77.8 Sequential Answer Clusters

One audio stretch may answer Q18, Q19, Q20 in order — stay aligned.

If Q19 missed, do not delay — Q20 may still be clear; return if time at section end (mental note only; no replay).

77.9 Why Questions

Reason answers often follow:

  • because of + noun
  • due to + noun
  • so they could + verb

Extract core noun phrase within limit: because of funding delays → funding delays (two words).

77.10 Spelling and Numbers Again

SAQ loses marks identically to completion on spelling.

Phone/postcode items rare in SAQ but dates common.

77.11 Guessing in SAQ

Semantic guess from topic if missed:

  • Biology lecture + What gas → maybe carbon dioxide if carbon context mentioned elsewhere — risky; better skip-flag.

77.12 Practice Materials Design

When creating SAQ drills, ensure one clear answer per question — ambiguous keys harm learning.

Examples

Example 1: Who

Q: Who manages the volunteer programme?
Audio: “Sarah Chen coordinates all volunteer shifts.”
A: Sarah Chen (two words — within three)

Example 2: How many

Q: How many workshops are offered?
Audio: “We run four workshops each term.”
A: 4 / four

Example 3: Why

Q: Why was the event rescheduled?
Audio: “Heavy snow made the road unsafe.”
A: heavy snow / unsafe roads — choose best noun phrase within limit

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Minimal Answer

Q: Where should visitors park? (NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS)
Audio: “Use the north car park behind the sports hall.”

Too long: north car park behind sports hall
Correct: north car park OR car park — if TWO WORDS max, north car park = 3 words → car park only if question accepts generic; north car park is 3 — trim to north carpark invalid.

Correct TWO WORDS: north car wrong semantics → sports hall wrong (behind hall not at hall) → north park odd → Best: north car park exceeds → re-read limit.

If TWO WORDS: north carpark (hyphen?) → north lot if paraphrase allowed — usually car park (2 words) if sufficient.

Lesson: Limit drives extraction ruthlessly.

Worked Example 2: Paraphrase

Q: What skill do interns develop?
Audio: “They gain confidence presenting to clients.”
A: presenting / client presenting — match limit

Worked Example 3: Distractor Times

Q: When does the film start?
Audio: “Doors open at six thirty; screening begins at seven fifteen.”
A: 7:15 / seven fifteen — not 6:30

Practice Exercises

Practice 1 — Section 2 (Visitor Centre)

Transcript (original):

The heritage centre opens daily at nine. Last entry is four thirty. Guided tours depart from the main hall at ten and two. Photography is forbidden in the archive room. The café closes half an hour before the centre.

Questions (NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER): 1. Opening time?
2. Last entry time?
3. Where do tours start?
4. Where is photography banned?
5. How long before closing does the café shut?

Practice 2 — Section 3

Transcript (original):

Tutor: Biggest methodology flaw?
Aisha: We didn’t control for age.
Tutor: Sample size?
Aisha: Eighty-three participants.
Tutor: Funding source?
Aisha: Health charity grant.

Questions: 6. What variable wasn’t controlled?
7. How many participants?
8. Who funded the study?

Practice 3 — Section 4

Transcript (original):

The Permian extinction occurred roughly 252 million years ago. Volcanic activity in Siberia released massive carbon dioxide, acidifying oceans. Marine reptiles recovered over millions of years; dinosaurs later dominated terrestrial niches.

Questions: 9. Name of extinction event?
10. How long ago?
11. Which region’s volcanoes?
12. Gas released?
13. Which marine group recovered?

Practice 4 — Mixed WH- drill

Transcript (original):

Why did bees decline? Pesticide exposure and habitat loss. Who led the UK study? Professor Holt. How were hives monitored? Using ** wireless sensors**.

  1. Two causes of decline? (THREE WORDS MAX — pick one if single answer)
  2. Study leader?
  3. Monitoring method?

Practice 5 — Tricky limits

Q: What must students bring? (ONE WORD ONLY)
Audio: “Bring a calculator; phones aren’t allowed.”

Solutions (with WHY)

Practice 1

  1. 9 / nine / 9 am
  2. 4:30 / four thirty
  3. main hall
  4. archive room
  5. half an hour / 30 minutes

WHY wrong: café close time ≠ centre close — question 5 asks gap before centre closing.

Practice 2

  1. age / control for age — within limit
  2. 83 / eighty-three
  3. health charity / charity grant

Practice 3

  1. Permian extinction (may need TWO WORDS: Permian) if limit
  2. 252 million years
  3. Siberia
  4. carbon dioxide
  5. marine reptiles

Practice 4

  1. If ONE cause ONE WORD: pesticides OR habitat loss (two words) — read instruction
  2. Professor Holt / Holt
  3. wireless sensors

Practice 5

calculator — phones forbidden distractor

Review

  • SAQ = question word → answer type.
  • Minimal accurate phrase within limit.
  • Distinguish multiple mentions — match exact question target.
  • Same spelling/number rules as all Listening.
  • Sections 3–4 add paraphrase layer.
  • Skip-flag-return applies.

Quiz

  1. “Who” questions expect what answer type?
  2. Typical SAQ word limit?
  3. SAQ vs sentence completion check difference?
  4. Why answers often follow which structures?
  5. How many vs how much?
  6. Film start vs doors open — lesson?
  7. ONE WORD — “carbon dioxide” fits?
  8. Sequential cluster strategy?
  9. Article counting rule?
  10. Missed SAQ — leave blank penalty?

Assignment

  1. Write 15 SAQ from one Section 4 transcript; include 5 Why/How.

  2. Minimal answer drill: given long audio phrases, trim to limit.

  3. Timed: 5 SAQ from fresh audio — target 5/5 spelling.

  4. WH- prediction table for 20 questions without listening.

Revision Notes

SHORT ANSWER

Circle WH- word → predict type
Minimal words; respect limit
Not a full sentence on sheet
Why → because/due to phrase core
How many → number only often enough
Multiple times → match question scope
Spelling counts
Paraphrase in S3–4

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Who answers rarely need titles unless limit allows — Patel may suffice if uniquely identified.

Exam Strategy: For When, write format consistently (time vs date) as heard.

Exam Strategy: Don’t copy question words into answer (What: what time wrong).

Challenge

Listen to a 2-minute news clip. Write 8 SAQ for a partner. Swap. One-play only. Discuss ambiguous questions — refine until each has one defensible key.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 listeners answer in noun phrases by default — avoids accidental clause overflow past word limits.

Band 9 Secret: They note two candidate answers pencil-light when speaker contrasts (opens six, starts seven) — confirm before transfer.

Band 9 Secret: SAQ at end of Section 4 are never sacrificed — easy marks if limits respected; Band 9 protects time for final questions.

Extended Practice Set F — Science Museum Guide (Section 2)

Transcript (original):

The planetarium show runs every hour on the half hour from ten thirty am. Children under eight must sit with an adult. Photography is forbidden during shows because of laser equipment. Tickets are not sold separately — they’re included in general admission, currently fourteen pounds for adults. Groups of fifteen or more should email groups@scitech.org at least two weeks ahead. The access lift is located behind the ticket desk. Wheelchair spaces hold four viewers per show.

Short answers (NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER): 11. Show start pattern?
12. Age requiring adult supervision?
13. Why no photography?
14. Ticket inclusion?
15. Adult admission price?
16. Minimum group size for email booking?
17. Lift location?
18. Wheelchair spaces per show?

Solutions:

Q Answer WHY wrong fails
11 hourly / half hour Every hour on half hour
12 under eight / 8 Explicit age rule
13 laser equipment Reason given
14 general admission Not sold separately
15 14 / fourteen pounds Current adult price
16 15 / fifteen Minimum group
17 behind ticket desk Lift location
18 4 / four Capacity limit

Appendix 77.A — WH- Question Transformation

Convert statements to SAQ (practice paraphrase):

Statement SAQ
The lab closes at six pm. When does the lab close?
Dr Nguyen led the trial. Who led the trial?
Funding came from a charity. Where did funding come from? / Who funded?
They chose method B because of cost. Why was method B chosen?

Write 10 transformations weekly from Chapter 79 transcripts — builds reverse paraphrase skill for Section 3–4.

Extended Theory — Multi-Answer Scope

When question asks for one cause but audio lists three, extract first emphasised or explicitly labelled main:

“Three factors mattered — cost, distance, and timing — but cost dominated decisions.”

Answer: cost — WHY not distance/timing: dominance marker “dominated” signals primary.

Extended Practice Set G — University Office Hours (Section 1–2)

Transcript (original):

Student: When is the dissertation office open?
Staff: Tuesday and Thursday, ten to four.
Student: Who handles extension requests?
Staff: Ms O’Brien in room 204.
Student: Formatting queries?
Staff: Online FAQ only — no appointments.
Student: Binding service cost?
Staff: Eight pounds per copy, two-day turnaround.

Questions (NO MORE THAN THREE WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER): 11. Office open days?
12. Extension contact?
13. Room number?
14. Formatting help method?
15. Binding price?
16. Turnaround time?

Solutions: 11-Tuesday and Thursday | 12-Ms O’Brien / O’Brien | 13-204 | 14-online FAQ / FAQ | 15-8 pounds / eight pounds | 16-two days / 2 days — WHY not appointments for formatting: explicitly rejected.

Extended Exercises Set H (41–50)

  1. SAQ typical limit?
  2. Why question — extract what phrase type?
  3. How many — answer form often?
  4. Where — minimal answer example?
  5. Who — title required?
  6. Sequential 3 answers missed — action?
  7. SAQ vs gap fill check difference?
  8. Doors open vs event start lesson?
  9. Copy full clause — limit risk?
  10. Blank penalty?

Solutions: 41-3 words and/or number common | 42-noun phrase core of reason | 43-number alone often | 44-building name | 45-only if needed | 46-skip-flag-continue | 47-SAQ standalone grammar | 48-match question scope | 49-exceed limit zero | 50-no penalty guess

Appendix 77.B — Minimal Answer Decision Tree

Question word identified?
 ├─ Who → proper noun / role noun
 ├─ When → time/date (shortest valid)
 ├─ Where → place name (not full address unless needed)
 ├─ How many → number (+ unit if essential)
 ├─ Why → cause noun phrase core
 └─ What → thing/concept noun
Check word limit → trim to minimal sufficient → verify spelling

Print and use during first five practice tests until internalised.

Appendix 77.C — SAQ in Full Test Context

In 40-question tests, SAQ items typically cluster in Section 2–3 (6–8 total). Missing one SAQ rarely changes band alone; missing six SAQ because of systematic limit violations drops band — treat word limits as strictly as spelling.

Band 9 rule: After writing SAQ, count words on fingers before moving to next question — 2 seconds per item, zero limit errors over full prep cycle.

Final note: Short-answer items reward concise precision — practise trimming adjectives until only the essential noun or number remains. This habit alone can recover two to three marks per test lost to word-limit violations.

Chapter 78: Accents, Paraphrase & Distractors

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Comprehend British, Australian, North American, and New Zealand English accents in exam conditions.
  • Recognise systematic paraphrase patterns linking audio to question stems and options.
  • Classify distractors and predict when speakers deploy corrections, hedges, and false trails.
  • Train accent weak spots using targeted exposure without transcript dependency.
  • Map synonym families from the Academic Word List to Listening paraphrase in Section 4.
  • Maintain accuracy when speakers use idiomatic expressions, fillers, and false starts.
  • Build a personal “distractor reflex” that pauses before accepting first-heard plausible answers.

Theory / Explanation

78.1 Why This Chapter Is Cross-Cutting

Every Listening question type (Chapters 72–77) depends on three invisible skills:

  1. Accent tolerance — phonetic variation does not change meaning.
  2. Paraphrase recognition — answers reword source speech.
  3. Distractor resistance — wrong choices sound plausible.

Mastering these raises all section scores simultaneously — especially the jump from Band 6.5 to 8.0.

78.2 Accent Landscape in IELTS

Accent Features to notice Common contexts
British (RP & regional) Non-rhotic /r/; glottal stops in cities Sections 1–4 UK settings
Australian Diphthong shifts; rising intonation Tours, university life
North American Rhotic /r/; flapped /t/ Exchange programmes, research
New Zealand Vowel shifts near Australian Agriculture, ecology

Exam fairness: Accents are standard educated varieties — not obscure dialect poetry.

78.3 Accent Training Protocol (4 Weeks)

Week 1 — Diagnostic:
Play 5-minute clips from each accent; transcribe 20 content words. Score errors by accent.

Week 2 — Weak accent immersion:
Daily 15 min weakest accent only — news, lectures, podcasts.

Week 3 — Mixed rotation:
Alternate accents each day; one timed section.

Week 4 — Exam simulation:
Full tests; no transcript until after scoring.

Tooling: BBC, ABC Australia, NPR, RNZ — all freely available online.

78.4 Phonological Traps by Accent

Trap Example
/æ/ vs /a:/ cast vs cart (context disambiguates)
Missing /r/ park → “pahk” (UK)
/t/ as /d/ water → “wader” (US)
Linking next item sounds like nex-titem
Numbers thirty vs thirteen — stress final vs first syllable

Drill: Minimal pair dictations daily (13/30, 14/40, 15/50).

78.5 Paraphrase Mechanics

Paraphrase types:

Type Audio Question/Option
Synonym purchase buy
Antonym structure not uncommon fairly common
Generalisation Labrador and poodle dogs
Specificisation vehicles buses and trams
Nominalisation They decided to expand expansion
Voice change Active transport reduces emissions Emissions reduced by active transport

Section 4 favours nominalisation — AWL nouns (implementation, distribution, correlation).

78.6 Paraphrase Prediction Exercise

Before listening, rewrite question keywords:

Q: What reduces traffic congestion?
Predict audio: ease gridlock, cut bottlenecks, improve flow, reduce jams

Build prediction webs in margin — 10 seconds each question.

78.7 Distractor Taxonomy (Advanced)

Code Name Behaviour
D1 Echo trap Option repeats audio word; wrong
D2 Premature answer Correct topic, wrong detail
D3 Corrected info First value replaced
D4 Temporal shift Past plan vs current plan
D5 Scope creep True but not answering stem
D6 Partial clause Half true, half false
D7 Attractive extreme always, never, all
D8 Mentioned in passing Brief reference, not focus

Band 8+ habit: Label distractor type in error log — speeds pattern recognition.

78.8 Speaker Correction Signals

Listen for:

  • Sorry, I mean…
  • Actually…
  • No, wait…
  • Let me rephrase…
  • Stress shift + repetition

Rule: Final confirmed value wins unless question asks initially.

78.9 Hedges vs Definite Statements

Hedge Implication for MCQ
might, could, perhaps Weaker commitment
generally, often Moderate claims — often correct
must, definitely, clearly Strong — check if question asks certainty

Attitude questions: Hedges signal qualified agreement, not full endorsement.

78.10 Idiom and Colloquialism

Section 1–2 may include:

  • “That’ll cost you an arm and a leg” → expensive (paraphrase in option)
  • “We’re snowed under” → very busy

Don’t panic — context defines meaning. Idioms rarely form gap answers verbatim unless Section 2 cultural tour.

78.11 False Starts and Fillers

“So, um, the—the main point is…”

Ignore disfluency; capture main point post-repair.

78.12 Building Paraphrase Fluency from Reading

When reading Part 5 chapters, note how authors reword ideas. Same skill as Listening paraphrase.

Weekly task: Take one paragraph; write 3 paraphrase versions; record one as lecture; practice gaps.

78.13 Accent + Distractor Combo Trap

Australian speaker says “Tuesday at half past two” quickly; note shows 2:30 Tuesday; option echoes “Tuesday at two” missing half past — D2 premature.

78.14 Cognitive Load Management

Accent decoding + paraphrase + distractors = high working memory load.

Reduce load: - Preview thoroughly ( frees slots ) - Automate spelling of common AWL - Skip-flag-return prevents rumination

78.15 Self-Assessment Rubric

Rate 1–5 weekly:

Skill Score
Accent A comprehension
Accent B comprehension
Paraphrase prediction hit rate
Distractor resistance
Correction detection

Target: all ≥4 before exam.

Examples

Example 1: Accent — Number

Australian speaker: “It’ll be thirty dollars.”
Stress on first syllable THIR-ty — don’t confuse with thirteen.

Example 2: Paraphrase

Audio: “The policy aims to curb emissions.”
Gap: The policy tries to ___ emissions.
Answer: reduce / cut — curb paraphrase

Example 3: Distractor D3

Audio: “Meet at eight—oh, venue changed, make it nine.”
Answer: 9 — eight is D3

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Echo Trap MCQ

Audio: “Tourism hasn’t destroyed the village entirely.”

Option C: Tourism has completely destroyed the village.

Analysis: Contains tourism + destroyed from audio (D1/D6) but contradicts hasn’t entirely.

Eliminate C.

Worked Example 2: Nominalisation Section 4

Audio: “Researchers implemented a new sampling protocol.”
Summary gap: Implementation of a new ___ protocol.
Answer: sampling

Worked Example 3: Accent Place Name

British: “Worcester” sounds like “Wooster”
Spelling on form must match official: Worcester

Practice Exercises

Practice 1 — Accent Identification

Listen mentally to these lines (read aloud or with partner):

  1. UK: “Can’t park there — it’s a loading bay.”
  2. US: “The parking lot closes at midnight.”
  3. AU: “Reckon we’ll need to register this arvo.”
  4. NZ: “The bins get collected on Thursday.”

Questions: Match line to accent 1–4. Define arvo. US term for loading bay area?

Practice 2 — Paraphrase Matching

Match audio phrase (1–6) to question word (A–F).

Audio phrases:
1. alleviate pressure
2. a substantial proportion
3. prior to commencement
4. undermine confidence
5. subsequent investigation
6. primarily attributable to

Question gaps:
A before start
B mainly caused by
C reduce pressure
D later inquiry
E large share
F weaken confidence

Practice 3 — Distractor Hunt

Transcript (original):

We considered locating the lab in Building C, but noise from the ventilation system made that ** impractical. Building A** was too small. We finally chose Building D, next to the courtyard.

Questions:
1. Where is the lab?
2. Why not Building C?
3. Why not Building A?

List distractor codes (D1–D8) for wrong answers: Building C, Building A, considered Building C.

Practice 4 — Correction Chain

Transcript (original):

The discount applies to students only — actually, staff qualify too if they enroll before May — sorry, June — the first.

Questions:
- Who qualifies?
- Enrollment deadline?

Practice 5 — Section 4 Paraphrase Heavy

Transcript (original):

Coral bleaching occurs when elevated sea temperatures stress symbiotic ** algae. Without algae, corals lose colour and photosynthetic support. Mass bleaching events doubled in frequency** since the 1980s. Mitigation requires ** limiting global warming** to 1.5 degrees.

Paraphrase questions:
1. Bleaching triggered by high ___
2. Corals depend on algae for ___
3. Events now happen ___ as often
4. Solution: cap ___ rise

Solutions (with WHY)

Practice 1

1-UK, 2-US, 3-AU, 4-NZ (typical patterns)
Arvo = afternoon (Australian)
US parking lot vs UK car park

Practice 2

1-C, 2-E, 3-A, 4-F, 5-D, 6-B — classic AWL paraphrase pairs

Practice 3

  1. Building D — final choice
  2. noise / ventilation noise — C impractical why
  3. too small — A

Distractors: “Building C” = D4 temporal (considered not final); “considered C” = D2 premature

Practice 4

  • staff and students / both — correction expands eligibility
  • June 1 / first of June — May distractor D3

Practice 5

  1. sea temperatures / temperatures
  2. photosynthesis / photosynthetic support → noun photosynthesis ONE WORD
  3. twice / double — doubled frequency
  4. temperature / global warming — within limits

Review

  • Accents are trained, not innate talent.
  • Paraphrase = meaning bridge; AWL nominalisation dominates Section 4.
  • Distractors follow predictable codes — log them.
  • Corrections override; hedges modulate MCQ strength.
  • Preview prediction reduces cognitive load.
  • Integrate accent drills with number minimal pairs.

Quiz

  1. Name three IELTS accent varieties.
  2. Nominalisation example?
  3. D1 echo trap — define.
  4. Correction signal phrase?
  5. thirteen vs thirty — stress rule?
  6. AWL helps which section most?
  7. D7 attractive extreme — example word?
  8. Paraphrase prediction when done?
  9. US rhotic /r/ means?
  10. Final value vs initial — default rule?

Assignment

  1. 7-day accent rotation journal — 15 min/day; note 5 new words each.

  2. Build personal paraphrase table: 50 AWL verb → noun pairs.

  3. Re-do missed mock questions; tag each error D1–D8 or accent/spelling.

  4. Minimal pair audio self-test: 13/30, 14/40, 15/50, 16/60 — score accuracy.

Revision Notes

ACCENTS / PARAPHRASE / DISTRACTORS

4-week accent protocol
Paraphrase: synonym, nominalisation, voice
Predict before listen
D1 echo, D3 corrected, D5 scope, D7 extreme
"Sorry I mean" → update answer
Hedges ≠ strong MCQ unless qualified Q
13/30 stress minimal pairs daily
Error log by distractor code

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: If an option quotes the audio exactly, suspicion rises — verify meaning match before selecting.

Exam Strategy: Section 4 nouns often nominalise verbs from the lecture — train implement → implementation.

Exam Strategy: Under accent stress, write numbers immediately — defer spelling words until speaker repeats if possible.

Challenge

One week: no transcripts allowed. Score two full Listening tests. Only then review audio with transcript — colour-code paraphrase vs distractor segments.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 listeners predict accent from context (Melbourne study → Australian likely) — primes ear before first word.

Band 9 Secret: They treat paraphrase as default expectation — exact match suspicion unless Section 1 spelling name.

Band 9 Secret: Distractor reflex: pause 0.5 seconds on “too easy” answers — catches D3 corrections others miss.

Band 9 Paraphrase Web (original sample)

Question: Why did participation fall?

Prediction web: cost, time, lack of interest, poor advertising, inconvenient schedule, competition from other events

Audio match: “Clashes with the football calendar suppressed turnout.” → paraphrase schedule conflict / competing events — not literal football if limit requires generic other events within rules.

Extended Practice Set F — Mixed Accent Passages

Passage 1 (British — read aloud or partner):

The pharmacy on High Street closes at half five weekdays.

Passage 2 (American):

Prescriptions get filled at the drugstore on Main, open till five thirty.

Passage 3 (Australian):

Scripts are ready this arvo at the chemist near the footy ground.

Questions:
11. British closing time?
12. American term for pharmacy?
13. Australian term for afternoon?
14. Which passage uses “chemist”?

Solutions: 11-half five / 5:30 | 12-drugstore | 13-arvo | 14-Passage 3 — WHY: same concept (pharmacy) three paraphrase variants — trains accent + lexical variation simultaneously.

Extended Practice Set G — Distractor Classification

Transcript:

We planned to launch in January, but regulatory approval delayed us until March. Budget was adequate; the issue was documentation errors. Marketing wanted April anyway for seasonal reasons — rejected.

Classify distractors for question Launch month:
- January: D___
- April: D___
- Budget inadequate: D___

Answers: January-D4 (temporal initial plan) | April-D2 (mentioned not chosen) | Budget inadequate-D6 (partial false — budget was fine).

Extended Theory — Connected Speech and Accents

Elision: next day → /neksteɪ/
Assimilation: ten people → /tem pi:pəl/
Intrusion: go away → /gəʊwəweɪ/

Training: IPA optional but minimal pair + phrase dictation mandatory. Band 9 candidates spend 5 minutes/day on connected speech clips — not because exam tests IPA, but because unsegmented speech causes misaligned word boundaries in Section 4.

Chapter 79: Listening Practice Bank

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Complete ten full original IELTS-style Listening sections (100 questions) under timed conditions.
  • Apply question-type strategies from Chapters 71–78 across realistic section progressions.
  • Self-mark using detailed answer keys with WHY explanations for every item.
  • Simulate exam-day pacing: preview windows, one-play discipline, and transfer practice.
  • Identify personal weak sections by scoring each bank section separately.
  • Use transcripts for post-test analysis without relying on them during first attempt.
  • Build stamina for the full 40-question, 30-minute Listening marathon.

How to Use This Practice Bank

Recommended Protocol

  1. Attempt first — one play only, no transcript, strict 30 minutes (+10 transfer if PBT).
  2. Mark using Solutions section — record raw score /10 per section.
  3. Analyse — tag errors: spelling (S), distractor (D), paraphrase (P), accent (A), pace (T).
  4. Replay missed segments with transcript once — note paraphrase path.
  5. Retry missed question types in isolation after 48 hours.

Scoring Grid (photocopy or duplicate)

Section Score /10 S D P A T
1A
1B
2A
2B
3A
3B
4A
4B
5A
5B

Target progression: Sections 1–2 ≥9/10 consistently before obsessing over Section 4.

Theory / Explanation

79.1 Why a Dedicated Practice Bank?

Chapters 71–78 taught techniques. This chapter supplies volume — the condition under which techniques become automatic. Research on skill acquisition (overlearning) shows that stable performance requires varied repetition beyond initial understanding.

79.2 Bank Structure

Block Sections Context mix
Block 1 1A, 1B Social forms & bookings
Block 2 2A, 2B Monologue tours & facilities
Block 3 3A, 3B Academic discussions
Block 4 4A, 4B Lectures (science/society)
Block 5 5A, 5B Mixed full tests (40 Q each)

Each section = 10 questions with full transcript and explained key.

79.3 Question-Type Distribution (Approximate)

Across 100 questions:

  • Completion (form/note/table/sentence/summary): ~45%
  • Multiple choice: ~25%
  • Matching: ~15%
  • Map/plan/diagram: ~10%
  • Short answer: ~5%

Mirrors official test balance.

79.4 Timing Guidance

Allow ~30 seconds preview per question average across section — adjust by item density.

Section 4: front-load preview during Section 3 playback if your test centre permits booklet preview (policy varies — practice both).

79.5 Recording Your Own Audio (Optional)

Reading transcripts aloud with a partner simulates accent variety. Pause between question groups as in real tests.

SECTION 1A — Gym Membership Enquiry

Context: Two speakers. Form completion.

Questions 1–10

Complete the form below. Write NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS AND/OR A NUMBER for each answer.

APEX FITNESS — Membership Application

Field Details
Name Lucas ___________
Date of birth ___________ 2001
Address 22 ___________ Lane
Membership type ___________
Start date ___________
Monthly fee £___________
Emergency contact ___________
Medical note No ___________ issues
Referral source ___________
Free gift sports ___________

Transcript — Section 1A

Staff: Apex Fitness, membership line.
Lucas: Hi, I’d like to join. I’m Lucas Fernandez — F-E-R-N-A-N-D-E-Z.
Staff: Date of birth?
Lucas: Fourteenth of March two thousand one.
Staff: Address?
Lucas: Twenty-two Maple Lane.
Staff: Membership level?
Lucas: The premium one — includes pool access.
Staff: When should it start?
Lucas: First of September.
Staff: That’s forty-nine pounds monthly.
Staff: Emergency contact name?
Lucas: Elena Fernandez — my sister.
Staff: Any heart or asthma issues?
Lucas: No asthma — I’m fine.

SECTION 4B — Lecture: Sleep and Memory

Questions 1–6 — Summary (ONE WORD)

Complete summary.

Sleep consolidates memories by transferring information from hippocampus to cortex. REM sleep supports procedural skills; deep sleep aids factual recall. Students sacrificing sleep show twenty percent lower retention. Naps under thirty minutes boost alertness without harming night sleep. Blue light from screens delays melatonin.

Root cause: Unfamiliar parasite term — add to AWL science list.

Fix rule: Section 4 biology terms → pre-study list of 30 common organisms/pests.

WHY correct: Explicitly named Varroa mites.

WHY virus wrong: Not mentioned.

Chapter 80: Advanced Listening Strategies

Part: Part 4 — Listening

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Execute Band 8–9 listening routines that protect Sections 1–2 perfection while maximising Section 4 yield.
  • Apply cognitive strategies: chunking, shadowing, and dual-channel preview during instruction windows.
  • Design personalised 4-week Band 7.5→8.5 Listening escalation plans from error-log data.
  • Handle worst-case scenarios: audio issues, lost place, panic mid-section, and post-miss recovery.
  • Integrate corpus-informed collocation training with lecture-topic prediction.
  • Use semi-authentic materials (podcasts, MOOCs) without diluting IELTS format practice.
  • Maintain peak performance across computer-delivered and paper-based delivery modes.

Theory / Explanation

80.1 The Band 8+ Profile

Band 8 Listening (35–36/40 raw) differs from Band 7 (30–31) not by “better ears” but by:

Dimension Band 7 Band 8+
Section 1–2 17–18/20 19–20/20
Spelling loss 2–3 0–1
Distractor capture occasional rare
Section 4 pace loses 2–3 loses 0–1
Preview discipline inconsistent automatic
Recovery after miss rumination skip-flag-return

Strategic insight: Band 8 is built on eliminating cheap losses, not decoding impossible audio.

80.2 The 19/20 Rule

Before attempting exotic Section 4 tricks, enforce:

Sections 1 and 2 combined: minimum 19/20 for three consecutive mocks.

If below 19: - Drill form/table completion (Chapter 72) - Spelling dictation 15 min/day - Number minimal pairs - Map orientation (Chapter 73)

Why: Each Section 1–2 error has higher opportunity cost than one Section 4 paraphrase miss.

80.3 Dual-Channel Preview (Advanced)

During Section N playback, advanced candidates preview Section N+1 questions if booklet policy allows (many centres permit turning ahead during instructions — verify in your familiarisation test).

Protocol: 1. Listen to Section 2 audio fully — no preview steal during dense map section if it costs answers. 2. During Section 2 final items, if audio pace allows margin, skim Section 3 headings only — not during map turns. 3. Never preview Section 4 at expense of current section marks.

Risk: Illegal in some invigilation styles — practice official CDT interface rules.

80.4 Chunking Spoken Academic English

Section 4 lectures follow rhetorical chunks:

Chunk Signals Question target
Hook surprising fact rarely tested first
Definition X is defined as completion
Example for instance detail
Contrast however MCQ
Conclusion in summary main idea

Train ear to hear discourse frames — content slots into pre-built skeleton.

80.5 Shadowing for Section 4 Speed

Shadowing: Speak along with lecturer 0.5 sec behind — daily 10 min with Section 4 transcripts (practice material only).

Benefits: - Faster phoneme prediction - Reduced lag on paraphrase - Improved working memory for numbers mid-sentence

Caution: Shadow after scored attempt — don’t memorise specific tests for exam.

80.6 Topic Prediction Matrix

Section 4 topics rotate but cluster:

Cluster Subtopics AWL focus
Life science bees, coral, migration species, habitat, decline
Physical science plastics, energy, climate emissions, particles, renewable
Social science sleep, memory, urban planning policy, behaviour, infrastructure
History/archaeology excavation, dating artefacts, settlement
Technology AI ethics, data privacy algorithm, surveillance

Pre-study: 30-minute vocabulary primer night before mock on predicted cluster — not exam cram, long-term rotation.

80.7 Collocation Listening

Band 9 recognises chunks, not word lists:

  • mitigate the effects
  • pose a threat
  • a substantial body of evidence

When gap expects noun after *mitigate the ___,* ear waits for collocation pattern.

Cross-reference Chapter 70 (Collocations) — read 20 entries weekly aloud.

80.8 The Error Log 2.0 (Listening-Specific)

Extend Chapter 6 log:

Date Q# Section Type Heard Wrote Code Root Rule

Codes: SP spell, DS distractor, PR paraphrase, AC accent, PC pace, AL alignment, TR transfer

Weekly review: If ≥40% one code → single drill type all week.

80.9 Computer-Delivered Optimisation

CDT-specific tactics:

  • Scroll lock: Note question number on scrap if interface scrolls.
  • Highlight tool: Mark limit words in stem digitally.
  • Double-click accidents: Confirm before change on MCQ.
  • Typing muscle memory: Practice @, hyphenated compounds, British -ise.
  • No transfer buffer: Type during gap — don’t defer to end.

Simulate on official familiarisation test minimum twice.

80.10 Paper-Based Transfer Mastery

Advanced transfer (8 minutes active + 2 check):

Minute Action
0–2 Section 1 transfer + verify
2–4 Section 2
4–6 Section 3
6–8 Section 4
8–10 Global number scan + spelling

Never transfer while second-guessing Section 4 — booklet closed, sheet only.

80.11 Panic Recovery Protocol

Trigger: Realise three consecutive misses.

STOP sequence: 1. S — breathe (physiological sigh, Chapter 6) 2. T — touch question number physically — re-anchor 3. O — orient to next clean question 4. P — preview that question’s limit words

Mind script: “Next question is independent data.”

80.12 When Audio Quality Fails

Raise hand immediately during section if volume drops — examiners may adjust or note incident.

If glitch already passed — do not replay; guess from context; flag invigilator after section.

Document incident on test-day report if offered.

80.13 Semi-Authentic Materials (Supplementary)

Material Use Avoid
BBC In Our Time Section 4 lecture rhythm substituting for timed tests
TED-Ed (no subtitles) Paraphrase training only easy topics
University open lectures AWL exposure ignoring question types
Podcast interviews Accent + Section 3 no preview discipline

Ratio: 70% IELTS-format timed / 30% enrichment.

80.14 From 7.5 to 8.5: Four-Week Plan

Week Focus Deliverable
1 19/20 rule S1–2 3 section pairs scored
2 Distractor codes D1–D8 tagged error log
3 Section 4 shadowing + AWL 4 lectures shadowed
4 2 full mocks exam simulation 34+ target

Adjust upward if starting below 30 raw.

80.15 Band 9 Mental Model

Band 9 listeners think like examiners designing items:

  • “What would I paraphrase?”
  • “Where would I place a correction?”
  • “Which option echoes audio wrongly?”

Reverse-engineering item design builds anticipatory listening.

80.16 Sleep, Nutrition, and Listening

Sleep deprivation: 5–6 hours reduces auditory working memory ~15–20% (general cognitive literature — treat as risk factor).

Test week: Stable caffeine; avoid experimental energy drinks; hydrate — dehydration affects concentration.

Morning LRW: Protein + complex carb breakfast; not heavy fat delaying alertness.

80.17 Group vs Solo Advanced Training

Solo Group
Timed mocks Peer question writing
Shadowing Live map description games
Error log Debate MCQ (Section 3 simulation)

Combine both — solo for exam fidelity, group for generative paraphrase.

80.18 Retake Listening Strategy

If Listening alone blocks requirement:

  • Compare five TRFs — stable 6.5 vs one-off 7.0 dip
  • Change one variable: e.g., 4 weeks accent focus OR spelling clinic
  • Avoid retake within 5 days unless diagnostic proved external factor

80.19 Ethical Boundaries

Do not: - Memorise leaked “predicted answers” - Use hidden earpieces - Submit proxy test-taker

Do: - Use official materials - Build genuine English competence

Band 9 without ethics is worthless outside the test room.

80.20 Capstone Integration

Listening excellence supports Speaking fluency (chunking), Writing spelling (AWL), Reading speed (paraphrase). Part 4 completes when:

  • Mock average ≥ target raw 3 times
  • Error log codes diversify (no single code >30%)
  • Section 1–2 ≥19/20 stable
  • Transfer under 8 minutes without error

Examples

Example 1: 19/20 Rule Check

Mock S1 S2 S1+S2
A 9 10 19 ✓
B 8 9 17 ✗ → drill forms
C 10 9 19 ✓

Proceed to Section 4 intensity only after two consecutive ✓.

Example 2: Chunking Lecture

Audio: “However, the primary limitation — and this is crucial — was sample size.”

Chunk parse: Contrast marker → limitation focus → emphasis crucial → answer sample size incoming.

Example 3: CDT Typing

Gap: NO MORE THAN TWO WORDS → public housing typed; autocorrect tries Public Housing — acceptable if case-insensitive; verify no extra space causing “public housing” double space error in strict systems.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Error Log → Drill

Log: 8/10 errors code PR in Section 4 over 3 mocks.

Drill: AWL paraphrase webs — 20 nouns/day; summary completion Chapter 76 exercises ×5.

Re-test: Section 4 only — target 8/10 → achieved 9/10.

Worked Example 2: Panic Recovery

Candidate misses Q32–34 in Section 4; heart rate spikes.

STOP applied at Q35 preview; captures Q35–40; finishes 37/40 raw vs projected 34 if ruminated.

Worked Example 3: Four-Week Escalation

Start: 31/40 (7.0). Week 1: spelling + S1–2 → 33. Week 2: distractors → 34. Week 3: shadowing → 35. Week 4: mocks → 36/36/37 → register Band 8.0–8.5.

Solutions (with WHY)

Exercise 1

Personal — if S1+S2 <19, delay Section 4 advanced work until fixed. WHY: higher ROI.

Exercise 2

Sample: “Urban beekeeping grew forty percent” = definition/stat hook; “Varroa mites devastate” = problem; “Register with National Beekeepers” = procedure — mirrors question targets.

Exercise 3

Sample nodes: solar, turbine, grid, storage, intermittency, subsidy, carbon-neutral, retrofit, emissions, infrastructure — WHY: primes ear for lecture synonyms.

Exercise 4

Under 4 min with zero misalignment — WHY: transfer errors are preventable procedure failures.

Exercise 5

Lag >1 sec → continue daily; WHY: shadowing reduces processing delay.

Exercise 6

Peer review identifies trap plausibility — WHY: designing items reveals examiner logic.

Exercise 7

Under 3 min typing 20 items — WHY: CDT rewards keyboard fluency.

Exercise 8

4A → life science; 4B → psychology — WHY: topic rotation planning.

Exercise 9

Sample: If I miss two answers, then I STOP breathe before next preview — WHY: implementation intentions automate under stress.

Exercise 10

Need +5 raw from 31→36: +1 S1 spelling, +1 S2 map, +2 S4 paraphrase, +1 S3 MCQ — WHY: distributed gains safer than S4-only obsession.

Review

  • Band 8+ = 19/20 rule + Section 4 chunking + zero spelling negligence.
  • Error log codes drive weekly drills.
  • CDT vs PBT need different procedural mastery.
  • Panic STOP protocol preserves remaining marks.
  • Shadowing + AWL + collocation = Section 4 triangle.
  • Semi-authentic materials supplement, never replace, timed format tests.
  • Ethical prep only.

ADVANCED LISTENING

19/20 on S1+S2 before S4 tricks
Chunk: define → example → contrast → conclude

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Last mock one week before test — not night before; allows error-log fix without fatigue cram.

Exam Strategy: On test morning, hum Section 1 number rhythm during check-in — warms digit ear without studying new content.

Exam Strategy: If target Band 8.0, never accept Section 1 below 9/10 in final three mocks — one slip equals two Section 4 paraphrase saves.

Challenge

Score 36/40 on two consecutive official-style tests with: - S1+S2 ≥19 both times - ≤1 spelling error total across both tests - Post-mortem under 45 minutes each

Document error codes — if PR still >25%, repeat Chapter 78 + 79 Block 4.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 candidates simulate invigilator instructions aloud before mocks — eliminates surprise when real instructions match familiarisation script.

Band 9 Secret: They pre-commit guess rules (always guess MCQ after eliminating two) — removes micro-decisions under fatigue.

Band 9 Secret: Listening prep ends 48 hours before test — only sleep, light AWL review, STOP card — neural consolidation beats volume cram.

Band 9 Exam-Week Schedule (original)

Day Activity
-7 Full mock + log
-6 S1–2 perfection drill
-5 Section 4 shadowing only
-4 Light Section 3 MCQ
-3 Review error log rules
-2 20-min accent clip
-1 STOP card + sleep
Test Execute procedure

Final Word

Listening at Band 9 is industrial consistency: the same preview, the same spelling vigilance, the same recovery — repeated until boring. Boredom in practice produces calm on test day. That calm is the ultimate advanced strategy.

6.0 20–22
6.5 23–25
7.0 26–29
7.5 30–31
8.0 32–34
8.5 35–36
9.0 37–40

Use official TRF for final confirmation; mocks estimate trends.

Chapter 81: Reading Overview & Skills

Part: Part 5 — Reading

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Describe the structure, timing, and scoring of the IELTS Academic and General Training Reading tests with precision.
  • Distinguish between question types and map each to an appropriate reading strategy.
  • Apply a three-pass reading methodology under strict time constraints.
  • Identify how band descriptors translate into observable reading behaviours at Bands 5, 7, and 9.
  • Build a personalised Reading preparation schedule integrated with vocabulary and grammar work from earlier parts of this book.
  • Diagnose whether Reading weakness stems from language, technique, or time management.
  • Execute transfer and checking procedures that protect against careless errors in the final minutes.

Theory / Explanation

81.1 Format Overview: Academic vs General Training

The IELTS Reading test lasts 60 minutes with no extra transfer time. You receive the question paper and answer sheet together; answers must be written on the answer sheet before the hour ends.

Feature Academic Reading General Training Reading
Passages 3 long texts 3 sections (Section 1: 2–3 short texts; Sections 2–3: longer)
Source types Journals, textbooks, magazines, newspapers Notices, advertisements, workplace documents, general interest
Difficulty curve Passage 1 easiest → Passage 3 hardest Section 1 easiest → Section 3 hardest
Total questions 40 40
Marks 1 mark per correct answer 1 mark per correct answer

Why this matters: Academic candidates often prepare only with scientific passages and are shocked by humanities or historical texts in Passage 1. General Training candidates who ignore Section 3’s academic-style passage underperform despite strong performance on notices and ads.

81.2 The 40-Question Architecture

Regardless of module, you face 40 questions converted to a band score via a conversion table that varies slightly between test versions. You do not need 40/40 for Band 9; historically, 39–40 raw marks often yield Band 9 in Academic Reading, while 37–38 may suffice depending on test difficulty.

Question types (not always all present in one test):

  1. Multiple choice
  2. Identifying information (True/False/Not Given)
  3. Identifying writer’s views/claims (Yes/No/Not Given)
  4. Matching information
  5. Matching headings
  6. Matching features
  7. Matching sentence endings
  8. Sentence completion
  9. Summary/note/table/flow-chart completion
  10. Diagram label completion
  11. Short-answer questions

Why taxonomy matters: Each type tests a different cognitive operation—global structure (headings), local detail (TFNG), inferential stance (YNNG), lexical precision (completion). Treating all items as “find the answer in the text” produces systematic failure on headings and NG items.

81.3 What Reading Actually Measures

IELTS Reading is not a vocabulary test alone, nor a speed-reading contest. It assesses:

  • Reading for gist — skimming for main idea and text organisation
  • Reading for detail — locating specific information
  • Reading for inference — understanding implicit meaning and writer attitude
  • Reading for purpose — recognising why information is included
  • Following logical argument — tracking cause, contrast, concession, example

The official band descriptors (see Part 1, Chapter 3) emphasise understanding complex discourse at higher bands. A Band 9 candidate handles dense syntax, nominalisation, and abstract referents without losing the macro-argument.

81.4 The Three-Pass Method

Under exam conditions, most successful candidates use a structured multi-pass approach rather than reading every word once:

Pass 1 — Orientation (30–60 seconds per passage) - Read title, subtitle, first paragraph opening, topic sentences, conclusion signals. - Note passage structure: problem–solution? chronological? compare–contrast?

Pass 2 — Question-driven (bulk of time) - Read questions first for the current group of items. - Deploy skimming or scanning as appropriate (Chapter 82). - Answer questions in order when possible; flag uncertain items.

Pass 3 — Verification (final 3–5 minutes) - Transfer all answers to the answer sheet if not done continuously. - Revisit flagged items. - Check word limits, spelling, grammatical fit for gap-fills.

Why three passes: A single linear read satisfies neither global questions (headings) nor scattered detail (matching information). Orientation prevents getting lost; verification catches transfer errors that cost more marks than hard questions.

81.5 Time Allocation Models

There is no single correct split, but these models serve as baselines:

Model Passage 1 Passage 2 Passage 3 Check
Equal (20-20-20) 20 min 20 min 20 min embedded
Front-loaded 17 min 20 min 23 min —
Progressive 15 min 20 min 22 min 3 min

Why Passage 3 often receives more time: Difficulty and question density increase; easier marks in Passage 1 should not cannibalise Passage 3. Band 7+ candidates typically complete Passage 1 slightly under time to bank minutes for Passage 3.

81.6 Language Threshold vs Technique Ceiling

Reading scores stall for two distinct reasons:

Language threshold: Unknown vocabulary, inability to parse complex clauses, weak reference tracking (what does “this” refer to?). Fix via Parts 2–3 of this book and extensive reading.

Technique ceiling: Adequate comprehension but wrong strategy—reading entire passage before questions, misjudging NG, matching headings by keyword repetition. Fix via Parts 5–8 skills chapters.

Diagnostic question: If you read a passage untimed and score 90%+ on comprehension questions, but timed score is Band 6, technique and time are the bottleneck. If untimed comprehension is also weak, language is primary.

81.7 Paraphrase as the Core Mechanism

Almost every correct answer is a paraphrase of passage wording, not a copy. IELTS designers deliberately avoid identical strings in question and text (except when testing precise terminology in gap-fills).

Paraphrase types:

Type Passage Question
Synonym “rapid expansion” “quick growth”
Antonym + negation “not uncommon” “fairly frequent”
Word class change “decision” (noun) “decided” (verb)
General ↔︎ specific “mammals” “whales and dolphins”
Clause restructuring “Because X, Y occurred” “Y occurred due to X”

Why paraphrase awareness accelerates improvement: Candidates who hunt for identical words miss answers and declare items “Not Given” incorrectly.

81.8 Answer Sheet Discipline

  • Write answers directly on the answer sheet during the test if your centre permits (most do).
  • Use pencil as instructed.
  • For multiple choice, write the letter (A, B, C, D).
  • For True/False/Not Given, write the full word or abbreviation as instructed.
  • Never leave blanks — no penalty for guessing.

Why continuous transfer: The Listening test already separates transfer time; Reading does not. Candidates who fill the answer sheet only at the end frequently leave questions blank when time expires.

81.9 Band Progression: Observable Behaviours

Band 5–5.5: Handles simple factual retrieval in straightforward texts; struggles with dense Passage 3; NG confused with False; headings chosen by word match not logic.

Band 6.5–7: Consistent detail location; reasonable NG discrimination; headings mostly correct except on abstract paragraphs; time pressure causes last 5 questions to suffer.

Band 8–9: Accurate inference and writer stance; headings aligned to paragraph function; vocabulary gaps do not block macro-understanding; time managed with 2–3 minutes for review.

Examples

Example 1: Passage Structure Recognition

Opening sentence: “For decades, urban planners assumed that widening roads would reduce congestion.”

Signal: Historical belief likely to be challenged. Expect “however,” research findings, or policy reversal. Questions may ask what current evidence shows vs past assumption.

Example 2: Question Type → Strategy Mapping

Question Strategy
Matching headings Read paragraph topic sentences; ignore detail examples
TFNG Locate named entity; compare statement precisely
Summary completion Predict grammar (noun/verb/adj.); scan for paraphrase
Multiple choice Eliminate distractors using NG logic for extreme options

Example 3: Paraphrase in Action

Passage: “The initiative failed to gain traction among rural communities.”

Question: “The scheme was unpopular in countryside areas.” → TRUE (failed to gain traction = unpopular; rural = countryside)

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Diagnosing a Band 6.0 Plateau

Profile: Academic candidate; Practice Test average 26/40 (Band 6.5); always runs out of time on Passage 3; TFNG accuracy 55%.

Analysis: - Raw score suggests technique issues, not total language failure. - TFNG below 70% indicates NG/False confusion (Chapter 83). - Time overrun → skip-flag-return not implemented.

Prescription: Two weeks TFNG drills (untimed accuracy first); implement 20-20-20 timing; one Passage 3 daily with post-mortem.

Worked Example 2: Choosing Passage Order

Scenario: Candidate strong on factual retrieval, weak on inference.

Strategy: Complete Passage 1 and 2 in order (bank easy marks). For Passage 3, pre-read all question types: if matching headings present, do headings first while memory of structure is fresh; then detail questions.

Why: Headings require freshest structural memory; leaving them until end after fatigue reduces accuracy more than leaving a short-answer item.

Worked Example 3: Raw Score to Band Estimate

Academic Reading: 30/40 correct.

Approximate band: 7.0 (always verify with specific test key). If target is 7.5, need ~32–33/40 — identify which passage loses most marks and drill that passage’s dominant question type.

Exercises / Passages

  4. Name three question types that test global understanding.
  5. What is the three-pass method in one sentence?

  8. Penalty for wrong answers?
  9. Band 6 technique vs language: how distinguish?
  10. When transfer answers in Reading?
