  12. What does Pass 1 (orientation) include?
  13. Multiple choice: write answer as —?
  14. NG confused with which answer most often?
  15. Highest band approximate raw score Academic?

Exercise Set B — Applied Strategy (16–25)

  1. You finish Passage 1 in 22 minutes — adjustment?
  2. Passage title: “The Reinvention of Silk” — predict content type.
  3. Question asks writer’s opinion — likely question type?
  4. 35/40 untimed, 27/40 timed — primary issue?
  5. Last 5 questions always wrong — likely cause?
  6. Design weekly 5-hour Reading plan referencing Parts 2–3.
  7. Error log entry for TFNG False marked NG — root cause category?
  8. When guess vs leave blank?
  9. Passage 3 has headings + TFNG + summary — suggested order?
  10. Candidate reads entire passage before questions — risk?

Mini-Passage 1: Urban Heat Islands

Read the excerpt and answer questions 26–30.

Cities retain heat more effectively than surrounding countryside, a phenomenon urban climatologists term the heat island effect. Concrete and asphalt absorb solar radiation during daylight hours and release it slowly overnight, keeping nocturnal temperatures several degrees higher than in adjacent rural zones. Vegetation, by contrast, moderates temperature through evapotranspiration—a process largely absent on built surfaces. Recent interventions, including green roofs and expanded tree canopies, have demonstrated measurable cooling in pilot districts, though scale remains limited relative to metropolitan sprawl.

  1. Heat islands are cooler at night than rural areas. (T/F/NG)
  2. Evapotranspiration occurs on built surfaces. (T/F/NG)
  3. Green roofs have produced no measurable results. (T/F/NG)
  4. The heat island effect involves higher rural temperatures. (T/F/NG)
  5. Pilot cooling projects cover most of the metropolis. (T/F/NG)

Solutions

1–15: 1. 60 minutes | 2. 40 | 3. Passage 3 | 4. Matching headings, matching information (global placement), summary with options | 5. Orient, answer question-driven, verify | 6. General Training | 7. Answers rarely copy wording | 8. None | 9. Untimed vs timed comparison | 10. Continuously during hour | 11. Equal 20-20-20; progressive 15-20-22+3 | 12. Title, structure, topic sentences | 13. Letter A/B/C/D | 14. False | 15. ~39–40 (varies)

16–25: 16. Speed up P1 next time; bank time for P3 | 17. Historical/material science or trade history | 18. Yes/No/Not Given | 19. Time/technique | 20. Time pressure or fatigue | 21. Sample: 2 hr timed passages; 1 hr TFNG; 1 hr vocab AWL; 1 hr review log | 22. Over-caution on NG | 23. Always guess | 24. Headings → TFNG → summary | 25. Time loss; no question focus

26–30 with explanations:

  1. FALSE — Passage states nocturnal city temperatures are “several degrees higher,” not cooler.

  2. FALSE — Evapotranspiration is “largely absent on built surfaces”; it occurs with vegetation.

  3. FALSE — Green roofs “have demonstrated measurable cooling”; statement contradicts text.

  4. FALSE — Heat island means cities are hotter; rural zones are cooler comparatively.

  5. NOT GIVEN — Scale “remains limited relative to metropolitan sprawl” but we are not told exact proportion or “most”; “limited” ≠ “none,” and “most of metropolis” is not confirmed or denied precisely.

Review

  • Reading = 60 minutes, 40 questions, no extra transfer time.
  • Academic Passage 3 and GT Section 3 demand the most attention.
  • Separate language barriers from technique barriers via untimed testing.
  • Use three-pass methodology; protect final minutes for checking.
  • Paraphrase recognition is the single highest-leverage comprehension skill.
  • Every blank should be filled — no guessing penalty.

Quiz

  1. GT Section 1 typical text types?
  2. Passage 3 time allocation strategy?
  3. Three-pass method phases?
  4. Primary fix if untimed >> timed score?
  5. TFNG tests writer facts or views?
  6. Approximate raw score for Band 7 Academic?
  7. Why read title before body?
  8. Answer sheet: pencil or pen?
  9. Paraphrase type: “utilise” → “use”?
  10. Band 9 behaviour under time pressure?

Assignment

  1. Complete one full Academic Reading test under strict 60-minute conditions. Score by question type; write 200-word diagnosis using language vs technique framework.

  2. Build a personal time allocation table for three passages; test it on two practice tests and adjust.

  3. Create a paraphrase journal: 20 pairs from any practice test, categorised by paraphrase type.

  4. Read Part 1 Chapter 7 (Time Management) and integrate Reading-specific rules into one-page exam-day card.

Revision Notes

READING OVERVIEW

60 min | 40 Q | no transfer time
Academic: 3 passages (P3 hardest)
GT: 3 sections (S3 academic-style)

Three-pass: Orient → Question-driven → Verify
Time models: 20-20-20 or 15-20-22+3

Language threshold vs technique ceiling
  untimed high + timed low = technique/time

Paraphrase = core mechanism
Always guess; check word limits
Question type → strategy (not one-size-fits-all)

Exam Tips

  1. Start Passage 1 confidently — secure early marks before anxiety peaks.
  2. Read instructions — “ONE WORD ONLY” violations = zero marks even if concept correct.
  3. Underline names, dates, numbers in question paper as you read questions.
  4. Do not panic on one hard question — 90-second rule, then flag and move.
  5. Matching headings: write candidate headings lightly in margin while reading.
  6. Circle question numbers you skip; return in order if possible.
  7. Spelling counts in gap-fills — copy from text when allowed.
  8. GT candidates: do not neglect Section 3 academic preparation.
  9. Wear a watch if centre clock is hard to see.
  10. Last 3 minutes: scan answer sheet for blanks and format errors.

Challenge

The 55-Minute Simulation

Complete a full Reading test in 55 minutes (5-minute penalty). Then use the saved 5 minutes only for checking flagged items and answer sheet. Repeat weekly until raw score within 2 marks of your 60-minute performance. This builds buffer for test-day anxiety and slow centre conditions.

Stretch target: Identify the single question type that costs you most marks across three tests; achieve 85%+ on that type alone in untimed drill before next mock.

Band 9 Strategies

  1. Pre-read all question types for the current passage in 30 seconds before reading text — builds a mental map of what to notice.

  2. Track discourse markers (however, nevertheless, conversely, it follows that) as logical GPS; Band 9 items often hinge on contrast and concession.

  3. Maintain dual focus: macro-structure (paragraph function) and micro-precision (quantifiers, modals, negation) simultaneously.

  4. NG discipline: Band 9 candidates mark NG when one element of the statement is neither confirmed nor contradicted — not when the topic is “different.”

  5. Vocabulary in context: unknown words are resolved through collocational and syntactic frames, not panic — read the clause, not the word in isolation.

  6. Post-test analysis at criterion level: tag errors as paraphrase miss, NG logic, time, spelling, or grammar fit — never “I was unlucky.”

  7. Cross-module transfer: AWL and collocation work (Part 3) directly reduces Reading latency; treat vocabulary chapters as Reading prep.

  8. Simulate distraction: occasional practice in non-silent environments builds resilience for imperfect centre acoustics and clock visibility.

  9. Headings last pass: even Band 9 candidates re-read only first/last sentences of paragraphs for headings confirmation, never full re-read.

  10. Target 38+ raw consistently on recent Cambridge-style tests before test day; margin accounts for harder live forms and nerves.

Next: Chapter 82 — Skimming, Scanning & Keywords

Chapter 82: Skimming, Scanning & Keywords

Part: Part 5 — Reading

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Define skimming, scanning, and intensive reading and deploy each at the correct stage of the IELTS Reading test.
  • Extract keywords and search terms from questions using systematic annotation rules.
  • Recognise synonym chains and reference chains that connect questions to distant passage locations.
  • Avoid the “keyword trap” where identical words appear in distractors but not in answers.
  • Combine skimming for structure with scanning for detail within a single passage under time pressure.
  • Apply keyword transformation rules for names, numbers, dates, and abstract concepts.
  • Evaluate your own reading speed and adjust strategies rather than attempting to read every word.

Theory / Explanation

82.1 Three Reading Speeds

IELTS Reading demands three distinct reading speeds, not one:

Mode Purpose What the eyes do Typical duration
Skimming Gist, structure, tone Move quickly; read topic sentences, titles, transitions 1–2 min per passage
Scanning Locate specific information Hunt for keywords and paraphrases; ignore ir relevant paragraphs Seconds per item
Intensive reading Understand logic of a difficult clause Slow, parse grammar, resolve reference 15–45 sec per segment

Why three speeds: Candidates who skim when they should scan miss detail; candidates who scan when they should skim fail headings and main-idea items.

82.2 Skimming: The Architecture of a Passage

Skimming answers: What is this passage about, and how is it organised?

Skimming protocol:

  1. Read the title and any subtitle or epigraph.
  2. Read the first sentence of each paragraph (often the topic sentence in academic prose).
  3. Read the last sentence of the introduction and conclusion paragraphs.
  4. Note signpost words: firstly, in contrast, the implications, in conclusion.
  5. Ignore examples, statistics, and names on first pass unless the question targets them.

Paragraph function labels (write in margin):

  • INTRO — thesis or problem statement
  • HIST — background
  • ARG — claim
  • EVID — study/data/example
  • CONC — counterargument or limitation
  • SUM — conclusion or future direction

Why label paragraphs: Matching headings and matching information become faster when each paragraph’s function is pre-identified.

82.3 Scanning: Locating the Needle

Scanning answers: Where in the passage is this specific information?

Scanning protocol:

  1. Annotate the question — underline 2–4 keywords (nouns, names, numbers, distinctive terms).
  2. Predict paraphrase — write a synonym beside each keyword if possible.
  3. Visual search — eyes move in Z-pattern or paragraph-by-paragraph until anchor found.
  4. Read intensively — 2–3 sentences around the match to confirm answer.

Scan anchors:

  • Proper nouns — capitalised names, places, organisations (often unchanged in text and question).
  • Numbers — dates, percentages, quantities (may appear as words: “half” = 50%).
  • Distinctive terminology — technical terms less likely to be paraphrased.
  • Rare words — low-frequency nouns that stand out visually.

Why anchors work: Even in 900-word passages, anchors reduce search space from 100% to ~10% of text.

82.4 Keyword Selection Rules

From any question, extract keywords using this hierarchy:

Priority 1 — Unparaphrasable: names, numbers, place names, titles
Priority 2 — Content words: nouns and main verbs carrying meaning
Priority 3 — Modifiers: only if they distinguish similar concepts (e.g., “annual” vs “monthly”)

Delete as keywords:

  • Grammar words: the, a, is, of, have
  • Generic verbs: make, do, get, be (unless central to meaning)
  • Words repeated throughout passage (e.g., “technology” in a tech passage)

Example:

Question: “What did Henderson discover about nocturnal feeding in 2019?”

Keywords: Henderson | nocturnal feeding | 2019
Paraphrase predictions: Henderson (unchanged) | night-time eating | 2019 (unchanged)

82.5 The Keyword Trap

Examiners deliberately place question words in wrong sections to trap scanners who match words without meaning.

Trap type 1 — Same word, wrong context

Passage A discusses “plastic recycling rates.” Passage B discusses “recycling water in agriculture.” Question about water recycling — word “recycling” appears in both; only B is correct.

Trap type 2 — Distractor in multiple choice

Option B repeats three words from the passage but reverses causal direction.

Trap type 3 — False comfort in TFNG

Statement includes “always” and passage says “often” — same topic, different quantifier → FALSE, not TRUE because keywords match.

Defence: After locating keywords, read the full sentence and compare propositional content, not word overlap.

82.6 Synonym Chains and Reference Tracking

Advanced scanning requires following reference chains:

Passage excerpt: “The expedition reached the plateau in March. It documented seventeen species previously unknown to science. These findings were later disputed.”

  • “It” = expedition
  • “These findings” = seventeen species documentation

Question: “Which journey recorded new species?” → expedition (via chain, not keyword in question)

Synonym chain example:

Passage term Question term
remuneration pay
workforce employees
terminate end

Build active synonym networks from Part 3 vocabulary chapters.

82.7 Skim-Scan Integration per Question Type

Question type Skim first? Scan method
Matching headings Yes — full passage skim Re-read paragraph openings
TFNG Light skim for structure Scan for statement subject
Matching information Yes — label paragraphs A–G Scan question keywords per paragraph
MCQ Optional Scan stem keywords; read surrounding context
Summary gaps Skim summary structure Scan for grammar + meaning fit
Short answer No full skim needed Direct scan for question words

82.8 Eye Movement and Physical Technique

  • Finger or pencil guide — acceptable; keeps line focus under stress.
  • Do not mouth words — subvocalisation slows speed; practice silent reading.
  • Peripheral vision batching — read phrases, not single words.
  • Return sweep — after scanning paragraph, note if topic shifted before next paragraph.

Why physical technique matters: Band gains from eliminating regressions (re-reading same line unnecessarily).

82.9 When to Abandon Scanning

If anchor not found in 90 seconds:

  1. Mark question flagged.
  2. Move to next question (often later text provides context).
  3. Return in Pass 3 with broader skim knowledge.

Why: Sequential obsession on one item costs 3–4 easier marks elsewhere.

Examples

Example 1: Keyword Extraction

Question: “According to the passage, why did the Meridan project fail to attract investors?”

Keywords: Meridan project | fail | attract investors
Scan for: Meridan (name), investment/funding/finance vocabulary, failure verbs (collapsed, withdrew, stalled)

Example 2: Skimming Labels

Passage on renewable energy:

  • ¶1 INTRO — climate targets
  • ¶2 HIST — fossil fuel dominance
  • ¶3 ARG — solar cost reduction
  • ¶4 EVID — 2022 study data
  • ¶5 CONC — grid storage problem
  • ¶6 SUM — policy recommendations

Headings question: ¶5 likely matches “The obstacle to continuous supply” not “Solar panel manufacturing.”

Example 3: Keyword Trap

Statement: Training programmes always improve retention.
Passage: “Structured onboarding often correlates with higher retention.”

Same topic (training/onboarding, retention) — but always vs often → FALSE.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Full Scan Sequence

Question 14: “What material did Kowalski use in the 2017 prototype?”

Step 1 — Keywords: Kowalski | 2017 | prototype | material
Step 2 — Scan: Find “Kowalski” → paragraph 4, line 3
Step 3 — Intensive read: “…Kowalski’s 2017 prototype employed a graphene composite rather than conventional polymers.”
Step 4 — Answer: graphene composite (check word limit: TWO WORDS → “graphene composite”)

Worked Example 2: Skim Then Headings

Paragraph opening: “Despite initial enthusiasm, several municipalities abandoned bike-share schemes within two years.”

Heading options:
A. Financial incentives for cyclists
B. Early withdrawal from rental programmes
C. Health benefits of urban cycling

Process: Skim signals “abandoned” + “within two years” = early withdrawal → B. Option C is topic-related trap (cycling mentioned elsewhere).

Worked Example 3: Reference Chain

Passage: “The committee issued revised guidelines. They mandated quarterly audits. This requirement provoked opposition from small firms.”

Question: “Who mandated quarterly audits?”
Chain: they = committee → Answer: the committee

Exercise Set B — Keyword Practice (11–20)

Extract keywords and one paraphrase prediction for each:

  1. “When was the fortress at Almaris first excavated?”
  2. “What do proponents of vertical farming cite as the main advantage?”
  3. “How many participants completed Phase Two of the trial?”
  4. “Which country pioneered the deposit-return scheme?”
  5. “Why does the author doubt the longevity of the agreement?”

16–20. Identify trap risk (low/medium/high) for each:

  1. Question about “banking” in passage on financial services and river ecology.
  2. Question with unique name “Dr. Eliza Chen.”
  3. Question with keyword “development” in urban planning passage.
  4. TFNG with “never” in statement.
  5. MCQ option copying five words from passage.

Mini-Passage: The Svalbard Seed Vault

Skim the passage in 90 seconds and label each paragraph’s function (INTRO/HIST/EVID/CONC/SUM). Then answer 21–25.

(A) Deep inside a sandstone mountain on the Norwegian archipelago of Svalbard, the Global Seed Vault preserves duplicate samples of crop diversity from gene banks worldwide.

(B) The facility, opened in 2008, was conceived as a failsafe against regional catastrophes—war, flood, or institutional collapse—that might destroy national collections.

(C) In 2017, unexpected permafrost melt breached the vault’s access tunnel, raising questions about long-term assumptions regarding Arctic stability.

(D) Engineers subsequently installed waterproof barriers and drainage systems; nevertheless, climatologists argue that design revisions alone cannot offset accelerating warming trends.

(E) Despite such challenges, deposits continue to arrive from partners on every inhabited continent, reflecting sustained international commitment to agricultural resilience.

  1. Paragraph B function?
  2. Scan: What year did the vault open?
  3. Scan: What natural event caused the 2017 incident?
  4. Scan: What was installed after the breach?
  5. Paragraph E suggests the project has been abandoned. (T/F/NG)

Solutions

1–10: 1. Rapid read for gist/structure | 2. Visual search for specific info | 3. Headings, matching info, global items | 4. Names/numbers | 5. Same word, wrong meaning/section | 6. however, in contrast, furthermore | 7. Faster headings/info matching | 8. Prevent one item consuming all time | 9. Slows reading speed | 10. “This” refers to prior noun phrase

11–15 keywords:

  1. Almaris | fortress | first excavated (+ paraphrase: initial dig/discovery date)
  2. vertical farming | proponents | main advantage (+ paraphrase: supporters/benefit)
  3. Phase Two | trial | how many participants (+ paraphrase: completed/finished/number)
  4. country | pioneered | deposit-return scheme (+ paraphrase: first introduced/bottle refund)
  5. author | doubt | longevity | agreement (+ paraphrase: sceptical/duration/treaty)

16–20 trap risk: 16. High | 17. Low | 18. High | 19. Medium (quantifier) | 20. High (MCQ copy trap)

21–25:

  1. HIST (background/conception)
  2. 2008 — stated directly in B
  3. Permafrost melt — “unexpected permafrost melt breached the access tunnel”
  4. Waterproof barriers and drainage systems — “Engineers subsequently installed…”
  5. FALSE — Deposits “continue to arrive”; “sustained international commitment” contradicts abandonment

Review

  • Skim for structure; scan for detail; read intensively only at answer location.
  • Select keywords by hierarchy: names/numbers first, then content words.
  • Keyword trap: word match ≠ correct answer — verify proposition.
  • Track reference chains (it, this, these, such).
  • Label paragraph function during skim for headings and matching information.
  • Use 90-second rule — flag and move to protect overall score.

Quiz

  1. Skimming reads every word? (Y/N)
  2. Best anchor type for scanning?
  3. “Often” vs “always” in TFNG →?
  4. Paragraph topic sentence usual location?
  5. Delete “the” as keyword? (Y/N)
  6. Signpost “nevertheless” signals?
  7. Scan found keyword — next step?
  8. Subvocalisation should increase? (Y/N)
  9. Matching headings: skim or scan first?
  10. Reference “they” requires what?

Assignment

  1. Take one Academic passage; time skim at 90 seconds; write paragraph function labels; verify against headings key.

  2. Create 15-question keyword extraction drill from past papers; include paraphrase predictions.

  3. Record one passage: count how many times you re-read a line (regression). Target 50% reduction next attempt.

  4. Build personal synonym list (30 pairs) from one Reading test wrong answers.

Revision Notes

SKIMMING & SCANNING

Skim = gist/structure (topic sentences, signposts)
Scan = locate (keywords, anchors)
Intensive = parse answer zone

Keywords: names > numbers > content words
Delete: grammar words, passage-wide repeats
Predict paraphrase BEFORE scanning

Traps: same word, wrong context/quantifier/causality
Reference chains: it/this/these → antecedent

90-sec rule → flag → return Pass 3
Paragraph labels: INTRO HIST ARG EVID CONC SUM

Exam Tips

  1. Underline question keywords in the first 5 seconds of each item.
  2. Circle names and dates in passage margin when they appear during skim.
  3. Never scan for “development” alone — combine with second anchor.
  4. Headings skim: first + last sentence of each paragraph only.
  5. Numbers appear as words — scan for both “50%” and “half.”
  6. If two paragraphs match, compare both intensively — one will fail a detail test.
  7. Pencil guide is allowed and professional — use it.
  8. Do not skim examples for headings — they rarely define paragraph purpose.
  9. Question order often follows passage order — use sequential scanning when stuck.
  10. Build AWL synonym networks (Chapter 69) — scanning speed depends on them.

Challenge

The Blind Scan Drill: Take 10 detail questions from a passage you have not skimmed. Scan only — no prior skim — and record accuracy. Then skim 90 seconds and repeat same questions. Compare times and scores. Goal: skim adds accuracy without adding more than 2 minutes total per passage.

Speed target: Locate anchor for any named entity within 30 seconds in Passage 1–2 texts.

Band 9 Strategies

  1. Simultaneous structure map: While scanning for Q7, update mental paragraph map if Q7 reveals new structural information — no separate re-read needed.

  2. Pre-emptive paraphrase: Before eyes leave the question, generate 2–3 synonym candidates; scan for all simultaneously.

  3. Negation spotting during scan: Band 9 readers notice not, un-, fail to, lack in answer zone instantly — critical for TFNG and MCQ elimination.

  4. Discourse-level skim: Identify whether passage is descriptive, argumentative, or problem-solution in first 20 seconds — predicts where opinions vs facts cluster.

  5. Minimal intensive zone: Read minimum window (often one sentence before and after match) — extra reading introduces distractor material.

  6. Cross-paragraph scan: Matching information may require scanning entire passage once with question list visible — batch scan all questions per passage.

  7. Reject regression habit: Band 9 candidates re-read only flagged items in Pass 3, never compulsively.

  8. Keyword deletion mastery: Strip questions to skeleton; prevents fixation on repeated low-value terms.

  9. Visual chunking: Read in sense groups (The 2017 prototype / employed a graphene composite / rather than conventional polymers) — faster and more accurate.

  10. Integrate Listening skill: Chapter 78 paraphrase tracking in Listening trains Reading scan recognition — cross-train both modules.

Next: Chapter 83 — True/False/Not Given & Yes/No/Not Given

Chapter 83: True/False/Not Given & Yes/No/Not Given

Part: Part 5 — Reading

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish True/False/Not Given (TFNG) from Yes/No/Not Given (YNNG) and apply the correct logic to each.
  • Execute a step-by-step verification protocol for every TFNG/YNNG statement.
  • Identify the seven statement patterns that most frequently cause False vs Not Given confusion.
  • Recognise how quantifiers, modals, comparatives, and absolutes alter truth value.
  • Locate the minimum text evidence required to justify each answer choice.
  • Avoid the three cognitive biases that push candidates toward incorrect NG answers.
  • Achieve 80%+ accuracy on TFNG/YNNG in timed conditions through structured drill.

Theory / Explanation

83.1 Two Related but Distinct Question Types

Identifying Information (TFNG) — Does the statement agree with the facts in the passage?

Answer Meaning
TRUE Statement matches passage information (may be paraphrased)
FALSE Statement contradicts passage information
NOT GIVEN Passage neither confirms nor contradicts the statement

Identifying Writer’s Views/Claims (YNNG) — Does the statement agree with the writer’s views or claims?

Answer Meaning
YES Writer holds this view or makes this claim
NO Writer expresses the opposite view or contradicts the claim
NOT GIVEN Writer’s position on this specific claim is not stated

Critical distinction: TFNG can be answered from any information in the text, including reported facts from studies. YNNG requires evidence of authorial stance — attitude, evaluation, recommendation, or explicit claim attributed to the writer.

Example:

Passage: “Critics argue that the policy is ineffective.”
Statement: “The policy is ineffective.” → TFNG: NOT GIVEN (critics’ view, not confirmed as fact). YNNG depends on whether the writer endorses critics — if writer adds “This criticism is well founded,” then YES for writer’s view.

83.2 The Verification Protocol

Apply this sequence for every statement:

Step 1 — Decompose the statement
Identify subject, verb, object, qualifiers (all, some, never, may, most).

Step 2 — Locate the topic
Scan for subject or paraphrase (Chapter 82).

Step 3 — Compare propositions
Ask: “If I accept the passage as true, is the statement necessarily true, necessarily false, or undetermined?”

Step 4 — Check qualifiers separately
Even if topic matches, always vs sometimes → FALSE.

Step 5 — NG test
Ask: “Does the passage say anything about this specific aspect?” If one element is missing → NG.

Why protocol beats intuition: Under time pressure, intuition overuses NG (safe guess) or TRUE (keyword match).

83.3 TRUE/YES Conditions

Statement is TRUE/YES when:

  • Passage states the same proposition in paraphrase.
  • Passage states a specific case that satisfies a general statement in the question (careful — sometimes this is FALSE if question overgeneralises).
  • Logical entailment: passage says “all participants completed the survey”; statement “every participant finished the survey” → TRUE.

Not TRUE merely because:

  • Topic is discussed.
  • Some words match.
  • You know from outside knowledge.

Outside knowledge rule: IELTS ignores your encyclopaedic knowledge. If passage doesn’t say it, it’s NG even if “everyone knows” it.

83.4 FALSE/NO Conditions

Statement is FALSE/NO when:

  • Passage states the opposite (antonym, reversed causality, different agent).
  • Passage provides a counterexample to an absolute in the statement.
  • Passage says X happened; statement says X did not happen.
  • Quantifier mismatch where passage clearly restricts scope: “some” in text vs “all” in statement → FALSE (not NG) when passage explicitly limits scope.

Common FALSE patterns:

Statement Passage Answer
X causes Y Y causes X FALSE
All birds migrate Many birds migrate FALSE
Plan was adopted Plan was rejected FALSE
Method is cheaper Method is costlier FALSE

83.5 NOT GIVEN Conditions

Statement is NOT GIVEN when:

  • Topic appears but specific detail in statement is absent.
  • Passage is silent on comparison, degree, reason, or frequency asked in statement.
  • Passage mentions related concept but not the exact claim.

NG decision tree:

  1. Found relevant section? No → NG
  2. Found section — does it confirm statement? Yes → TRUE/YES
  3. Does it contradict statement? Yes → FALSE/NO
  4. Neither confirm nor contradict → NG

Why NG is not “I didn’t find it”: NG requires confirming the passage does not address the specific claim after thorough scan — not giving up after 10 seconds.

83.6 The Seven NG/FALSE Confusion Patterns

Pattern 1 — Partial match
Passage discusses benefits; statement claims “main benefit is X.” Passage lists benefits without ranking → NG.

Pattern 2 — Different entity
Passage: “Company A expanded.” Statement: “Company B expanded.” → FALSE if B mentioned as not expanding; NG if B not mentioned at all.

Pattern 3 — Time shift
Passage: past tense event. Statement: present/future without support → NG unless implied.

Pattern 4 — Causal overreach
Passage: correlation mentioned. Statement: causation claimed → NG unless cause stated.

Pattern 5 — Absolute language
Statement: always/never/all. Passage: often/rarely/most → FALSE.

Pattern 6 — Reported speech vs fact
Passage quotes sceptic. Statement asserts sceptic’s view as fact → TFNG NG or FALSE depending on writer’s endorsement.

Pattern 7 — Comparison without basis
Statement: “X is more efficient than Y.” Passage discusses X efficiency only → NG.

83.7 TFNG vs YNNG: Side-by-Side

Passage excerpt: “It would be premature to conclude that artificial tutors replace human mentors entirely.”

Statement TFNG YNNG
Artificial tutors have replaced human mentors. FALSE (premature to conclude replacement) YES — writer implies full replacement has NOT occurred / is not yet valid; writer’s view is that conclusion is premature → NO to “have replaced”
Some schools use artificial tutors. NG if not mentioned NG if not mentioned
Human mentors remain important. NG unless stated YES if “premature to conclude replacement” implies humans still necessary

Rule: YNNG tracks evaluative language — premature, unfortunately, surprisingly, should, must, it is clear that.

83.8 Order and Location

TFNG/YNNG question sets usually follow passage order — statement 1 early in text, statement 7 later. Use this to bound scanning.

Exception: Occasional out-of-order item — do not force fit; if expected zone fails, expand search once then NG.

83.9 Frequency in the Test

Typically 5–7 TFNG and/or 3–5 YNNG per full Reading test. Combined, they often represent 25–30% of questions — mastery here yields disproportionate band gains.

Examples

Example 1: TRUE

Passage: “Honeybees orient using polarised light patterns.”
Statement: “Bees navigate with the aid of polarised light.”
Answer: TRUE — orient using = navigate with aid of; paraphrase match.

Example 2: FALSE

Passage: “The treaty came into force in 1992.”
Statement: “The agreement was implemented before 1990.”
Answer: FALSE — 1992 contradicts before 1990.

Example 3: NOT GIVEN

Passage: “Solar installations grew rapidly in Spain.”
Statement: “Solar installations grew faster in Spain than in Portugal.”
Answer: NOT GIVEN — Spain’s growth stated; Portugal not compared.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Qualifier Trap

Passage: “Most respondents favoured remote work at least part-time.”
Statement: “All respondents preferred working from home.”
Decomposition: all vs most; preferred vs favoured part-time
Answer: FALSE — quantifier and scope both contradicted.

Worked Example 2: TFNG vs YNNG

Passage: “While advocates celebrate the reform as overdue, the data presented here suggests gains have been uneven across regions.”

Statement A: “Reform gains have been uneven.” → TFNG: TRUE (data suggests uneven gains)
Statement B: “The writer celebrates the reform.” → YNNG: NO (writer reports advocates celebrate; writer’s own view emphasises uneven gains — not celebration)

Worked Example 3: NG Discipline

Passage: “The excavation uncovered pottery shards dating to the fourth century.”

Statement: “The excavation was led by Professor Nabil.”
Scan: Professor Nabil not mentioned anywhere.
Answer: NOT GIVEN — not FALSE (passage doesn’t say someone else led; silence on leadership)

Exercises / Passages

Passage: Bioluminescence in Marine Environments

Bioluminescence—the production of light by living organisms—is widespread among deep-sea species where sunlight never penetrates. Researchers once assumed that glowing served primarily to attract mates, but subsequent observations have documented at least four distinct functions, including predator confusion and cooperative hunting signals.

The chemical mechanism relies on luciferin oxidising in the presence of luciferase, releasing energy as photons. While terrestrial fireflies employ a similar biochemical pathway, marine variants often operate at near-freezing temperatures, requiring adapted enzymes that remain catalytically active under pressure exceeding two hundred atmospheres.

Commercial applications remain speculative. A Norwegian firm has experimented with bioluminescent markers for fishing gear to reduce seabird bycatch, yet trials published in 2021 showed only a modest reduction and raised concerns about ecological disturbance. Several commentators have urged caution before scaling such technologies, though the passage author notes that peer-reviewed long-term studies are still scarce.

Questions 1–10

Questions 1–6: TFNG

  1. Bioluminescence occurs only in deep-sea organisms.
  2. Scientists originally believed bioluminescence was mainly related to reproduction.
  3. Fireflies and marine organisms use identical enzymes for light production.
  4. Bioluminescent fishing gear has eliminated seabird bycatch.
  5. The 2021 trials demonstrated significant ecological harm.
  6. Long-term peer-reviewed studies of commercial markers are widely available.

Questions 7–10: YNNG (writer’s views)

  1. The writer believes attracting mates is the sole function of bioluminescence.
  2. The writer considers commercial deployment of bioluminescent markers premature without more evidence.
  3. The writer argues that terrestrial bioluminescence is scientifically unimportant.
  4. The writer is optimistic that adapted enzymes will soon power household lighting.

Exercise Set B — Quick Logic (11–20)

Classify without passage: what answer type is most likely?

  1. Statement adds “only” not in original concept.
  2. Statement reverses cause and effect from passage.
  3. Passage silent on topic of statement entirely.
  4. Statement uses “might”; passage says “does.”
  5. Writer quotes critic; statement attributes quote to writer.

Solutions

1. FALSE — “widespread among deep-sea” does not mean only deep-sea; fireflies (terrestrial) mentioned elsewhere in passage context of biochemistry.

2. TRUE — “Researchers once assumed that glowing served primarily to attract mates” = originally believed mainly reproduction.

3. FALSE — “similar biochemical pathway” but marine variants require “adapted enzymes” — not identical.

4. FALSE — “only a modest reduction” contradicts eliminated.

5. NOT GIVEN — trials “raised concerns about ecological disturbance” but did not demonstrate significant harm — concerns ≠ proven harm.

6. FALSE — Author notes long-term peer-reviewed studies are “still scarce” — contradicts “widely available.”

7. NO — Writer states at least four distinct functions; mate attraction is one historical assumption, not writer’s sole view.

8. YES — Commentators urge caution; author notes scarce long-term studies — aligns with caution before scaling; writer presents evidence supporting premature concern.

9. NOT GIVEN — Fireflies mentioned for comparison; writer never evaluates terrestrial importance.

10. NOT GIVEN — Enzymes discussed for marine context; household lighting never mentioned.

11. Likely FALSE (absolute “only”)
12. FALSE
13. NOT GIVEN
14. FALSE or TRUE depending on modal shift — “might” weaker than “does”
15. YNNG often NO or NG — rarely YES unless writer agrees

Review

  • TFNG = factual match; YNNG = writer’s view match.
  • Protocol: decompose → locate → compare → qualifier check → NG test.
  • FALSE/NO = contradiction; NG = no confirmation AND no contradiction on specific claim.
  • Absolutes (all, never, only) vs hedges (some, often) → usually FALSE.
  • Outside knowledge invalid.
  • Questions mostly follow passage order.

Quiz

  1. TFNG tests facts or views?
  2. Passage says “often”; statement “always” →?
  3. Topic mentioned; detail absent →?
  4. YNNG: writer quotes opponent — statement = opponent view →?
  5. NG means “I couldn’t find it quickly”? (Y/N)
  6. Opposite causality →?
  7. Comparison absent → usually?
  8. TRUE requires word-for-word match? (Y/N)
  9. Most common TFNG error at Band 6?
  10. Typical TFNG count per test?

Assignment

  1. Complete 40 TFNG items from practice tests; log each NG error as FALSE-missed or TRUE-missed.

  2. Write 10 original TFNG statements for Passage in Chapter 91; swap with study partner.

  3. One-page decision tree poster for FALSE vs NG — memorise.

  4. Timed drill: 13 minutes for 7 TFNG (exam pace) — repeat until 6/7+.

Revision Notes

TFNG / YNNG

TFNG = statement vs PASSAGE FACTS
YNNG = statement vs WRITER'S VIEWS

TRUE/YES  = paraphrase match / entailment
FALSE/NO  = contradiction (incl. quantifier/absolutes)
NOT GIVEN = topic may appear; SPECIFIC claim undetermined

Protocol: decompose → scan → compare → qualifiers → NG test

FALSE vs NG:
  contradicts? → FALSE
  silent on detail/comparison/cause? → NG

Never use outside knowledge
Order usually follows passage
Watch: all/most, always/often, cause/correlation

Exam Tips

  1. Underline qualifiers in statements before scanning.
  2. NG is not default — earn NG by confirming absence after scan.
  3. FALSE is underused — if passage says the opposite, choose FALSE confidently.
  4. YNNG: find writer’s evaluative verbs and adverbs first.
  5. One element rule: if ANY part of statement unsupported and none contradicted → NG.
  6. Do not combine sentences from different paragraphs to justify TRUE.
  7. Reported speech — attribute to speaker unless writer agrees.
  8. Chronology: dates must align exactly for TRUE.
  9. Write full word TRUE or FALSE as instructed — check centre convention.
  10. Review NG items last — they take longest; secure TRUE/FALSE first.

Challenge

NG Audit: Take 10 questions you marked NG. For each, write one sentence proving no contradiction exists AND specific information is absent. If you cannot write both, reconsider FALSE or TRUE. Retrain until NG selections drop but accuracy rises.

Target: 85% TFNG accuracy untimed, then 75% timed within 18 minutes per passage set.

Band 9 Strategies

  1. Instant qualifier flagging: Band 9 readers circle all, never, primary, only before reading passage — predicts FALSE in 80% of cases.

  2. Writer voice isolation: In YNNG, mentally strikethrough all reported speech and citations; evaluate only authorial sentences.

  3. Minimal evidence rule: One precise sentence sufficient for TRUE/FALSE — no accumulation of weak hints.

  4. NG stinginess: Band 9 candidates mark NG only when they can state what exact element is missing (“comparison with Portugal,” “leadership of excavation”).

  5. Parallel statement batching: Read statements 1–3 before scanning; scan once for cluster — reduces repeated scanning.

  6. Modal logic: may, could, suggests in passage cannot support will, must, proves in statement → FALSE or NG.

  7. Distinguish absence from denial: Silence → NG; explicit denial → FALSE — never conflate.

  8. Post-mortem taxonomy: Classify errors as qualifier, paraphrase, NG/FALSE confusion, or location — one drill per category weekly.

  9. YNNG from conclusion paragraphs: Writer views often crystallise in final 2 paragraphs — weighted scan.

  10. Simulate hardest item first: Practice Cambridge Passage 3 TFNG sets until NG/FALSE accuracy exceeds 90% untimed.

Next: Chapter 84 — Matching Headings

Chapter 84: Matching Headings

Part: Part 5 — Reading

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain what matching headings tests and why it is among the highest-discrimination IELTS Reading question types.
  • Apply a paragraph-function analysis method rather than keyword matching for heading selection.
  • Manage the heading list strategically, including elimination of used headings and distractor headings.
  • Distinguish main idea from supporting detail, example, and counterargument within paragraphs.
  • Handle special cases: introduction paragraphs, short paragraphs, and paragraphs with dual themes.
  • Complete matching headings sets within 8–10 minutes per passage without sacrificing accuracy.
  • Recognise the five distractor heading types examiners deploy repeatedly.

Theory / Explanation

84.1 What Matching Headings Measures

Matching headings requires selecting the best title for each paragraph (or section) from a list of headings. There are always more headings than paragraphs — typically 8–10 headings for 5–7 paragraphs.

This question type tests:

  • Reading for gist at paragraph level
  • Discourse awareness — what job does this paragraph perform?
  • Abstraction ability — convert specific detail into general label
  • Distraction resistance — reject headings that mention paragraph details but miss main idea

Why it discriminates bands: Band 5 candidates match keywords (“whales” in paragraph → heading with “whales”). Band 8 candidates match function (“paragraph explains why whale migration timing shifted”).

84.2 The Golden Rule: Function Over Keywords

Wrong method: Find word overlap between paragraph and heading.
Right method: Ask “If I removed this paragraph, what would the reader lose from the argument structure?”

Paragraph function categories:

Function Heading signal words
Historical background origins, early, tradition, emergence
Problem statement challenge, difficulty, concern, gap
Explanation of mechanism how, process, principle, mechanism
Evidence/example case study, illustration, findings (specific)
Comparison contrast, unlike, compared with
Evaluation/critique limitation, weakness, debate, controversy
Solution/proposal approach, remedy, initiative, recommendation
Implication/conclusion significance, future, therefore, broader impact

84.3 Step-by-Step Protocol

Step 1 — Read all headings first (2 minutes)
Group headings mentally: which sound similar? which are clearly distractors?

Step 2 — Skim passage structure (90 seconds)
Label each paragraph’s apparent function in margin (Chapter 82).

Step 3 — Work paragraph by paragraph
Read first 2 sentences + last sentence. Select best heading. Cross out used heading.

Step 4 — Difficult paragraphs last
Leave ambiguous paragraphs; eliminate headings already assigned; return with remaining options.

Step 5 — Verify (1 minute)
Check no heading reused; check introduction/conclusion not mismatched.

Why cross out used headings: Prevents double assignment — a common marking disaster.

84.4 Introduction and Conclusion Paragraphs

Introduction (Paragraph A often):
Usually overview of topic + thesis or roadmap — NOT detailed evidence.
Heading trap: specific detail heading when overview needed.

Conclusion (final paragraph):
Often future directions, broader significance, or summary of implications.
Heading trap: heading describing middle-section evidence.

Example:
Intro discusses “renewable energy transition” broadly.
Wrong heading: “The role of lithium mining” (appears in paragraph 4).
Right heading: “The shift away from fossil dependence”

84.5 The Five Distractor Heading Types

Type 1 — Detail heading
Captures one example, not whole paragraph.

Type 2 — neighbouring paragraph heading
Perfect for adjacent paragraph — tests careful boundary reading.

Type 3 — Passage-wide theme heading
True of entire passage, not specific paragraph.

Type 4 — Opposite/contrast heading
Paragraph mentions X to contrast with Y; distractor focuses on X alone.

Type 5 — Keyword magnet
Shares 2–3 words with paragraph but wrong abstraction level.

84.6 Short and Dual-Theme Paragraphs

Short paragraphs (3–4 sentences):
Often transitional — connect previous idea to next. Read both adjacent paragraphs before deciding.

Dual-theme paragraphs:
Rare but possible — one paragraph presents problem AND solution. Choose heading that covers dominant function (usually the second half if solution is emphasised).

84.7 Roman Numerals and Answer Format

Paragraphs labelled A, B, C… or i, ii, iii… depending on test. Headings listed as i–x. Write Roman numerals on answer sheet (e.g., iv, vii).

Check: Some tests include Example paragraph already matched — do not reassign.

84.8 Time Management

Matching headings on one passage: target 8–10 minutes including skim.

Order strategy debate:

  • Headings first: Best when headings present — fresh structural memory.
  • Other questions first: Some candidates save headings until after detail questions reveal structure.

Recommendation for Band 7+: Headings first or immediately after 90-second skim — detail questions may bias toward keyword headings.

84.9 Common Errors and Fixes

Error Fix
Keyword matching Function labelling during skim
Reusing heading Cross out on question paper
Ignoring final sentence Read paragraph closure — often states main point
Choosing too broad Ask: does this heading fit ONLY this paragraph?
Leaving hardest blank Elimination from remaining headings

Examples

Example 1: Detail Trap

Paragraph: Discusses three cities’ bike-share failures, focusing on Paris’s financial losses.

Headings:
i. The environmental promise of cycling
ii. Financial unsustainability in early schemes
iii. Government regulation of transport

Correct: ii — financial losses dominate; environmental promise is passage-wide (Type 3 distractor).

Example 2: Function Label

Opening: “Until recently, linguists treated whistled languages as mere curiosities.”

Function: HIST + setup for revision — heading likely about revised understanding or new recognition, not “whistling techniques” (detail).

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Full Paragraph Analysis

Paragraph C: “When the expedition drilled through the ice shelf, instruments registered microbial activity at depths previously considered sterile. The discovery forced geobiologists to revise models of subsurface energy sources. Similar readings were later replicated in Antarctica, though sample sizes remained small.”

Analysis:
- Sentence 1: discovery event
- Sentence 2: impact on scientific models — main idea
- Sentence 3: supplementary confirmation + limitation

Best heading: “Revising assumptions about life beneath ice” — captures revision theme; not “Antarctic drilling equipment” (detail trap).

Worked Example 2: Elimination Method

7 paragraphs, 10 headings. After assigning 5 confident matches, 2 paragraphs remain, 3 headings remain:

    1. Public resistance to vaccination
    1. Statistical methods in epidemiology
    1. Long-term immunity unanswered questions

Paragraph F discusses surveys showing 30% vaccine hesitancy but focuses on unknown duration of immunity.
Eliminate vi — hesitancy mentioned but paragraph pivot is immunity uncertainty → x.

Worked Example 3: Introduction Paragraph

Paragraph A: “Glass, once a symbol of architectural modernism, now embodies tensions between sustainability goals and energy-intensive manufacturing.”

No mention of specific manufacturing data (that’s paragraph B). Heading must capture symbolic tension/setup — not “energy costs of furnaces.”

Exercises / Passages

Passage: The Revival of Urban Wetlands (Headings Practice)

List of Headings

  1. Engineering challenges of water filtration
  2. A historical decline in natural marshland
  3. Biodiversity gains in pilot projects
  4. Conflict between developers and conservationists
  5. The economic case for restoring flood plains
  6. How cities lost their wetlands originally
  7. International policy frameworks since 2010
  8. Measuring carbon sequestration in peat
  9. Public access versus habitat protection
  10. Early scepticism among municipal planners

Paragraphs

A For centuries, wetlands within city boundaries were regarded as obstacles to expansion—drained, paved, and built over until scarcely three percent of original marshland survived in most metropolitan regions by the mid-twentieth century.

B Modern planners initially dismissed restoration proposals as impractical, citing contamination, mosquito control, and liability fears, until several high-profile floods demonstrated that hard infrastructure alone could not absorb storm surges.

C In Seoul, planners removed a concrete highway to expose a buried stream, creating Cheonggyecheon—a project that within five years recorded increased bird species counts and measurable reductions in surrounding air temperature.

D Real-estate consortiums have repeatedly challenged rezoning efforts, arguing that undeveloped parcels sacrifice tax revenue, even as insurers raise premiums in flood-prone districts lacking natural buffers.

E Economists now compile cost-benefit analyses weighing reduced flood damage and healthcare savings from improved air quality against upfront land acquisition expenses—analyses that increasingly favour restoration when thirty-year horizons are applied.

Questions 1–5: Match paragraphs A–E to headings i–x.

Exercise Set B — Distractor Identification (6–10)

  1. Heading captures one statistic in paragraph — distractor type?
  2. Heading perfect for paragraph C but question asks paragraph D — error type?
  3. Heading true for whole passage — distractor type?
  4. Paragraph contrasts two views; heading mentions only first — type?
  5. Why read last sentence of paragraph?

Solutions

1–5:

A → vi (or ii — both historical decline; vi “How cities lost wetlands originally” best matches “drained, paved, built over” causal history; ii also acceptable in practice but vi more precise on mechanism of loss)

Note: In real IELTS only one fits exactly; here ii = historical decline (outcome), vi = how they lost (process). Prefer vi.

B → x — “Early scepticism among municipal planners” matches dismissed restoration, impractical, liability fears.

C → iii — Biodiversity gains (bird species) + environmental benefit in pilot project (Cheonggyecheon).

D → iv — Developers vs conservationists conflict explicit.

E → v — Economic case / cost-benefit analyses favour restoration.

6. Type 1 — detail heading
7. Boundary/neighbour error
8. Type 3 — passage-wide
9. Type 4 — opposite/contrast partial
10. Last sentence often states main point or implication

Review

  • Match paragraph function, not keywords.
  • Skim first; read opening + closing sentences per paragraph.
  • Cross out used headings.
  • Watch five distractor types: detail, neighbour, passage-wide, partial contrast, keyword magnet.
  • Introduction = overview; conclusion = implications.
  • Target 8–10 minutes; use elimination on hard paragraphs.

Quiz

  1. More headings or paragraphs?
  2. Golden rule of matching headings?
  3. Write answer format on sheet?
  4. First step in protocol?
  5. Detail trap definition?
  6. Introduction paragraph heading characteristic?
  7. Recommended order: headings first or last?
  8. Dual-theme paragraph: choose?
  9. Paragraph skim: read every example? (Y/N)
  10. Common Band 5 error?

Assignment

  1. Take 3 Cambridge passages with headings; score and classify each wrong answer by distractor type.

  2. Write 5 original paragraphs + 8 headings each (include 3 distractors) for study group.

  3. Timed drill: 5 paragraphs in 8 minutes — repeat until 4/5+ consistently.

  4. Create function-label glossary (10 labels) for your error log.

Revision Notes

MATCHING HEADINGS

Function > keywords
Read: first 2 sentences + last sentence
Cross out used headings (Roman numerals)

Distractors:
  1 detail/example
  2 neighbouring paragraph
  3 whole-passage theme
  4 partial contrast
  5 keyword magnet

Intro = overview/thesis
Conclusion = implications/future
Elimination when stuck
8-10 min per passage set
Do early (after skim) for Band 7+

Exam Tips

  1. Never assign heading because of one shared word.
  2. Write Roman numerals carefully — iii vs viii.
  3. Example paragraph — copy given answer; don’t reassign.
  4. If two headings similar, decide which paragraph only one fits.
  5. Transitional paragraphs — check if heading fits bridge function.
  6. Don’t leave blanks — elimination increases guess accuracy.
  7. Margin notes: one-word function label per paragraph during skim.
  8. Return to hardest after other questions if doing headings later.
  9. Verify uniqueness — duplicate heading = one wrong.
  10. Practice abstracting — turn 80-word paragraph into 5-word label daily.

Challenge

Heading-Only Pass: Read 5 passages without answering other question types — headings only, 8-minute limit each. Score 90%+ before reintegrating full passage timing.

Stretch: Write correct heading for each paragraph before looking at options — then match. Builds abstraction muscle.

Band 9 Strategies

  1. Predict heading before viewing list — then find closest option; eliminates keyword magnet pull.

  2. Thesis mapping: Identify passage macro-argument in intro; each paragraph heading should slot into that map.

  3. Distractor pre-marking: While reading heading list first, mark pairs that differ only in scope (detail vs overview).

  4. Paragraph boundary discipline: If sentence belongs to previous topic, don’t let it hijack heading.

  5. Abstract nouns preferred: Band 9 headings in answer keys favour nominalisation (“Revision of…” / “Implications for…”) — match that register.

  6. One-pass assignment: Assign heading on first read unless genuinely torn — Band 9 candidates avoid overthinking loops.

  7. Confirm with deletion test: “If I delete this paragraph, which heading becomes unnecessary?”

  8. Integrate with TFNG: Headings reveal where opinions vs facts live — accelerates YNNG later in same passage.

  9. Review only ambiguous pairs in Pass 3 — confident matches untouched.

  10. Corpus exposure: Read academic article abstracts daily — same gist skill as heading selection.

84.10 Extended Practice Passage

Paragraph samples for heading practice:

G. Longitudinal tracking of participants revealed that benefits persisted twelve months after programme completion, suggesting behavioural change rather than temporary compliance—a finding policymakers cite when defending budget renewals against austerity cuts.

H. Nevertheless, replication attempts in rural districts with lower baseline literacy yielded ambiguous results, prompting calls for context-sensitive redesign rather than wholesale abandonment.

Best headings for G: Outcomes sustained beyond intervention period / Evidence of lasting behavioural impact
Best headings for H: Mixed results in different regional contexts / Limits to generalising urban trial success

Why G is not “Policy budget defence”: Budget renewal appears as secondary citation; paragraph function is persistence of benefits (evidence outcome).

84.11 Cross-Reference with Other Question Types

Matching headings interacts with other items on the same passage:

  • After headings, TFNG on paragraph detail becomes faster — you know where each topic lives.
  • Matching information reuses paragraph function labels from headings skim.
  • Summary completion follows passage order — headings map shows which paragraph supplies each gap zone.

Integrated strategy: Never treat headings as isolated — they are the structural key to the whole passage.

84.12 Frequency and Mark Weight

Matching headings typically appears once per test, covering 5–7 paragraphs = 5–7 marks (up to 17.5% of Reading). Missing 2 headings costs approximately 0.5 band in raw score terms — disproportionate impact relative to time invested.

ROI calculation: 8 minutes on headings securing 6/7 beats 8 minutes on one hard TFNG cluster securing 3/7.

Additional Exercises (14–20)

  1. Paragraph opens with “For example” — likely function? (EVID/detail)
  2. Heading shares three words with paragraph — still verify? (Y/N)
  3. Two headings differ only: “Problem” vs “Solution” — read paragraph pivot word?
  4. Example paragraph already matched — action?
  5. 10 headings, 6 paragraphs — minimum distractors? (4)
  6. Conclusion paragraph often matches headings containing? (implications/future)
  7. Time spent on headings should not exceed? (~10 min)

Solutions 14–20: 14. EVID/detail | 15. Yes | 16. Yes (however/therefore) | 17. Copy given; skip | 18. 4 | 19. implications, future, significance | 20. ~8–10 minutes

Headings Vocabulary — Abstraction Ladder

Train moving from concrete to abstract — the skill headings demand:

Concrete (paragraph) Abstract (heading)
Beavers build dams Ecosystem engineering by keystone species
2010 export ban to Japan Geopolitical use of supply restrictions
Schools visit trial sites Growing public engagement with conservation
Shredding before vats Preparatory processing of raw inputs

Daily drill: one paragraph → three abstraction levels → pick heading level.

Historical Passage Headings Practice

Paragraph: “Medieval guilds regulated apprenticeship length and tool quality, yet could not prevent periodic famine-driven wage collapse when grain prices spiked.”

Headings options:
A. The economic limits of craft regulation
B. Famine causes in medieval Europe
C. Tool manufacturing techniques

Answer: A — guild regulation + limits (could not prevent collapse); B is detail trap (famine mentioned but paragraph function is regulation limits).

Timing Log Template

Passage Headings Qs Time Correct Error type
1 6
2 5

Target: 6/7 correct in ≤9 minutes by Week 4 of headings drill.

Next: Chapter 85 — Matching Information & Features

Chapter 85: Matching Information & Features

Part: Part 5 — Reading

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Distinguish matching information from matching features, matching sentence endings, and matching headings.
  • Apply a systematic paragraph-indexing method for matching information questions.
  • Match features (people, dates, theories, places) to statements using evidence-based confirmation.
  • Handle questions that require scanning the full passage non-sequentially.
  • Avoid the “first match” trap when multiple paragraphs mention the same keyword.
  • Manage NB (nota bene) instructions when more than one answer may use the same letter.
  • Complete matching sets efficiently by batching scans and using elimination.

Theory / Explanation

85.1 Three Matching Subtypes

Matching information — Which paragraph contains the following information?
Statements describe facts, ideas, or findings; answers are paragraph letters (A, B, C…).

Matching features — Match statements to a list of named features (researchers, countries, inventions, periods).
Features may be used once only or more than once depending on instructions.

Matching sentence endings — First half of sentence given; choose correct ending from list.
Tests grammar + meaning cohesion; usually in order.

Why separate strategies: Matching information scans paragraphs as containers; matching features scans names as anchors; sentence endings test syntactic and semantic fit.

85.2 Matching Information: Core Logic

Question: “Which paragraph mentions the role of fungi in nutrient cycling?”

Method:

  1. Index passage during skim — one-line gist per paragraph in margin.
  2. Read statement — underline 2–3 unique content words.
  3. Predict paraphrase — nutrient cycling → decomposition, soil enrichment, organic matter breakdown.
  4. Scan paragraph index first — narrow to 2–3 candidates.
  5. Intensive read candidate paragraphs — confirm specific information present, not mere word overlap.
  6. Assign letter — if two paragraphs qualify, NB rule may allow duplicate letters; if “each paragraph once only,” pick best fit.

Critical: Statement must be ** substantively present**, not implied from unrelated content.

85.3 The First-Match Trap

Scenario: Three paragraphs mention “climate change.” Only one discusses insurance industry adaptation.

Trap: First paragraph with “climate change” selected.
Fix: Verify full statement proposition in intensive read.

Verification question: “Could I quote one sentence proving this statement?” If no → keep scanning.

85.4 NB (Nota Bene) Instructions

Many matching tasks state: “You may use any letter more than once.”

Implications:

  • Same paragraph letter may answer 2–3 questions.
  • Do not eliminate a paragraph after one use.
  • Conversely, some questions may share one paragraph — normal.

When each letter once only (rare in information matching): treat like headings — cross out used paragraphs.

85.5 Matching Features: People and Theories

Format: Box lists names (Dr. Reyes, Professor Tanaka, Wilson…) or categories (Theory A, Period 1…).

Method:

  1. Highlight all feature names in passage on first read (circle in text).
  2. Annotate margin — what is attributed to each person/theory.
  3. Match statement to attributed content, not general topic.

Trap: Person mentioned in paragraph but statement describes colleague’s view.

Example:

Passage: “Wilson disputed Tanaka’s estimate.”
Statement: “Questioned a colleague’s figures” → Wilson, not Tanaka.

85.6 Matching Sentence Endings

Format:
Stem: “The primary obstacle to desalination expansion…”
Endings: A. …has been identified as energy consumption. B. …was resolved in the 1990s.

Method:

  1. Read stem — note grammar (what follows verb? noun phrase? clause?).
  2. Eliminate ungrammatical endings — wrong part of speech, subject-verb disagreement.
  3. Scan passage for paraphrase of completed sentence meaning.
  4. Test two finalists — read full sentence aloud (silently) for cohesion.

Order: Usually follows passage order — use sequential positioning.

85.7 Non-Sequential Scanning Strategy

Matching information breaks passage-order convention. Efficient approach:

Batch method:
Read statements 1–3. Scan entire passage once with all three in mind. Assign letters. Repeat for 4–6.

Index method:
Build paragraph gist map upfront; match from map before deep scanning.

Why batch: Reduces full passage re-reads from 7 to 2–3.

85.8 Paragraph Gist Index Template

Para Gist (5–8 words)
A Intro: wetland loss history
B Planner scepticism, flood proof
C Seoul stream restoration success
D Developer vs conservation conflict
E Economic cost-benefit analyses

When statement arrives, match against Gist column first.

85.9 When No Paragraph Fits

Rarely, trick questions occur. If genuinely no match after full scan:

  • Re-read NB instruction.
  • Check paraphrase predictions — too literal?
  • Flag and return — later questions may reveal structure.

Do not force — wrong letter loses mark; flagged return may clarify.

Examples

Example 1: Matching Information

Statement: “Reference to a city that reversed earlier transport infrastructure decisions.”

Scan index: Paragraph C (Seoul, highway removed) → C

Example 2: Matching Features

Features: i. Dr. Mensah ii. The Hartwell Report iii. UNESCO

Statement: “Argued that heritage status could hinder ecological interventions.”

Passage: “The Hartwell Report cautioned that UNESCO designation sometimes constrains wetland modification.”

Answer: ii

Example 3: Sentence Endings Grammar Filter

Stem: “Researchers have yet to determine whether…”

Eliminate: endings starting with noun phrases without clause; past-only endings when “whether” requires future/present subordinate clause.

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Information Match with Paraphrase

Statement: “An example of monetary valuation applied over decades.”

Passage paragraph E: “…cost-benefit analyses… when thirty-year horizons are applied.”

Paraphrase link: monetary valuation = cost-benefit; decades = thirty-year horizons → E

Worked Example 2: Feature Disambiguation

Statement: “Documented microbial activity in extreme cold.”

Passage: Mensah led Arctic team; Tanaka replicated in Antarctica.

Both cold — read statements carefully: “extreme cold” + “documented” — Mensah’s Arctic expedition first documented → i. Dr. Mensah if statement matches Arctic original discovery.

Worked Example 3: Sentence Ending Selection

Stem: “Unlike earlier models, the revised simulation…”
Passage: “…the revised simulation incorporates feedback from ocean currents.”

Ending G: “…accounts for marine circulation patterns.”
Grammar: simulation accounts → fits. Meaning: ocean currents = marine circulation → G

Exercises / Passages

Passage Excerpt: Four Paragraphs on Coral Bleaching

A Coral reefs occupy less than one percent of ocean floor yet support roughly a quarter of marine species, making their decline a disproportionate ecological concern.

B Elevated sea temperatures trigger expulsion of symbiotic algae, leaving corals pale and unable to synthesise sufficient nutrients—a process widely termed bleaching.

C In 2016, Australian researchers deployed underwater shade cloths over selected reef sections, measuring partial recovery within six months though scalability remained uncertain.

D Economists affiliated with the Pacific Tourism Council estimated that bleaching-related closures could reduce regional GDP by 0.4 percent annually unless diversification strategies succeed.

Questions 1–8

Matching information — which paragraph contains:

  1. A statistic about species dependent on reefs
  2. Description of the biological mechanism of bleaching
  3. An experimental intervention whose wider application is unclear
  4. Predicted economic consequences linked to reef health

Matching features — Match to i. Australian researchers ii. Pacific Tourism Council iii. Symbiotic algae

  1. Organisms whose removal causes nutrient deficiency in corals
  2. Group providing figures on tourism-related GDP impact
  3. Team that tested physical shading as a remedy

Matching sentence endings

  1. The bleaching phenomenon occurs when corals…
    A. …reject algae due to heat stress.
    B. …migrate to deeper water automatically.
    C. …increase algae production indefinitely.

Exercise Set B (9–12)

  1. NB instruction means?
  2. First-match trap — define?
  3. Sentence endings: eliminate first by?
  4. Feature matching: circle what in passage first?

Solutions

1. A — “quarter of marine species” = statistic about species dependence
2. B — expulsion of symbiotic algae, pale, nutrients = mechanism
3. C — shade cloths experiment; “scalability remained uncertain”
4. D — GDP reduction 0.4% = economic consequences

5. iii — symbiotic algae expulsion causes nutrient problem
6. ii — Pacific Tourism Council economists
7. i — Australian researchers deployed shade cloths

8. A — heat stress triggers algae expulsion (B and C contradict passage)

9. Same letter may be used more than once
10. Selecting first paragraph with keyword without full proposition match
11. Grammar/cohesion
**12. Feature names (people, organisations, theories)

Review

  • Matching information = which paragraph contains X — build gist index.
  • Matching features = match to named list — circle names, track attributions.
  • Sentence endings = grammar filter then meaning scan — usually in order.
  • Avoid first-match trap — verify full statement.
  • NB: letters may repeat.
  • Batch scan statements to reduce re-reading.

Quiz

  1. Information matching answers are?
  2. Features matching answers are?
  3. Sentence endings test primarily?
  4. NB allows?
  5. Verification question for information match?
  6. Non-sequential type?
  7. Index method uses?
  8. Person mentioned ≠ person responsible for view — which type?
  9. Batch scanning reduces?
  10. Each letter once only — treat like?

Assignment

  1. Create gist index for 3 full passages; time index build at 90 seconds.

  2. Complete 20 matching information items; log first-match trap errors.

  3. Write 5 sentence-ending stems with 3 endings each; include 1 ungrammatical distractor.

  4. Feature matching: diagram attributions for one passage (who said what).

Revision Notes

MATCHING INFORMATION & FEATURES

Information → paragraph letter (A-G)
  gist index + paraphrase + verify proposition
  NB: letters repeat OK

Features → name/theory from list
  circle names; track who claimed what

Sentence endings → grammar first, meaning second
  usually IN ORDER

First-match trap → verify with quote test
Batch scan statements 1-3 together

Exam Tips

  1. Build gist index during skim — pays off for information matching.
  2. NB highlighted — underline on question paper.
  3. Feature names: annotate in passage margin on first encounter.
  4. Sentence endings: read A+B as complete sentence before choosing.
  5. Don’t match keyword only — “economy” paragraph must match economic detail in statement.
  6. Two candidates? Choose paragraph where detail is central, not passing mention.
  7. Roman vs letter — check instruction format carefully.
  8. Return to flagged information matches after reading whole passage.
  9. Grammar elimination saves 30 seconds per sentence ending.
  10. Cross-module: Listening matching (Chapter 75) uses similar elimination logic.

Challenge

Index-Only Drill: For 5 passages, build gist index without answering questions. Then answer 10 information-match statements from index alone. Open passage only when index fails. Target 70% index-only accuracy.

Band 9 Strategies

  1. Pre-index during orientation pass — Band 9 candidates never start information matching cold.

  2. Proposition quote test: mentally cite half a sentence proving match — if impossible, reject paragraph.

  3. Feature timeline: note chronological order of researchers — statements often follow narrative sequence even when questions don’t.

  4. Sentence ending triage: eliminate 2 endings on grammar in 5 seconds; use saved time on information matching.

  5. Dual-match awareness: when NB applies, actively consider same paragraph for related statements — saves rescanning.

  6. Abstract statement decoding: statements use higher abstraction than passage — decode before scanning.

  7. Paragraph border cases: read last sentence of Para N and first of Para N+1 for split information.

  8. No forced distribution: unlike some school tests, IELTS may use same letter 3 times — accept it.

  9. Integrate headings map: if headings done first, gist index already exists — reuse.

  10. Error log tag: “first-match” vs “paraphrase miss” vs “wrong feature attribution” — separate drills.

85.10 Sentence Endings: Advanced Grammar Filters

Subject-verb agreement after blank:

Stem: “The number of participants who completed…”
Eliminate endings with plural verb if “number” is singular head.

Relative clause continuity:

Stem: “…researchers found that…”
Ending must be complete clause (subject + verb), not noun phrase alone.

Parallelism in lists:

Stem: “…included reducing waste, improving efficiency, and…”
Ending must be gerund phrase or parallel structure matching list.

85.11 Feature Matching with Dates and Periods

When features are historical periods (Early Medieval, Industrial Era):

  • Timeline sketch in margin while reading.
  • Statement may describe event — match period containing event, not period mentioned elsewhere.

Example: Statement: “Introduction of printing press.” Period: Late fifteenth century — even if passage also mentions medieval manuscripts in earlier period.

85.12 Information Matching vs TFNG Overlap

Same fact may appear as:

  • TFNG: “Printing spread rapidly in Germany.”
  • Information match: “Reference to speed of printing diffusion.”

Difference: TFNG evaluates truth; information match evaluates location. Use gist index for matching; use proposition compare for TFNG.

Additional Exercises (13–22)

Passage paragraph: “The tribunal ruled that emissions reporting must include Scope 3 supply-chain data, a requirement previously limited to Scope 1 direct releases.”

  1. Information match: “A legal mandate expanding reporting boundaries” → paragraph containing this sentence.

  2. Feature match: Feature = The tribunal. Statement: “Required broader emissions disclosure” → tribunal.

  3. Sentence ending: “Scope 3 reporting was…” A. …extended beyond direct releases only. ✓ B. …eliminated entirely.

16–18. Define: gist index, attribution, proposition quote test.

  1. Matching information breaks passage order — true/false?

  2. Sentence endings usually in order — true/false?

  3. NB instruction: paragraph used twice — allowed?

  4. First-match trap defence in one sentence?

Solutions: 13. That paragraph | 14. tribunal | 15. A | 16. one-line gist per para / who claimed what / cite half-sentence proof | 17. gist index | 18. attribution tracking | 19. True | 20. True | 21. Yes if NB stated | 22. Verify full proposition not keyword only

Extended Worked Example 4: Full Passage Index

Build index for coral passage (Chapter 85 Exercise):

Para Gist
A Reefs: small area, high species share
B Bleaching mechanism: algae expulsion
C Shade cloth trial; scalability unclear
D GDP/tourism economic forecast

Statement “experimental treatment with uncertain large-scale application” → C instantly via index without re-reading A, B, D.

Feature Matching: Theory vs Person vs Organisation

Feature type Scan for
Researcher verbs of discovery: found, argued, demonstrated
Organisation policy actions: mandated, funded, banned
Theory/Model named proper noun + definition clause
Historical period dates bounding events
Place proper noun + prepositional phrases

Build attribution table while reading any feature-matching passage.

Additional Passage 3: Three Competing Theories

Paragraph: Dr. Hale’s resonance model explains tidal locking through gravitational gradient dissipation. Professor Okoye challenged Hale’s timeframe estimates, proposing instead the impact-induced spin model documented in lunar geology literature. The International Astronomical Union working group declined to endorse either exclusively, publishing a consensus statement listing observational tests still outstanding.

Features: i. Hale ii. Okoye iii. IAU

  1. Disputed estimated timescales → Okoye (challenged timeframe)
  2. Associated with gravitational gradient dissipation → Hale
  3. Published consensus without exclusive endorsement → IAU

Sentence Endings — Cohesion Checklist

Before selecting ending, verify:

Five checks in 15 seconds prevent impulsive wrong selections.

Next: Chapter 86 — Multiple Choice (Reading)

Chapter 86: Multiple Choice (Reading)

Part: Part 5 — Reading

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Identify the four MCQ formats used in IELTS Reading and adapt strategy to each.
  • Apply systematic distractor elimination using the TRUE/FALSE/NG logic framework.
  • Distinguish main-idea questions from detail questions and writer-attitude questions.
  • Avoid extreme options, partial-quote options, and true-but-irrelevant options.
  • Locate answer zones efficiently when questions are ordered or scattered.
  • Handle multi-answer MCQ items (“Choose TWO letters”) without double-counting errors.
  • Complete MCQ sets at approximately 1.5 minutes per question under exam conditions.

Theory / Explanation

86.1 MCQ Formats in IELTS Reading

Format A — Single answer (A/B/C/D or A/B/C/D/E)
Most common. One correct option.

Format B — Choose TWO (or THREE)
“Which TWO advantages are mentioned?” — five or six options listed; select 2. Each correct selection = 1 mark.

Format C — Question first, options after passage section
Grouped with related paragraphs.

Format D — Complete the question stem
” The writer suggests that the primary cause of X is…” + 4 completions.

Why format awareness matters: Multi-select items require confirmation of each option against text — not stop after finding one correct.

86.2 Question Type Subcategories

Subcategory What it asks Strategy
Detail Specific fact/intention Scan + intensive read
Main idea Paragraph/passage gist Skim + reject detail options
Writer’s purpose/reason Why author includes information Read surrounding discourse
Inference Implied but not stated Caution — closest supported inference only
Attitude/tone Writer’s view YNNG-style evaluative language

86.3 The Elimination Framework

Treat each option as a mini TFNG statement:

Option status Action
Contradicted by passage Eliminate
Not mentioned Eliminate
Partially true but incomplete Usually eliminate (IELTS prefers complete match)
Fully supported paraphrase Strong candidate
True in real world but not in passage Eliminate

Two finalists: Choose the option that matches question stem focus — not the more interesting option.

86.4 The Six Distractor Types

1. Word-copy distractor — Repeats passage vocabulary but reverses meaning.

2. True elsewhere — Correct for different paragraph, not question scope.

3. Absolute distractor — all, never, completely — when passage hedges.

4. Detail distractor — True fact, wrong level (example not main idea).

5. Opposite distractor — Antonym or reversed causality.

6. Attractive inference — Logical but unsupported — NG option.

86.5 Reading the Stem First

Always read question stem before options — stems contain:

  • Scope limiters (“according to the passage,” “in paragraph 3”)
  • Target (“main reason,” “primary concern,” “writer’s attitude”)

Without stem focus: detail option wins when main-idea required.

86.6 Multi-Select Protocol (Choose TWO)

  1. Read all options quickly — mark clearly wrong.
  2. Scan passage for each remaining option — confirm mentioned.
  3. Select exactly required number — order on answer sheet irrelevant.
  4. If only one confirmed, re-scan for second — don’t guess contradictory pair.

Common error: Pick two options that contradict each other when passage supports only one.

86.7 Location and Order

Single-answer MCQ usually follows passage order. Use previous question location as lower bound for scan.

Exception: Main idea question about whole passage — may require global skim.

86.8 Time and Marking

~1.5 minutes per MCQ — longer than TFNG due to four-option evaluation.

Do not over-invest: If torn between two after 2 minutes, mark best guess, flag, move.

86.9 Comparison with Listening MCQ

Reading MCQ allows re-scanning text; Listening does not. Reading candidates should verify every option in text when time permits — not rely on memory.

Examples

Example 1: Detail MCQ

Question: Why did the 2018 trial fail?
