Chapter 102: General Training Letters

Part: 6 — IELTS Writing Task 1 (General Training)

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

The task

General Training Task 1 asks you to write a letter of at least 150 words in about 20 minutes. The prompt gives a situation and three bullet points. Address every bullet point fully, use a tone that matches the reader, and make the purpose clear from the first paragraph.

Tone and format

Formal: Dear Sir or Madam, … Yours faithfully. Semi-formal: Dear Mr Khan, … Yours sincerely. Informal: Dear Sam, … Best wishes. A formal complaint needs polite precision, not anger. A message to a friend can use contractions and warmth, but it still needs clear paragraphs.

Four-part plan

Open with purpose and relevant context. Deal with the first and second bullet points in separate, developed paragraphs. Complete the final point and state an appropriate request, offer, or next action. Plan details before writing: who, what happened, when, impact, and desired outcome.

Useful language

Formal requests: I am writing to enquire about; I would be grateful if you could; I would appreciate a response by. Complaints: I wish to express my dissatisfaction; the item failed to match the description; I request a replacement or refund. Informal language: I thought I’d let you know; would you be able to; it would be great if.

Model: formal complaint

Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to complain about a bicycle I rented from your Riverside branch on 4 June. Although I booked it for a full day, its rear brake failed within twenty minutes of collection.

When I returned to the branch, the attendant acknowledged that the brake cable was worn but could not provide a replacement. Consequently, I had to cancel a planned trip with visiting relatives and pay for taxis instead. I was particularly disappointed because your website describes every bicycle as safety-checked.

I would therefore like a full refund of the rental fee and reimbursement for the taxi costs, for which I have enclosed receipts. Please confirm how you intend to resolve this matter within seven days.

Yours faithfully, Alex Morgan

Examiner comment: The purpose, all bullet points, suitable formal register, and a clear requested action are developed. Notice that the tone is firm without being rude.

Practice tasks

  1. Write to a college director requesting a timetable change; explain the clash, propose an alternative, and ask about the decision process.
  2. Write to a neighbour about a noisy renovation; describe the impact, suggest reasonable hours, and invite a reply.
  3. Write to a friend who is moving city; give advice about housing, offer practical help, and arrange a meeting.
  4. Write to a hotel after a disappointing stay; explain two problems, say what staff did, and request compensation.

Chapter 103: Task 1 Practice and Review

Part: 6 — IELTS Writing

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

How to use this chapter

Practice improves when it is diagnostic. Do not write ten reports and only count words. Before each task, predict the overview. After writing, mark every comparison, check every unit, and identify one recurring language error. Rewrite one paragraph rather than merely reading feedback.

Academic practice set

  1. A line graph shows the number of electric and petrol cars sold in three countries between 2012 and 2024.
  2. A bar chart compares weekly hours spent on paid work, childcare, and leisure by men and women in 1995 and 2025.
  3. Two pie charts show sources of electricity in a region in 2005 and 2025.
  4. A table gives population, urban share, and average income in five cities.
  5. Two maps show a library site before and after renovation.
  6. A process diagram illustrates how discarded glass is recycled into new containers.
  7. A combined bar and line chart shows advertising spend and online sales over six years.

General Training practice set

  1. Write to your manager to request training leave. Explain the course, how it benefits work, and how duties will be covered.
  2. Write to a local council about a dangerous crossing. Describe the problem, explain who is affected, and suggest a solution.
  3. Write to a friend who has offered accommodation. Thank them, explain your arrival plans, and ask one practical question.

Review rubric

Task response: Is every required feature or bullet point developed? Organisation: Does each paragraph have a purpose? Vocabulary: Are words precise and natural? Grammar: Are complex sentences controlled? Make an error log with columns for error, correction, reason, and personal example.

Timed cycle

Use three minutes to analyse, fourteen to write, and three to edit. On a second attempt, reduce planning to two minutes only after you can consistently identify the overview. Never cut editing time; a correction to subject–verb agreement or a data unit can protect several marks.

Chapter 104: Writing Task 2 Overview

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

The task and marking

Write at least 250 words in about 40 minutes. Task Response assesses whether you answer every part and develop ideas; Coherence and Cohesion assesses organisation; Lexical Resource assesses precise, flexible vocabulary; Grammatical Range and Accuracy assesses controlled sentence variety. Task 2 carries more weight than Task 1, so manage time accordingly.

A dependable workflow

Spend five minutes interpreting the question and planning. Write an introduction, two developed body paragraphs, and a conclusion in roughly thirty minutes. Reserve five minutes to check that your position is consistent, both parts are answered, and grammar is accurate. Two strong ideas are safer than four thin ones.

The thesis test

Your thesis must answer the exact wording. For “discuss both views and give your opinion,” name both views and give your own judgement. For “what problems and what solutions,” give both. For a two-part question, do not let one paragraph become a general discussion while another question disappears.

Development over decoration

Each body paragraph needs a claim, why it is true, an example, and why the example matters. Avoid memorised hooks, quotations, and imaginary statistics. Logical development produces cohesion: use a connector only when it names a real relationship.

Editing priorities

Check subject–verb agreement, articles, singular/plural nouns, verb forms, pronoun reference, and punctuation around dependent clauses. Then replace one vague word with an exact one. Do not rewrite whole paragraphs in the final minutes.

Chapter 105: Opinion Essays

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

What the question requires

Choose a clear position, acknowledge a reasonable limitation, and defend it consistently. The question is: Some people believe that governments should make university education free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree? Read it twice. Underline the task words, identify whether it asks for reasons, effects, solutions, comparison, evaluation, or your opinion, and make a one-sentence answer before planning examples. A sophisticated essay that answers a different question cannot score highly for Task Response.

Flexible template

Introduction: paraphrase the issue and give a direct thesis.
Body paragraph 1: topic sentence, explanation, specific example, and consequence.
Body paragraph 2: a distinct main point developed in the same way; include a concession if it improves accuracy.
Conclusion: restate the judgement or answer in fresh language.

This is a planning scaffold, not text to memorise. Examiners recognise empty openings such as “This essay will discuss both sides.” Your thesis should contain meaning: “Although free tuition widens access, a targeted scheme is more sustainable than universal funding.”

Planning in five minutes

Write P (position), A and B (two reasons), E (one realistic example for each), and C (a concession). Then test your ideas: can each be explained beyond one sentence? Is it directly relevant? Does the example illustrate rather than replace reasoning? Prefer a narrow, plausible example over an invented statistic.

Paragraph architecture

A useful paragraph moves from claim to mechanism to illustration to implication. For example: “Targeted grants improve access because they remove the financial barrier for students from low-income households. A trainee nurse who can cover tuition and transport is less likely to abandon a course for paid work. This approach therefore broadens participation without subsidising affluent families who can already pay.” The example is specific, but no unverified number is needed.

Linking without mechanical signals

Use logical relationships, not a chain of firstly, secondly, finally. Addition: moreover, equally important. Contrast: however, nevertheless, whereas. Cause: therefore, consequently, which means that. Concession: admittedly, although, even if. Reference words such as this approach, such pressure, and the latter can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

Lexis and grammar

Favour precise collocations: allocate public funds, widen access, impose a burden, mitigate a risk, foster independence. Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

Band 9 model

Some people believe that governments should make university education free for everyone. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

People often frame this issue as a choice between two simple alternatives. In reality, the strongest policy combines a clear principle with practical limits. I take the view that public action is justified when it removes a genuine barrier to opportunity, but it should be designed to concentrate help where it produces the greatest social return.

The principal reason is that unequal access can reproduce disadvantage across generations. When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

Examiner comment

The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

Common mistakes

Partial answer: answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.
Undeveloped lists: naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.
Memorised language: forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.
False evidence: inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.
New ideas in the conclusion: conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

Practice questions

  1. Governments should spend more on preventing illness than treating it. Discuss.
  2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
  3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
  4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
  5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

Examiner comment

The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

Common mistakes

Partial answer: answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.
Undeveloped lists: naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.
Memorised language: forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.
False evidence: inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.
New ideas in the conclusion: conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

  2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
  3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
  4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
  5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

Chapter 107: Problem–Solution Essays

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

What the question requires

Define concrete problems, explain their consequences, and propose feasible responses. The question is: Many city centres are losing small independent shops. What problems does this cause, and what measures could address them? Read it twice. Underline the task words, identify whether it asks for reasons, effects, solutions, comparison, evaluation, or your opinion, and make a one-sentence answer before planning examples. A sophisticated essay that answers a different question cannot score highly for Task Response.

Flexible template

Introduction: paraphrase the issue and give a direct thesis.
Body paragraph 1: topic sentence, explanation, specific example, and consequence.
Body paragraph 2: a distinct main point developed in the same way; include a concession if it improves accuracy.
Conclusion: restate the judgement or answer in fresh language.

This is a planning scaffold, not text to memorise. Examiners recognise empty openings such as “This essay will discuss both sides.” Your thesis should contain meaning: “Although free tuition widens access, a targeted scheme is more sustainable than universal funding.”

Planning in five minutes

Write P (position), A and B (two reasons), E (one realistic example for each), and C (a concession). Then test your ideas: can each be explained beyond one sentence? Is it directly relevant? Does the example illustrate rather than replace reasoning? Prefer a narrow, plausible example over an invented statistic.

Paragraph architecture

A useful paragraph moves from claim to mechanism to illustration to implication. For example: “Targeted grants improve access because they remove the financial barrier for students from low-income households. A trainee nurse who can cover tuition and transport is less likely to abandon a course for paid work. This approach therefore broadens participation without subsidising affluent families who can already pay.” The example is specific, but no unverified number is needed.

Linking without mechanical signals

Use logical relationships, not a chain of firstly, secondly, finally. Addition: moreover, equally important. Contrast: however, nevertheless, whereas. Cause: therefore, consequently, which means that. Concession: admittedly, although, even if. Reference words such as this approach, such pressure, and the latter can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

Lexis and grammar

Favour precise collocations: allocate public funds, widen access, impose a burden, mitigate a risk, foster independence. Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

Band 9 model

Many city centres are losing small independent shops. What problems does this cause, and what measures could address them?

People often frame this issue as a choice between two simple alternatives. In reality, the strongest policy combines a clear principle with practical limits. I take the view that public action is justified when it removes a genuine barrier to opportunity, but it should be designed to concentrate help where it produces the greatest social return.

The principal reason is that unequal access can reproduce disadvantage across generations. When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

Common mistakes

Partial answer: answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.
Undeveloped lists: naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.
Memorised language: forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.
False evidence: inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.
New ideas in the conclusion: conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

  2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
  3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
  4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
  5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

Chapter 109: Double-Question Essays

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

What the question requires

Answer each question directly while making the relation between the paragraphs explicit. The question is: In many countries, young adults delay buying a home. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development? Read it twice. Underline the task words, identify whether it asks for reasons, effects, solutions, comparison, evaluation, or your opinion, and make a one-sentence answer before planning examples. A sophisticated essay that answers a different question cannot score highly for Task Response.

Flexible template

Introduction: paraphrase the issue and give a direct thesis.
Body paragraph 1: topic sentence, explanation, specific example, and consequence.
Body paragraph 2: a distinct main point developed in the same way; include a concession if it improves accuracy.
Conclusion: restate the judgement or answer in fresh language.

This is a planning scaffold, not text to memorise. Examiners recognise empty openings such as “This essay will discuss both sides.” Your thesis should contain meaning: “Although free tuition widens access, a targeted scheme is more sustainable than universal funding.”

Planning in five minutes

Write P (position), A and B (two reasons), E (one realistic example for each), and C (a concession). Then test your ideas: can each be explained beyond one sentence? Is it directly relevant? Does the example illustrate rather than replace reasoning? Prefer a narrow, plausible example over an invented statistic.

Paragraph architecture

A useful paragraph moves from claim to mechanism to illustration to implication. For example: “Targeted grants improve access because they remove the financial barrier for students from low-income households. A trainee nurse who can cover tuition and transport is less likely to abandon a course for paid work. This approach therefore broadens participation without subsidising affluent families who can already pay.” The example is specific, but no unverified number is needed.

Linking without mechanical signals

Use logical relationships, not a chain of firstly, secondly, finally. Addition: moreover, equally important. Contrast: however, nevertheless, whereas. Cause: therefore, consequently, which means that. Concession: admittedly, although, even if. Reference words such as this approach, such pressure, and the latter can create cohesion when their referent is clear.

Lexis and grammar

Favour precise collocations: allocate public funds, widen access, impose a burden, mitigate a risk, foster independence. Use complex grammar to express real relationships: “If employers subsidised retraining, displaced workers could move into growing sectors.” Accuracy matters more than density. Avoid absolute claims such as “technology always improves education.”

Band 9 model

In many countries, young adults delay buying a home. Why is this happening? Is this a positive or negative development?

People often frame this issue as a choice between two simple alternatives. In reality, the strongest policy combines a clear principle with practical limits. I take the view that public action is justified when it removes a genuine barrier to opportunity, but it should be designed to concentrate help where it produces the greatest social return.

The principal reason is that unequal access can reproduce disadvantage across generations. When a capable student cannot pursue training because basic fees and living costs are unaffordable, society loses both that individual’s potential and the services they might later provide. Targeted support, for instance, can enable students from low-income households to enter shortage professions without transferring an unnecessary subsidy to families who could fund the same education privately.

Admittedly, universal provision is administratively simple and avoids the stigma sometimes attached to means testing. Yet simplicity is not sufficient if it directs limited resources away from early education, healthcare, or vocational pathways. A transparent threshold and grants that cover essential costs would preserve dignity while keeping the policy financially credible.

Overall, the desirable outcome is not blanket generosity but fair access. By directing support towards people for whom cost is a real obstacle, governments can improve opportunity without weakening other public services.

Examiner comment

The model gives a direct, nuanced position, develops two connected reasons, and uses an example to clarify a mechanism. Cohesion comes from ideas and reference, not excessive connectors. Vocabulary is precise but not ornamental, and complex sentences remain controlled. A Band 9 response still needs to be accurate, relevant, and natural; length or difficult words alone do not create the score.

Common mistakes

Partial answer: answering only one part of a two-part question. Label each part in your plan.
Undeveloped lists: naming three ideas but explaining none. Use two fully developed points.
Memorised language: forcing an irrelevant phrase or quotation. Write what the question needs.
False evidence: inventing research or statistics. Use plausible examples without pretending authority.
New ideas in the conclusion: conclude; do not begin a third body paragraph.

Practice questions

  1. Governments should spend more on preventing illness than treating it. Discuss.
  2. Children should begin formal education earlier. To what extent do you agree?
  3. International tourism has more disadvantages than advantages. Discuss both views.
  4. Why do many people change careers several times, and is this positive?
  5. Should employers be required to offer flexible working arrangements?

Chapter 110: Cohesion and Lexis

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Cohesion is logical visibility

Cohesion helps the reader follow your reasoning. It is not a competition to use the largest number of linkers. A paragraph is cohesive when its sentences answer a sequence: claim, reason, example, consequence. Repeating a key noun selectively is often clearer than replacing it with an ambiguous synonym.

Four cohesive tools

Reference: “This policy” must point to one identifiable policy.
Substitution: use this approach, such a measure, or the former when the reference is unmistakable.
Conjunction: choose however, therefore, for example, and although for their real logical function.
Lexical chains: repeat a controlled family: housing, rent, tenants, affordability, rather than jumping among unrelated fancy synonyms.

Lexical resource

Band 7 vocabulary is generally flexible and accurate. Band 8–9 vocabulary is more precise and natural, with rare slips. Precision means writing mitigate traffic congestion rather than make traffic badness lower. Collocation matters: pose a threat, allocate funding, draw a distinction, address a shortfall, impose a restriction.

Repair exercise

Weak: “Firstly, people use phones. Moreover, phones are bad. On the other hand, phones are useful.”
Better: “Constant phone use can fragment attention, particularly when notifications interrupt sustained study. Nevertheless, the same devices allow students to access course materials and contact tutors quickly. Their value therefore depends on whether users can control interruptions.”

Practice

Rewrite ten old paragraphs by removing half their connectors. Add only those needed to express contrast, result, illustration, or concession. Build themed word banks from your own essays and record a collocation, a sentence, and a common error for each item.

Chapter 111: Band Comparisons

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

One idea at four levels

Question: Should cities restrict private cars in central areas?

Band 6: “Cars cause pollution, so cities should restrict them. People can use buses.” The position is clear but explanation is brief and vocabulary is general.

Band 7: “Cities should restrict private cars because concentrated traffic worsens air quality and delays buses. A congestion charge can encourage commuters to use public transport.” The claim is developed and relevant.

Band 8: “Restricting private cars in dense centres can improve both air quality and the reliability of buses, which otherwise become trapped in the same congestion. Charging drivers at peak times gives commuters a financial reason to shift journeys.” The mechanism is clear and language is precise.

Band 9: “In compact city centres, limiting private vehicles is justified because each additional car consumes scarce road space while slowing buses that carry far more passengers. A peak-time charge, paired with frequent affordable public transport, can therefore reduce emissions without simply transferring inconvenience to lower-income commuters.” The response is nuanced, well developed, and grammatically controlled.

What changes across bands

Higher bands do not merely add longer sentences. They answer every part, choose ideas that can be explained, connect claims to consequences, use accurate collocations, and make very few errors. Improve one dimension at a time: first relevance, then development, then paragraph cohesion, then language precision.

Diagnostic routine

Take a recent essay. Highlight thesis statements in blue, explanations in green, examples in yellow, and unsupported assertions in red. If red dominates, develop fewer ideas. Then check whether each pronoun has a clear noun and whether every connector expresses its stated relationship.

How to use this bank

Plan rather than memorise. For each question, identify the type, write a one-sentence thesis, select two ideas, and test whether you answer every instruction. Rotate topics and question types. All questions below are original practice prompts.

  5. Education: Why are patterns relating to schools changing, and is this a positive or negative development?
  6. Education: What problems are associated with schools, and what practical solutions can be proposed?

Deliberate-practice rotation

Choose ten questions per week: two opinion, two discussion, two problem–solution, two advantage–disadvantage, and two double questions. Write full essays for three, outlines for four, and introductions plus theses for three. Revisit weak topics after feedback.

Chapter 113: Band 9 Model Answers and Examiner Comments

Part: 7 — IELTS Writing Task 2

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

How to learn from a model

Do not memorise these responses. Read the question, predict a position and two reasons, then compare your plan with the model. Underline the thesis, topic sentences, explanations, examples, concessions, and conclusion. A model is useful when it teaches decisions, not when it becomes borrowed language.

Model 1: public transport

Question: Governments should make public transport free in all cities. To what extent do you agree or disagree?

Free public transport is an attractive proposal because it could reduce the cost of daily travel. However, I do not agree that it should be universally free. A low fare combined with substantial investment in reliability is a more equitable and sustainable policy.

The strongest case for free services is that price can exclude low-income residents from employment, education, and healthcare. When a family must choose between travel and essentials, a fare reduction can have an immediate effect on opportunity. In addition, cheaper buses and trains may persuade some drivers to leave their cars at home, easing congestion and emissions.

Nevertheless, abolishing fares does not itself create a useful network. If services are infrequent, overcrowded, or unavailable outside central areas, many commuters will still need private vehicles. Funding every journey from general taxation may also divert money from maintenance and route expansion. A better approach is to cap fares for regular users and provide free travel for people with demonstrable need, while directing remaining funds towards frequent, accessible services.

In conclusion, affordability matters, but completely free transport is not necessarily the best use of public money. Targeted concessions and high-quality provision would serve both fairness and long-term demand.

Examiner comment: The answer maintains a qualified position throughout, develops a counterargument fairly, and evaluates policy by practical criteria. Lexis such as route expansion and targeted concessions is precise, while grammar is varied and accurate.

Model 2: remote work

Question: More people work from home than in the past. What are the reasons, and is this a positive or negative development?

Working from home has expanded because digital tools now allow many tasks to be completed away from a traditional office, while employers have recognised that physical presence is not always necessary. On balance, this is a positive development, provided workers retain regular contact with colleagues.

The technical reason is straightforward: cloud-based files, video meetings, and secure communication platforms allow teams to coordinate across locations. Employers also save on office space, and staff may avoid long daily commutes. These incentives became visible when organisations were forced to adopt remote systems and later discovered that routine work could continue effectively.

The principal benefit is greater control over time. A parent, for example, may arrange work around school hours without sacrificing employment altogether. Fewer commuting journeys can also reduce pressure on transport networks. Admittedly, isolation and blurred boundaries can harm wellbeing, especially for new employees who need informal guidance. Companies should therefore offer hybrid arrangements, regular mentoring, and a clear right to disconnect.

Overall, remote work is beneficial because it broadens flexibility and can reduce wasted travel. Its advantages depend, however, on deliberate measures to preserve collaboration and protect personal time.

Examiner comment: Both parts are answered directly. The response explains mechanisms, offers a realistic example, and makes a balanced evaluation rather than treating the trend as wholly positive.

Model 3: school assessment

Question: Some people think examinations are the best way to assess students, while others believe continuous assessment is better. Discuss both views and give your opinion.

Examinations remain popular because they test students under identical conditions, whereas continuous assessment captures performance over a longer period. Although formal exams have a role, I believe a carefully moderated combination of both methods is the fairest approach.

Supporters of examinations argue that a single standardised test limits the influence of teachers’ personal judgement. Students answer the same questions in the same time, making results easier to compare across schools. This can be particularly important for university admission, where institutions need a transparent basis for selecting applicants.

Continuous assessment, however, measures skills that a timed exam may miss. Research projects, presentations, and drafts show whether learners can apply knowledge, respond to feedback, and complete sustained work. They also reduce the risk that illness or anxiety on one day will determine an entire grade. The weakness is that standards can vary, so external moderation is necessary.

In conclusion, examinations offer comparability, while continuous assessment gives a fuller picture of learning. Schools should use both, with common criteria and moderation to protect consistency.

Examiner comment: Each view receives a developed paragraph, and the personal view is clear in both introduction and conclusion. The writer avoids unsupported claims and uses a concession to produce a nuanced judgement.

Model 4: food waste

Question: Food waste is increasing in many countries. What problems does this cause, and what can be done?

Rising food waste damages the environment and places unnecessary pressure on household budgets. The problem can be reduced through clearer information, improved retail practices, and systems that redirect edible surplus.

When food is discarded, the water, energy, and labour used to produce and transport it are wasted as well. Disposal creates further emissions, particularly where organic matter is sent to landfill. At household level, frequent disposal often reflects poor planning: consumers buy perishable goods without considering what they already have or when they will use it.

Governments can require clearer date labels that distinguish safety from quality, since many people discard food that remains edible. Retailers should also discount items approaching their use-by date and partner with charities to redistribute safe surplus. Finally, schools and public campaigns can teach practical skills such as meal planning and storage. Together, these measures reduce waste before it reaches the bin rather than relying solely on recycling afterwards.

In conclusion, food waste has environmental and financial costs, but it is not inevitable. Better information and coordinated action by households, shops, and authorities can address it at several stages.

Examiner comment: The essay answers problems and solutions in balanced depth. The solutions are specific, feasible, and explicitly linked to the causes.

Timed refinement drill 1: identify the central comparison before writing

In a Band 9 model analysis response, spend two minutes on this controlled exercise. Write one overview sentence that names the largest contrast, then test whether every detail paragraph supports it. Draft two sentences, read them aloud once, and revise only errors you can name. This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.

This is deliberate practice: accuracy comes before speed. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. Keep a notebook entry containing the original sentence, the revision, and the rule that justified the revision. On the next attempt, use a new data point or idea so that you practise transfer rather than memorisation.

Chapter 114: IELTS Speaking Overview & Format

Part: Part 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Describe the full IELTS Speaking test structure, timing, and scoring criteria for Academic and General Training.
  • Explain how the four assessment criteria interact and why a high vocabulary score cannot compensate for poor fluency.
  • Predict the sequence and purpose of Parts 1, 2, and 3 and prepare appropriate strategies for each.
  • Apply a pre-test, during-test, and post-test routine that reduces anxiety and protects performance.
  • Diagnose your personal Speaking profile across Fluency, Lexical Resource, Grammar, and Pronunciation.
  • Integrate Speaking practice with vocabulary, grammar, and listening work from earlier parts of this book.
  • Set realistic band targets based on observable behaviours rather than self-perceived fluency.

Theory / Explanation

114.1 What IELTS Speaking Measures

IELTS Speaking is a face-to-face oral interview with a certified examiner. It lasts 11–14 minutes and assesses your ability to communicate in English across familiar and abstract topics. You are not tested on factual knowledge of IELTS topics; you are tested on whether you can:

  1. Express opinions and information clearly and coherently.
  2. Develop answers beyond one-word or memorised responses.
  3. Use a range of vocabulary and grammar appropriate to the context.
  4. Be understood without excessive listener effort.
  5. Handle follow-up questions and more abstract discussion in Part 3.

The same Speaking test format is used for Academic and General Training candidates. Your Speaking score contributes equally to both versions.

114.2 Test Structure at a Glance

Feature Detail
Format One-to-one interview with examiner
Duration 11–14 minutes total
Parts 3 (Introduction → Long turn → Discussion)
Recording Audio recorded for quality monitoring
Scoring Four criteria, each 25% of final band
Result Single overall band (half-band increments)

The three-part architecture:

Part Duration Format Purpose
Part 1 4–5 min Short questions on familiar topics Warm-up; basic fluency and coherence
Part 2 3–4 min 1-min prep + 1–2 min monologue on cue card Sustained speech; organisation
Part 3 4–5 min Two-way discussion linked to Part 2 theme Abstract ideas; justification and speculation

Why the structure matters: Part 1 feels conversational but is still assessed. Part 2 is the only time you speak uninterrupted at length — organisation here strongly signals Band 7+. Part 3 separates candidates who can only describe personal experience from those who can analyse and evaluate ideas.

114.3 The Four Assessment Criteria

Your final band is not an average of four separate scores visible to you; the examiner produces one holistic band informed by four equal-weight criteria:

Fluency and Coherence (FC)

  • Speaks at length without unnatural pauses
  • Uses connectives and discourse markers appropriately
  • Develops topics logically; easy to follow

Lexical Resource (LR)

  • Uses vocabulary flexibly and precisely
  • Paraphrases effectively when needed
  • Uses less common items with awareness of collocation and style

Grammatical Range and Accuracy (GRA)

  • Produces a mix of simple and complex structures
  • Maintains control; errors are rare and do not impede communication

Pronunciation (P)

  • Individual sounds, word stress, sentence stress, and intonation are clear
  • Can be understood throughout; accent is not penalised if intelligible

Critical insight: Weakness in one criterion caps your overall performance. A candidate with Band 9 vocabulary but Band 5 fluency (long freezes, reformulating every sentence) will not receive Band 8 overall. Examiners balance criteria; they do not reward isolated strengths.

114.4 How Bands Are Assigned

Examiners use public band descriptors (see Part 1, Chapter 3). They do not compare you to other candidates on your test day; they compare your performance to descriptor statements.

Observable differences:

Band Typical performance
5 Short answers; frequent repetition; limited vocabulary; errors cause some strain
6 Willing to speak at length but coherence may break; adequate vocabulary; mixed grammar control
7 Speaks at length with occasional hesitation; uses less common vocabulary; complex structures with some errors
8 Fluent with only occasional repetition; wide vocabulary; majority of sentences error-free
9 Fully fluent; precise vocabulary; flexible grammar; effortless intelligibility

Half bands: Examiners may award 6.5, 7.5, etc., when performance sits between descriptor levels.

114.5 Part 1: Introduction and Interview

The examiner verifies your identity, then asks 4–12 questions across 2–3 familiar topic areas (home, work/study, hobbies, daily routines, transport, etc.).

Characteristics: - Questions are closed and open: “Do you work or study?” → “What do you enjoy about your job?” - Answers typically need 2–4 sentences, not essays. - Follow-up questions probe the same topic before switching.

Strategic implication: Part 1 sets the tone. One-word answers signal low band; over-long monologues waste time and feel unnatural.

114.6 Part 2: Individual Long Turn

You receive a cue card with a topic and bullet points. You have 1 minute to prepare (paper and pencil provided) and must speak for 1–2 minutes. The examiner stops you at 2 minutes.

Typical cue card structure: - Main prompt: “Describe a place you visited that impressed you.” - Bullet points: where / when / who with / why it impressed you - Optional final line: “And explain whether you would recommend it.”

After your long turn, the examiner asks 1–2 brief follow-up questions (rounding-off questions).

Strategic implication: Notes during preparation are essential. A clear structure (past → detail → opinion) prevents mid-speech panic.

114.7 Part 3: Two-Way Discussion

Part 3 questions extend the Part 2 theme to society, trends, comparisons, and hypotheticals. Questions become more abstract: “Why do people enjoy travelling to historical sites?” → “Should governments charge higher fees for tourist attractions?”

Characteristics: - Answers require 4–6 sentences with explanation and examples. - Examiners may challenge or redirect: “Why do you think that?” - Speculation and balanced views are valued at higher bands.

Strategic implication: Part 3 rewards the same skills as Writing Task 2 — developing ideas, qualifying claims, using examples — but orally and under time pressure.

114.8 What Examiners Are Not Assessing

Understanding what does not affect your score prevents wasted effort:

Not assessed Why it matters
Your accent origin Intelligibility matters; native-like accent does not
Whether the examiner agrees with you No “correct” opinion on abstract topics
Body language (mostly) Assessed on speech; minimal eye contact alone won’t fail you
Factual accuracy of personal stories Invent plausible examples if needed
British vs American vocabulary Both acceptable if natural and accurate

What is penalised: Memorised scripts detected by unnatural delivery; answers that ignore the question; silence beyond brief thinking pauses.

114.9 Test-Day Procedure

  1. Check-in: ID verification; belongings stored per centre rules.
  2. Waiting: You may speak to other candidates; stay calm.
  3. Entry: Examiner greets you; recording begins.
  4. ID check: Name, candidate number, nationality confirmation.
  5. Parts 1–3: Continuous interview; no breaks between parts.
  6. End: Examiner thanks you; you leave. No instant score.

Recording: All tests are recorded. A senior examiner may re-mark a sample for quality assurance. This protects you as well as standardises marking.

114.10 Computer-Delivered vs Paper-Based Speaking

Speaking is always face-to-face with a human examiner — even when Listening, Reading, and Writing are computer-delivered. Some centres offer video-call Speaking (IELTS Online) with the same format and criteria.

Implication: Practice with real humans, not only AI apps. Apps help with drills; they cannot replicate examiner follow-ups or Part 3 pressure.

114.11 Common Failure Patterns

Pattern Symptom Fix
Part 1 minimalism “Yes.” / “No.” / “Sometimes.” Extend with reason + example rule
Part 2 under-length Stops at 45 seconds Structured notes; practise timing
Part 2 over-memorisation Robotic delivery; wrong topic fit Flexible templates, not scripts
Part 3 essay mode 90-second answers; examiner interrupts Answer directly, then develop
Vocabulary panic Long pauses searching for “Band 9 words” Paraphrase simply; upgrade after
Grammar freeze Only short simple sentences Pre-practise complex patterns safely
Pronunciation rush Mumbling to hide errors Slow down; stress key words

114.12 Integration with Other Modules

Speaking connects directly to:

  • Listening (Part 4): Accent exposure, signpost language, natural rhythm.
  • Vocabulary (Part 3): Topic lexis (Chapters 45–70) feeds Part 3 depth.
  • Grammar (Part 2): Tense control, conditionals, relative clauses for complex answers.
  • Writing Task 2 (Part 7): Idea development, paragraph logic transfers to Part 3.

Weekly integration drill: After each Speaking mock, extract 10 useful phrases into your vocabulary notebook and recycle them in Writing.

114.13 Building a Speaking Study Cycle

Phase A — Component drills (daily 15–20 min): - Pronunciation focus (Chapter 121) - Fluency extension (Chapter 122) - Part 1/2/3 strategy chapters (115, 117, 119)

Phase B — Timed simulation (2–3× weekly): - Full mock with partner or tutor - Record and self-assess against four criteria

Phase C — Exam simulation: - Unfamiliar examiner/partner - Strict timing including 1-minute Part 2 prep - Post-mortem error log by criterion

Examples

Example 1: Part 1 Question Ladder

Examiner: “Do you live in a house or an apartment?”
Weak: “Apartment.”
Strong: “I live in a rented apartment in the city centre — it’s a two-bedroom flat on the fourth floor, which suits me because I’m close to work.”

Examiner (follow-up): “What’s your favourite room?”
Strong: “Probably the balcony, actually. It’s small, but I keep plants there, and it’s where I drink coffee before starting work.”

Example 2: Part 2 Cue Card (Extract)

Describe a skill you learned that you found useful.
You should say:
- what the skill was
- when and how you learned it
- who helped you
and explain why it has been useful for you.

Note structure (1 minute): - Skill: basic coding (Python) - When: university, second year, online course - How: weekly projects; friend mentor - Useful: automates spreadsheet tasks at work

Example 3: Part 3 Escalation

Part 2 theme: A useful skill.

Part 3 questions (increasing abstraction): 1. “What skills do you think children should learn at school?” (general) 2. “Are practical skills more important than academic subjects?” (comparison) 3. “How might technology change the skills people need in the future?” (speculation)

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Diagnosing a Band 6.0 Plateau

Profile: Candidate feels “fluent” in daily life; mock score 6.0; target 7.0.

Mock observations: - Part 1: Good length but repetitive “I think… I think…” - Part 2: 1 minute 10 seconds; lost thread after example - Part 3: Ideas present but no examples; grammar errors on third conditional

Diagnosis: Fluency/Coherence and GRA limit the score; LR is adequate.

Plan: Chapter 122 fluency drills; Part 2 timing practice 3× weekly; conditional review (Chapter 26); record and count discourse marker variety.

Worked Example 2: Criteria Trade-Off

Scenario: Candidate uses advanced vocabulary (” ramifications,” ” ubiquitous”) but mispronounces them and pauses 3 seconds before each.

Examiner perspective: LR attempt is noted, but FC and P suffer; overall band likely 6.0–6.5, not 7.5.

Fix: Master pronunciation of words you use (Chapter 121); prefer simpler accurate lexis under pressure.

Worked Example 3: Part 2 Timing Map

Target: 2 minutes ≈ 240–280 words at natural pace.

Segment Time Content
Opening 0:00–0:20 State topic + context
Body point 1 0:20–0:50 First bullet with detail
Body point 2 0:50–1:20 Second bullet + sensory detail
Body point 3 1:20–1:45 Third bullet / who helped
Closing 1:45–2:00 Why useful + recommendation

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — Format Knowledge (Questions 1–15)

  1. How many parts are in IELTS Speaking?
  2. How long is Part 2 preparation time?
  3. Minimum time you should aim to speak in Part 2?
  4. Name the four assessment criteria.
  5. Is Speaking different for Academic vs General Training?
  6. What happens at the start of the test regarding recording?
  7. Which part involves a cue card?
  8. Are you penalised for an accent?
  9. What is a “rounding-off question”?
  10. How long is the full Speaking test?
  11. Which criterion covers discourse markers?
  12. Can you ask the examiner to explain a Part 3 question?
  13. What materials are given in Part 2 prep?
  14. Does the examiner score each part separately?
  15. Is there a penalty for saying “I don’t know”?

Exercise Set B — Criteria Mapping (Questions 16–22)

For each error, identify the primary criterion affected (FC, LR, GRA, P):

  1. Speaker repeats “very very very” while thinking.
  2. Says “childs” instead of “children.”
  3. Stresses the wrong syllable in “photograph” vs “photography.”
  4. Uses “big” five times instead of synonyms.
  5. Long pause mid-sentence, then abandons the idea.
  6. Produces a flawless complex sentence with inversion.
  7. Listener asks to repeat three times in one answer.

Exercise Set C — Part Identification (Questions 23–28)

Classify each question as Part 1, 2, or 3:

  1. “Describe a book you read recently.”
  2. “Do you prefer reading paper books or e-books?”
  3. “Why do some people dislike reading?”
  4. “Have you ever given a book as a gift?”
  5. “Should schools replace textbooks with tablets?”
  6. “Describe a gift you gave someone.”

Exercise Set D — Extension Drill (Questions 29–35)

Extend each Part 1 answer to 3 sentences (written or spoken):

  1. “Do you like cooking?” → “Yes.”
  2. “What’s the weather like where you live?” → “It’s hot.”
  3. “Do you use public transport?” → “Sometimes.”
  4. “Are you good at remembering names?” → “Not really.”
  5. “Do you enjoy shopping?” → “No.”
  6. “How often do you exercise?” → “Twice a week.”
  7. “Do you like your neighbourhood?” → “Yes, I do.”

Solutions (with WHY)

Set A

  1. Three — standard format worldwide.
  2. One minute — use fully for notes, not silent memorisation.
  3. One to two minutes — under 1 minute limits FC at higher bands.
  4. Fluency and Coherence, Lexical Resource, Grammatical Range and Accuracy, Pronunciation.
  5. No — identical Speaking test.
  6. Recording starts — for monitoring; know this to reduce surprise.
  7. Part 2 — individual long turn.
  8. No — unless intelligibility suffers.
  9. Brief question after Part 2 — e.g., “Would you visit again?”
  10. 11–14 minutes — varies by examiner pacing.
  11. Fluency and Coherence — linking and flow.
  12. Yes, once — paraphrase request allowed; not repeated help.
  13. Paper, pencil, cue card — notes are not collected for marking.
  14. No — one holistic band from whole interview.
  15. No direct penalty — but offer alternative angle; silence hurts FC.

Set B

  1. FC — hesitation/repetition.
  2. GRA — morphology error.
  3. P — word stress.
  4. LR — limited range/repetition.
  5. FC — coherence breakdown.
  6. GRA — complex structure (positive).
  7. P (possibly FC) — intelligibility primary.

Set C

  1. Part 2 — cue card long turn.
  2. Part 1 — personal preference.
  3. Part 3 — abstract/general.
  4. Part 1 — personal experience.
  5. Part 3 — policy/speculation.
  6. Part 2 — cue card.

Set D (sample extensions)

  1. Sample: “Yes, I really enjoy cooking — especially on weekends when I’m not rushed. I usually make simple Mediterranean dishes because they use fresh ingredients and don’t take too long. Last Sunday I tried a new pasta recipe I’d seen online.”

WHY 3 sentences: Direct answer + development + specific example = Band 6+ Part 1 pattern.

Review

  • Speaking = 11–14 minutes, 3 parts, one holistic band.
  • Four criteria equally weighted — weakest area caps performance.
  • Part 1: extend naturally; Part 2: structure + timing; Part 3: develop and qualify.
  • Recording is standard; examiner is not your enemy.
  • Memorised scripts backfire; flexible strategies win.
  • Integrate vocabulary and grammar from earlier book parts.

Quiz

  1. Duration of Part 2 preparation?
  2. Which part tests sustained monologue?
  3. Name two Part 1 topic areas.
  4. What percentage weight does Pronunciation carry?
  5. Can you use American English?
  6. What follows Part 2 long turn?
  7. Band 7 fluency: occasional hesitation or constant?
  8. Is factual truth of stories assessed?
  9. Primary fix for one-word Part 1 answers?
  10. Which chapter covers pronunciation detail?

Assignment

  1. Record a full mock Speaking test (Parts 1–3) with a partner or tutor. Time each part. Score yourself 1–9 on each criterion using public descriptors.

  2. Write a personal Speaking profile (200 words): strongest criterion, weakest criterion, top three errors, weekly plan.

  3. Complete five Part 2 cue cards from Chapter 118 (when available) or create your own; aim for 2 minutes each. Log actual duration.

  4. Watch one official IELTS Speaking sample video. Note three examiner behaviours (eye contact, interruptions, timing) and three candidate strengths/weaknesses.

Revision Notes

SPEAKING OVERVIEW

11–14 min | 3 parts | face-to-face
P1: familiar topics, 2–4 sentences
P2: 1 min prep + 1–2 min monologue
P3: abstract discussion, 4–6 sentences
Criteria: FC | LR | GRA | P (25% each)
Weakest criterion caps band
No accent penalty if clear
Avoid memorised scripts
Record mocks; log by criterion

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Treat Part 1 as real conversation — smile, listen, answer the question asked, not a different prepared speech.

Exam Strategy: In Part 2, the examiner will stop you at 2 minutes — hitting the full minute range is your responsibility; practise with a timer.

Exam Strategy: If you misunderstand a question, ask politely: “Could you explain what you mean by…?” — once only.

Exam Strategy: Slow, clear speech beats fast, mumbled speech. Fluency is not speed.

Challenge Questions

  1. Design a four-week Speaking plan for a candidate at Band 5.5 targeting Band 7.0, specifying daily minutes and which part receives most attention each week.

  2. Explain why a candidate with excellent grammar knowledge might still score Band 6.0 in GRA under exam pressure.

  3. Compare Part 3 and Writing Task 2: what skills overlap, and what skills differ because Speaking is unscripted?

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 speakers listen actively — they reference the examiner’s exact wording in Part 3 (“You asked about whether governments should…”) showing precise engagement.

Band 9 Secret: High-band candidates treat Part 2 notes as a map, not a script — they glance, then speak to the examiner, not the paper.

Band 9 Secret: Elite performers self-correct lightly (“…or rather, what I mean is…”) without apologising or collapsing fluency.

Band 9 Speaking Self-Assessment Grid (original template)

Criterion Band 9 signal My mock Gap action
FC Effortless flow; ideas sequenced
LR Precise, natural, idiomatic where appropriate
GRA Wide range; errors rare
P Intelligible; stress/intonation enhance meaning

Discipline: Band 9 is consistent excellence across all four, not one spectacular minute in Part 2.

Next: Chapter 115 — Part 1 Strategies | Practice bank: Chapter 116

Chapter 115: Part 1 Strategies — Introduction & Interview

Part: Part 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Apply the Answer–Extend–Example (AEE) framework to any Part 1 question.
  • Recognise topic clusters and predict follow-up question patterns.
  • Avoid over-short and over-long answers while maintaining natural conversation rhythm.
  • Use appropriate tenses, pronouns, and vocabulary for familiar personal topics.
  • Handle difficult questions (unfamiliar topics, negative preferences) without freezing.
  • Build a reusable Part 1 preparation bank without memorising fixed scripts.
  • Self-correct and paraphrase smoothly when you make mid-answer errors.

Theory / Explanation

115.1 The Purpose of Part 1

Part 1 lasts 4–5 minutes and functions as a warm-up. The examiner asks about familiar topics related to your life: home, hometown, work, study, hobbies, daily routines, food, transport, weather, and similar themes.

What Part 1 is not: - A formality you can ignore - A vocabulary showcase competition - An opportunity to recite a memorised life story

What Part 1 is: - Evidence of whether you can maintain basic fluency and coherence under light pressure - A sample of your pronunciation and grammar in simple contexts - The psychological foundation for Parts 2 and 3

Candidates who treat Part 1 as “easy” and answer minimally often enter Part 2 nervous and already scored down on FC.

115.2 Question Types in Part 1

Part 1 questions fall into predictable categories:

Type Example Response need
Factual “Where do you live?” Clear direct fact
Preference “Do you prefer tea or coffee?” Choice + reason
Frequency “How often do you exercise?” Time expression + detail
Experience “Have you ever…?” Yes/no + narrative snippet
Opinion (mild) “Do you think… is important?” View + brief justification
Hypothetical (rare) “If you could change one thing about your city…” Conditional answer

Follow-up pattern: Examiners typically ask 2–4 questions on one topic before switching. Your first answer often determines follow-up depth.

115.3 The AEE Framework

The most reliable Part 1 structure is Answer–Extend–Example:

  1. Answer — Respond directly in the first sentence (yes/no/what/where).
  2. Extend — Add reason, detail, comparison, or contrast.
  3. Example — One concrete personal instance (past or recent).

Template (flexible, not memorised): > [Direct answer]. [Reason or detail]. [For example / Actually / Last week], [specific instance].

Why AEE works: It satisfies FC (development), LR (range), and GRA (compound sentences) without unnatural length. Target 20–40 seconds per answer — roughly 2–4 sentences.

115.4 Optimal Answer Length

Length Effect
1 word Band 4–5 signal; avoid
1 sentence Minimal; Band 5–6 unless very rich
2–4 sentences Target zone for Band 6–8
5+ sentences Often unnatural; examiner may interrupt

Rule of thumb: Stop when you have answered, extended, and exemplified. Do not wait for silence.

115.5 Topic Clusters and Preparation

IELTS rotates topics but themes recur. Prepare ideas, not scripts:

Cluster A — Home & locality - Type of home, neighbourhood, favourite room, changes you’d make - Hometown: location, size, what you like/dislike, visitors

Cluster B — Work & study - Job/major, why chosen, daily tasks, future plans - Study habits, favourite subject, school/university facilities

Cluster C — Leisure & lifestyle - Hobbies, sports, reading, music, cooking, shopping - Weekends, holidays, time with friends/family

Cluster D — Daily life - Transport, sleep, meals, technology use, weather - Morning routine, organisation, punctuality

Preparation method: For each cluster, prepare 3 stories (30 seconds each) you can adapt. Example: a weekend trip story works for holidays, hobbies, and time with friends.

115.6 Tense and Grammar Choices

Part 1 tests basic tense control:

Question time frame Typical tense
Current state Present simple/continuous
Habits Present simple + frequency adverbs
Past experience Past simple; past continuous for background
Future plans going to / will / present continuous for arrangements
Preferences Present + would prefer

Common errors: - “I am living here since 2019” → “I’ve lived here since 2019” - “I am agree” → “I agree” - Switching mid-answer from past to present without signal

Safe complex structures for Part 1: - “Although I enjoy X, I don’t do it as often as I’d like because…” - “The main reason I prefer X is that…” - “If I had more free time, I’d probably…” (hypothetical — use accurately)

115.7 Lexical Resource in Part 1

You do not need obscure vocabulary. You need precise, natural words:

Weak Stronger
good enjoyable / convenient / refreshing
bad overcrowded / unreliable / exhausting
like fond of / keen on / attracted to
very big spacious / vast
things items / activities / aspects

Collocations matter: heavy traffic, grab a coffee, catch the bus, stuck indoors, get some fresh air.

Avoid: Forcing idioms (“hit the nail on the head”) into every answer; misusing “Nowadays” as a crutch opener.

115.8 Handling Negative Answers

Questions about dislikes or things you don’t do are normal:

Question: “Do you enjoy cooking?”
Honest negative: “Not especially — I’m quite lazy in the kitchen, to be honest. I usually order delivery or eat at my parents’ place on Sundays. That said, I can make a decent omelette when I have to.”

Why this works: Direct honesty + extension + slight positive = natural, fluent answer. Never invent passion you cannot sustain in follow-ups.

115.9 Handling Unfamiliar Topics

If asked about something you rarely consider (e.g., singing, museums):

  1. Acknowledge honestly: “I don’t do that very often, actually.”
  2. Redirect with related experience: “But I do enjoy listening to music when I commute.”
  3. Speculate lightly: “I suppose I’d like to try it if I had a patient teacher.”

Do not: Say only “I don’t know” and stop.

115.10 Memorisation Traps

Examiners detect: - Scripted intros unrelated to the question - Topic mismatch (answer about “travel” when asked about “reading”) - Flat intonation on supposedly personal content - Grammar too perfect for spontaneous speech followed by breakdown in Part 3

Safe approach: Memorise structures and phrases, not full answers. Rotate examples.

115.11 Interaction Skills

Part 1 is a dialogue: - Listen to the full question; answer what was asked. - Don’t interrupt the examiner. - Eye contact (cultural norms permitting) shows confidence. - React naturally to surprising questions — brief “That’s an interesting question” is acceptable once per test, not every turn.

115.12 Common Part 1 Errors by Band

Band area Typical Part 1 behaviour
5 Mostly short; repetition; limited vocabulary
6 Willing to extend but formulaic; some errors
7 Fluent with occasional hesitation; varied vocabulary
8+ Natural, flexible, precise; smooth self-correction

Examples

Example 1: AEE Applied — Work

Q: “Do you work or are you a student?”
A: “I’m working full-time as a junior accountant at a logistics firm.”
E: “I chose accounting because I was always good with numbers, and this industry is quite fast-paced, which suits me.”
Ex: “For instance, last month I helped reconcile shipping invoices for three warehouses — it was stressful but satisfying.”

Example 2: Preference Question

Q: “Do you prefer hot or cold weather?”
Answer: “Definitely cold weather — I find heat draining, especially when humidity is high. In cold months I can layer up and stay active outdoors. Summer where I live gets uncomfortable; I tend to stay indoors with the air conditioning on.”

Example 3: Negative Preference

Q: “Do you like shopping?”
Answer: “Not really — crowded malls overwhelm me, and I hate queuing. I shop online for clothes and only visit physical stores when I need to try something on, like shoes.”

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Turning a Band 5 Answer into Band 7

Question: “How often do you use your phone?”

Band 5: “Every day. Many times.”

Revision steps: 1. Add frequency phrase: “Pretty much constantly throughout the day.” 2. Add reason: “I need it for work messages and navigation.” 3. Add example/limit: “I try to put it away after nine p.m., though, so I can sleep properly.”

Band 7 target: “I’d say I’m on my phone throughout the day — mainly for work emails and maps when I’m travelling between sites. I do try to disconnect after nine in the evening because otherwise I struggle to fall asleep.”

Worked Example 2: Follow-Up Chain

Topic: Hometown

# Question Strategy
1 Where’s your hometown? Direct location + size
2 What do you like about it? One like + example place
3 Has it changed much? Compare past/present
4 Would you live there in future? Opinion + condition

Planning note: Question 3 and 4 can share the same example (new metro system) if developed differently.

Worked Example 3: Self-Correction Without Panic

Mid-answer error: “I have went to the gym…”

Self-correction: “Sorry — I went to the gym yesterday, actually, for a yoga class.”

WHY: Light self-correction shows GRA awareness; apologising repeatedly hurts FC.

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — AEE Construction (Questions 1–10)

  1. Do you live in a house or an apartment?
  2. What do you usually do on weekends?
  3. Do you prefer mornings or evenings?
  4. How do you usually travel to work or school?

  6. What’s your favourite type of food?
  7. Do you like your name?
  8. How often do you watch TV or streaming services?
  9. Do you prefer spending time alone or with others?
  10. Is there anything you’d like to change about your daily routine?

Exercise Set B — Error Correction (Questions 11–16)

Improve these Part 1 answers:

  1. “Yes.” (Q: Do you like music?)
  2. “I am living in Tashkent since five years.”
  3. “Shopping is boring boring boring for me.”
  4. “I very like swimming because it is good.”
  5. “My hometown is good. Good people. Good food.” (Q: What do you like about your hometown?)
  6. 90-second answer about tea when asked only “Do you drink tea?”

Exercise Set C — Topic Cluster Mapping (Questions 17–22)

For each question, name the topic cluster (A/B/C/D from section 115.5):

  1. “Do you use public transport much?”
  2. “What’s your favourite subject?”
  3. “Do you often visit museums?”
  4. “Describe your favourite room.”
  5. “Do you work or study?”
  6. “How do you usually relax?”

Exercise Set D — Difficult Questions (Questions 23–28)

Plan honest 3-sentence answers for:

  1. “Do you enjoy dancing?” (you don’t)
  2. “Do you play a musical instrument?” (you don’t)
  3. “Do you like art?” (you rarely think about it)
  4. “Are you good at saving money?” (you’re not)
  5. “Do you enjoy crowded places?” (you dislike them)
  6. “Do you often give presentations?” (never)

Solutions (with WHY)

Set A (sample answers)

  1. Sample: “I live in a rented apartment near the city centre. It’s on the sixth floor, so I get quite a lot of light, which I appreciate. My favourite spot is the small balcony where I keep a few herbs.”

WHY: Fact + detail + personal touch = natural Band 7 pattern.

  1. Sample: “On Saturdays I usually sleep in, then meet friends for lunch. Sundays are quieter — I cook something simple and prepare for the week ahead.”

Set B

  1. Improved: “Yes — I’m especially into jazz and lo-fi beats when I’m working. I discovered a Korean pianist on a streaming playlist last year and listen to her almost daily.”

  2. Fixed: “I’ve lived in Tashkent for five years.” — Present perfect for duration.

  3. Fixed: Replace repetition with reason: “Shopping frustrates me because I dislike browsing without a clear goal.”

  4. Fixed: “I really enjoy swimming because it’s refreshing and low-impact on my knees.”

  5. Expanded: Name specifics: people, dish, atmosphere — one sentence each layer.

  6. Trimmed: “Yes, I drink tea most mornings — usually green tea without sugar. I rarely have it in the evening because caffeine keeps me awake.”

Set C

  1. D | 18. B | 19. C | 20. A | 21. B | 22. C

Set D (strategy notes)

  1. Acknowledge + related (enjoy watching) + open to trying.
  2. Acknowledge + enjoy listening + childhood stopped.
  3. Limited exposure + memorable exhibition + would visit more.
  4. Honest struggle + mobile banking helps + goal to improve.
  5. Dislike + reason (noise) + prefer quiet cafes/parks.
  6. Rarely + workplace meetings only + would like practice.

Review

  • Part 1 = 4–5 minutes, familiar topics, 2–4 sentences per answer.
  • Use AEE: Answer, Extend, Example.
  • Prepare topic clusters, not scripts.
  • Negative/unfamiliar answers are fine if developed honestly.
  • Tense accuracy and natural vocabulary beat rare words.
  • Listen and answer the actual question.

Quiz

  1. What does AEE stand for?
  2. Ideal sentence count for most Part 1 answers?
  3. How many questions typically on one topic before switching?
  4. What tense for “I’ve lived here since 2019”?
  5. Is saying “I don’t really do that” acceptable?
  6. Name two topic clusters.
  7. Why are one-word answers risky?
  8. What is a follow-up question?
  9. Should you memorise full Part 1 scripts?
  10. Which part follows Part 1?

Assignment

  1. Record 20 Part 1 answers (2 minutes total speaking spread across questions). Use AEE. Replay and mark FC/LR/GRA/P.

  2. Build a Part 1 idea bank: 4 clusters × 5 bullet points of personal facts you can reuse.

  3. Practise with a partner: 3 topic changes, 4 questions each, strict timing. Partner must flag answers under 2 sentences.

  4. Complete the question bank in Chapter 116 for timed drills (10 questions daily for one week).

Revision Notes

PART 1 STRATEGIES

4–5 min | familiar topics
AEE: Answer → Extend → Example
2–4 sentences | 20–40 sec each
Clusters: home | work/study | leisure | daily life
Honest negatives OK if developed
Structures yes, full scripts no
Self-correct once, move on
Listen → answer exact question

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Your first sentence must answer the question — examiners note directness immediately.

Exam Strategy: If you use a prepared example, adapt it to the exact wording — mismatch is a memorisation red flag.

Exam Strategy: Don’t ask “Should I say more?” — extend naturally; the examiner will interrupt if needed.

Exam Strategy: Warm up your voice before the test — hum, read aloud, or chat in English for 10 minutes.

Challenge Questions

  1. Why might a candidate who speaks English daily at work still score Band 6.0 in Part 1?

  2. Design five follow-up questions an examiner might ask after “Do you enjoy cooking?” — and sketch ideal answer angles for each.

  3. Compare Part 1 development strategy with Part 3 — what changes and what stays the same?

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 Part 1 answers feel effortlessly personal — small specific details (“a café on the corner that closes at four”) without rehearsed polish.

Band 9 Secret: High-band speakers vary sentence openings — not every answer begins with “Yes, I…” or “Well, I think…”

Band 9 Secret: They match register to topic — casual tone for hobbies, slightly more formal for work/study, never stiff or academic in Part 1.

Band 9 Model — Part 1 Mini-Set (original)

Q: “Do you prefer texting or calling?”
A: “It depends on the situation, really. If I need a quick confirmation — like running late for dinner — I’ll text. But if something’s complicated or emotional, I’d rather call because tone gets lost in messages. My mother, for instance, still prefers long phone calls on Sundays, and I’ve got used to that ritual.”

Q: “Has your preference changed over time?”
A: “Definitely. When I was a teenager I avoided phone calls entirely; now I appreciate them more, especially for staying in touch with relatives abroad. Video calls have become part of that too — we schedule them so time zones align.”

WHY Band 9: Natural qualification, clear examples, flexible grammar, zero strain.

Chapter 116: Speaking Part 1 Question Bank (500+)

Part: 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

  • Practise 500+ Part 1 questions across everyday topics
  • Internalise a flexible answer architecture (answer → detail → example → reflect)
  • Maintain fluency without sounding memorised

Theory (quick)

Part 1 lasts 4–5 minutes. Keep answers extended but natural (2–4 sentences). Avoid one-word replies and avoid Task 2 lectures.

Question Bank with Band 9 Models

Topic: Hometown

Q1. Do you like hometown?

Band 9 model answer
Well, regarding hometown, I’d say it depends on the day, but generally I try to be intentional about it. For example, I usually approach it in a practical way: I notice what actually improves my routine rather than what looks impressive. That said, I’m not rigid — if circumstances change, I’m happy to adapt. Overall, it’s something I value because it quietly shapes how productive and balanced I feel.
