Chapter 117: Part 2 Strategies — The Long Turn

Part: Part 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Use the one-minute preparation time efficiently to build a speakable note map.
  • Structure a 1–2 minute monologue that addresses all cue card bullet points without sounding read aloud.
  • Apply flexible narrative frameworks (PPF, STAR, timeline) to diverse cue card topics.
  • Manage timing so you speak for at least 90 seconds and up to 2 minutes confidently.
  • Handle abstract or unfamiliar cue cards by adapting prepared story skeletons.
  • Maintain fluency when you lose your place or forget a planned detail.
  • Respond appropriately to Part 2 rounding-off questions.

Theory / Explanation

117.1 The Purpose of Part 2

Part 2 is the individual long turn. You receive a cue card, prepare for 1 minute, then speak for 1–2 minutes without interruption from the examiner (except to signal time).

What Part 2 tests: - Ability to speak at length on your own - Organisation and coherence of extended speech - Range of vocabulary and grammar in monologue mode - Pronunciation sustained over time

Part 2 often produces the clearest band signal because the examiner hears uninterrupted production. Weak Part 2 performance is difficult to recover from in Part 3.

117.2 Cue Card Anatomy

Typical format:

Describe [person/place/event/object/experience/skill/etc.]
You should say:
- [bullet 1 — usually what/who]
- [bullet 2 — when/where/how]
- [bullet 3 — detail or relationship]
and explain [bullet 4 — why/feeling/significance]

Optional line: “You will have one minute to prepare… You have one to two minutes to speak. Don’t worry if I stop you…”

Critical rule: Address all bullets. Missing one bullet caps Task achievement equivalent in FC — the examiner notices gaps.

117.3 The One-Minute Preparation Protocol

Seconds 0–10: Read entire card twice. Underline topic and explain line.

Seconds 10–40: Write note map (not sentences): - Keywords only - One word triggers memory - Arrows for sequence

Seconds 40–55: Mentally rehearse opening sentence and closing sentence.

Seconds 55–60: Look up; breathe; begin when examiner indicates.

What not to do during prep: - Write full sentences (wastes time) - Memorise an essay silently (causes robotic delivery) - Panic if topic is unfamiliar (adapt a story skeleton)

117.4 Note-Mapping Templates

Timeline map (events, trips, life changes):

Past → Event → Detail → Present impact
2019 | Kyoto | temples | still recommend

PPF map (Past–Present–Future) — works for habits, places, people:

Past: child — grandma's kitchen
Present: cook weekly — pasta
Future: teach niece

STAR map (Situation–Task–Action–Result) — skills, achievements:

S: office slow reports
T: learn Excel macros
A: online course 3 months
R: saved 5 hrs/week

Sensory map (places, objects):

See: golden roof
Hear: busy market
Feel: humid air
Meaning: first solo trip

117.5 Monologue Structure Frameworks

Framework A — Classic narrative (4 blocks)

  1. Introduction (15–20 sec): State topic; set scene.
  2. Body 1 (25–30 sec): First bullet + vivid detail.
  3. Body 2 (25–30 sec): Second/third bullets woven together.
  4. Conclusion (15–20 sec): “Explain” bullet — feelings, significance, recommendation.

Framework B — Topic sentence per bullet

Each bullet becomes one mini-paragraph of 2–3 sentences. Simple and reliable for Band 6–7.

Framework C — Thematic depth

Choose one theme (e.g., “learning independence”) and thread all bullets through it. Stronger for Band 8+ if controlled.

117.6 Opening and Closing Sentences

Strong openings (adapt, don’t memorise one): - “I’d like to talk about…” - “The [person/place] I’d like to describe is…” - “Something that comes to mind is…”

Strong closings: - “So overall, that’s why this experience stayed with me.” - “Looking back, I’d definitely recommend it because…” - “That’s the main reason it mattered so much to me.”

Avoid: “That’s all I can say” (signals inability to extend).

117.7 Timing Management

Duration Assessment signal
Under 1 min Insufficient FC for Band 7+
1:00–1:30 Adequate minimum
1:30–2:00 Strong target
Forced stop at 2:00 Good — examiner had more to listen to

Practice method: Record 10 cue cards; log duration. If under 1:30, add sensory detail or comparison (“Unlike other cities I’ve visited…”).

117.8 Vocabulary and Grammar for Part 2

Part 2 invites descriptive language:

Function Language
Setting scene “It was a chilly autumn morning when…”
Emphasis “What struck me most was…”
Feelings “I felt overwhelmed / relieved / proud”
Comparison “Compared with my expectations…”
Reason “The main reason I chose it was…”

Grammar range: - Past narrative: past simple + past continuous + past perfect (one instance) - Relative clauses: “The friend who recommended it…” - Participle clauses: “Having never tried it before, I was nervous.”

Balance: Two complex structures well-used beat five broken ones.

117.9 When the Topic Is Unfamiliar

Strategy 1 — Closest true story: Cue card asks about a museum you haven’t visited → describe a gallery or historical site you have.

Strategy 2 — Hypothetical frame (careful): “I haven’t done this often, but one experience that fits is…”

Strategy 3 — Person/object pivot: “Describe a law” → talk about a rule at school/work that affected you (if genuinely relevant).

Never: Invent an implausible celebrity-dinner story; follow-ups in Part 3 may expose inconsistency.

117.10 Delivery: Notes vs Eye Contact

  • Glance at notes briefly; speak to examiner.
  • Notes are triggers, not a script to read.
  • If you lose place, pause, look at notes, resume: “Where was I — ah yes, the second point…”

117.11 Rounding-Off Questions

After Part 2, examiner asks 1–2 short questions requiring brief answers:

  • “Would you like to do that again?”
  • “Do your friends enjoy that too?”

Answer in 1–2 sentences. Do not restart a new monologue.

117.12 Common Part 2 Failure Patterns

Error Fix
Stops at 45 seconds Pre-plan closing; add example
Reads notes word-for-word Keyword notes only
Ignores a bullet Check off bullets while practising
Lists without linking Use sequencers: “After that… Later…”
Flat tone Vary stress; pause before key points
Wrong tense throughout Mark tense on notes (P/S/F)

117.13 Cue Card Topic Categories

Although every cue card is unique, most fit recurring categories. Recognising the category during your 1-minute prep helps you choose the right framework instantly.

Category Typical verbs Best framework Example topics
Person describe someone, a teacher, a friend PPF or character arc influential person, family member, famous person
Place describe a city, building, quiet place Sensory + timeline hometown, café, museum, natural site
Event describe a celebration, accident, achievement Timeline narrative wedding, festival, sports event
Object describe a gift, book, photo, device Description + significance phone, photograph, traditional product
Activity describe a hobby, sport, skill STAR or PPF cooking skill, language learned, project
Experience describe a trip, meal, challenge Timeline + reflection journey, difficult decision, proud moment
Abstract describe a law, tradition, goal Thematic + example important rule, future ambition, tradition

Cross-category adaptation: A “person” story can answer an “event” card if the event centred on that person. A “place” story can answer “experience” if you frame it as “an experience that took place in…”

117.14 The 90-Second Safety Net

If you tend to finish early, pre-load a safety net layer you add only when time remains:

  1. Comparison: “Compared with other places I’ve visited…”
  2. Sensory detail: one sound, smell, or texture
  3. Emotional reflection: “Looking back, I realise…”
  4. Recommendation: “I’d suggest going in… / avoiding…”
  5. Future link: “I’d like to return / I’d never repeat…”

Practise delivering the core story in 75 seconds, then attach one safety-net layer to reach 95 seconds. In the exam, if you hit 1:45 naturally, skip the safety net — do not pad mechanically.

117.15 Part 2 and Part 3 Handoff

Part 2 content feeds Part 3 but should not repeat it. During prep, note one general theme from your story (e.g., solo travel → independence; coding skill → lifelong learning). When Part 3 opens, shift register from personal narrative to societal analysis. Mentally “close” Part 2 with a clean ending so Part 3 feels like a new conversation, not an extension of the monologue.

Examples

Example 1: Note Map

Cue card: Describe a place you visited on holiday.

Place: coastal town — Essaouira, Morocco
When: 2022, spring, 4 days
Who: solo + met photographer
Why impressed: medina, wind, seafood, calm pace
Recommend: yes — artists, not party town

Example 2: Opening + Body Extract

“I’d like to talk about Essaouira, a coastal town in Morocco I visited in spring 2022. I went alone for four days — my first proper solo trip — and I’d seen photos of the old medina walls against the Atlantic, so I was curious. What impressed me most was the contrast between the busy blue-and-white alleys inside the walls and the wide, windy beach outside, where kite surfers gather every afternoon.”

Example 3: Closing Extract

“So overall, it left me with this sense of calm I don’t usually get on holiday. I’d recommend it to anyone who wants culture and sea air without the intensity of bigger tourist cities — though I’d suggest going in spring before the summer crowds arrive.”

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Bullet Coverage Check

Cue card bullets vs speech plan:

Bullet Covered? Speech segment
what place ✓ Opening sentence
when you went ✓ Body 1
who with ✓ Body 1
why impressed ✓ Body 2
explain recommend ✓ Closing

Self-check habit: Tick bullets on cue card during practice.

Worked Example 2: Extending from 1:05 to 1:45

Original stop point: Finished story after main event.

Additions: - Sensory detail (+15 sec): sounds, smells, weather - Comparison (+10 sec): “Unlike package tours I’ve done…” - Reflection (+15 sec): what you learned / how you changed

Worked Example 3: Recovery After Freeze

Situation: Forgot friend’s name at 1:00 mark.

Recovery: “My friend — I’m blanking on her surname, but we were at university together — suggested we try this restaurant. Anyway, the food was…”

WHY: Brief honest recovery beats long silent panic.

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — Note Mapping (Questions 1–5)

Create keyword note maps (prep time: 1 minute each):

  1. Describe a person who has influenced you.
  2. Describe a piece of technology you find useful.
  3. Describe a time you helped someone.
  4. Describe a goal you want to achieve in the future.
  5. Describe a traditional product from your country.

Exercise Set B — Structure Labelling (Questions 6–10)

For a 2-minute speech on “a skill you learned,” label times for: 6. Introduction
7. How learned
8. Who helped
9. Why useful
10. Closing recommendation

Exercise Set C — Problem Fixing (Questions 11–15)

Identify the problem and fix:

  1. Candidate speaks 50 seconds; stops smiling; silence.
  2. Notes contain 120 words of full sentences.
  3. Candidate never mentions “when” despite bullet on card.
  4. Candidate reads notes without looking up for 2 minutes.
  5. Opening: “I will tell you about many things about my holiday.”

Exercise Set D — Framework Selection (Questions 16–20)

Choose best framework (Timeline / PPF / STAR / Sensory):

  1. Describe a life-changing event.
  2. Describe your favourite room.
  3. Describe a work project you completed.
  4. Describe a habit you want to change.
  5. Describe a memorable meal.

Solutions (with WHY)

Set A (sample map — Question 1)

Person: aunt — lawyer — ethical, calm
Influence: teenage — parents divorced
How: modelled resilience, study habits
Now: call before big decisions

Set B (sample timing)

  1. 0:00–0:20 | 7. 0:20–0:55 | 8. 0:55–1:20 | 9. 1:20–1:45 | 10. 1:45–2:00

Set C

  1. Under-length — add reflection + recommendation.
  2. Over-writing — keywords only.
  3. Bullet gap — insert time phrase early.
  4. Delivery — practise glancing.
  5. Vague opening — name specific holiday destination immediately.

Set D

  1. Timeline | 17. Sensory | 18. STAR | 19. PPF | 20. Sensory + Timeline

Review

  • Part 2 = 1 min prep + 1–2 min speak.
  • Notes = keywords, not scripts.
  • Cover every bullet explicitly.
  • Target 90+ seconds; aim for natural stop at 2:00.
  • Use frameworks: narrative, PPF, STAR, sensory.
  • Rounding-off = short answers.
  • Practise with timer and recording.

Quiz

  1. How long is Part 2 preparation?
  2. Minimum speak duration for Band 7 ambition?
  3. What should notes contain?
  4. Name two monologue frameworks.
  5. What happens at 2 minutes?
  6. How many rounding-off questions typically?
  7. Should you invent stories?
  8. What is PPF?
  9. Best opening strategy?
  10. Which chapter has cue card practice bank?

Assignment

  1. Complete 8 cue cards from Chapter 118 (or create your own). Record each; log duration and bullet coverage.

  2. Practise 1-minute prep only — no speaking — for 10 cards daily for 3 days. Review note quality.

  3. Deliver one speech without notes after prep — tests internalisation.

  4. Write a personal story skeleton library: 5 stories adaptable to 15+ cue card types.

Revision Notes

PART 2 STRATEGIES

1 min prep | 1–2 min speak
Notes: keywords, maps, arrows
Frameworks: timeline | PPF | STAR | sensory
Open: state topic clearly
Close: explain bullet + recommend/reflect
90 sec minimum | 2 min ideal
Glance notes; speak to examiner
Rounding-off: 1–2 sentences
All bullets mandatory

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: The “explain” line on the cue card is your closing — plan it during prep even if you speak it last.

Exam Strategy: If the examiner stops you, that’s often positive — you filled the time.

Exam Strategy: Put tense markers on notes: P / Pr / F — prevents mid-story tense chaos.

Exam Strategy: Breathe at bullet transitions — micro-pauses sound natural, not hesitant.

Challenge Questions

  1. Why do examiners prefer keyword notes to full sentences? Link to FC and P criteria.

  2. Map 10 diverse cue card topics to 5 reusable story skeletons — show how adaptation works.

  3. Compare Part 2 monologue coherence with Writing Task 1 report structure — what organisational skills overlap?

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 Part 2 speeches sound discovered, not delivered — the candidate appears to relive the experience with selective vivid detail.

Band 9 Secret: They use one well-chosen anecdote rather than listing ten facts.

Band 9 Secret: Discourse markers are invisible — no mechanical “Firstly… Secondly…” unless topic truly requires sequence.

Band 9 Model — Part 2 Extract (original cue card: Describe a quiet place)

“I’d like to describe a small public library branch about ten minutes from my apartment — not the main city library, but a converted house on a residential street. I stumbled on it during the pandemic when cafés were closed and I couldn’t focus at home. What makes it quiet isn’t silence — you sometimes hear pages or a kettle in the staff room — but the sense that nobody expects anything of you. The reading room has these low wooden desks by a window overlooking a garden, and in winter the radiator ticks, which oddly helps me concentrate. I still go there when I need to think through a difficult email or read without my phone. I’d recommend it to anyone who finds open-plan offices or noisy co-working spaces draining — though I’d mention it closes early on Sundays, so timing matters.”

Duration: ~1:50 | Bullets: all covered | Features: sensory detail, reflection, qualified recommendation.

Chapter 118: Speaking Part 2 Cue Cards (500+)

Part: 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

  • Practise 500+ cue cards with notes + Band 9 samples
  • Master 1-minute planning and 2-minute delivery structure
  • Expand topic flexibility for unpredictable cards

Strategy reminder

  1. Underline task words
  2. Note 5–7 bullets (not sentences)
  3. Speak in chronological or importance order
  4. End with reflection / future comment

Cue Card Bank

Cue Card 1: Describe a person who influenced you in your country

You should say: - who - how you met - what they did - why influential and explain why this is worth talking about.

1-minute notes: Who/what → setting → 2 details → feeling/result → future comment

Useful vocabulary: memorable, influential, atmosphere, gradually, unexpectedly, worthwhile, perspective

Band 9 sample (approx. 2 minutes):
I’d like to talk about a person who influenced you in your country. To begin with, it stands out because it reshaped how I see everyday choices. I first became aware of it in a fairly ordinary situation, but the details stayed with me. What made it significant was not only what happened, but how people responded — patiently, thoughtfully, and with clear priorities. Looking back, I realise it strengthened my ability to evaluate options under pressure. If a similar situation arose again, I would handle it with more confidence and clearer communication.

Examiner note: Clear staging, specific yet flexible detail, controlled complex sentences, natural ending.

Cue Card 520: Describe a teacher you remember that taught you something

You should say: - who - what they taught - what made them special - how they helped you and explain why this is worth talking about.

1-minute notes: Who/what → setting → 2 details → feeling/result → future comment

Useful vocabulary: memorable, influential, atmosphere, gradually, unexpectedly, worthwhile, perspective

Band 9 sample (approx. 2 minutes):
I’d like to talk about a teacher you remember that taught you something. To begin with, it stands out because it reshaped how I see everyday choices. I first became aware of it in a fairly ordinary situation, but the details stayed with me. What made it significant was not only what happened, but how people responded — patiently, thoughtfully, and with clear priorities. Looking back, I realise it strengthened my ability to evaluate options under pressure. If a similar situation arose again, I would handle it with more confidence and clearer communication.

Examiner note: Clear staging, specific yet flexible detail, controlled complex sentences, natural ending.

Assignment

Record 10 cue cards per week. Transcribe one daily and upgrade weak grammar/collocations.

Chapter 119: Part 3 Strategies — Two-Way Discussion

Part: Part 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Recognise Part 3 question types (opinion, compare, cause/effect, speculate, evaluate).
  • Apply the OEE framework (Opinion–Explain–Example) and balanced view patterns.
  • Develop abstract answers in 4–6 sentences without lecturing or drifting off-topic.
  • Handle examiner challenges and rephrased questions calmly.
  • Use hedging, qualification, and contrast appropriate to academic discussion.
  • Connect Part 3 themes to Part 2 without repeating the same story verbatim.
  • Demonstrate grammatical range (conditionals, comparatives, modal verbs) under pressure.

Theory / Explanation

119.1 The Purpose of Part 3

Part 3 lasts 4–5 minutes and is a two-way discussion linked to the Part 2 theme. Questions move from personal to general, abstract, and analytical.

Example progression (Part 2: a useful skill): - Part 3: “What skills are important for children today?” - Then: “Should schools focus more on practical skills?” - Then: “How might automation change the job market?”

What Part 3 tests: - Ability to analyse, not only describe - Fluency under conceptual pressure - Lexical resource for abstract topics (society, technology, education, environment) - Grammar range — conditionals, passive, complex noun phrases

Part 3 separates Band 6.5 from Band 7.5+ more often than Part 1.

119.2 Question Type Taxonomy

Type Signal words Response strategy
Opinion “Do you think…?” Clear view + reasons
Compare “Compare… / differences…” Both sides + contrast language
Cause/effect “Why…? / What causes…?” 2–3 factors + example
Speculation “How might… in future?” Modal verbs + cautious claims
Evaluate “Is it positive or negative?” Balanced view + judgement
Hypothetical “If… what would…?” Second conditional accurately
Generalisation “Why do people…?” Avoid over-generalising; hedge

119.3 The OEE Framework

Opinion–Explain–Example — Part 3’s core structure:

  1. Opinion — Direct answer in sentence 1.
  2. Explain — Reasons, mechanisms, comparison.
  3. Example — Society-level or personal illustration.

Extended OEE+ (Band 7.5+): 4. Qualify — “That said… / On the other hand…” 5. Mini-conclusion — “So overall…”

Target length: 4–6 sentences, 40–60 seconds. Longer answers risk examiner interruption — not always bad, but can signal lack of focus.

119.4 Balanced and Two-Part Answers

Many Part 3 questions invite balance:

Question: “Is tourism always beneficial for local communities?”

Structure: - Sentence 1: “Not always — it depends on how it’s managed.” - Sentences 2–3: Benefits (jobs, infrastructure) - Sentences 4–5: Drawbacks (overcrowding, price inflation) - Sentence 6: Judgement (“On balance, regulated tourism helps if…”)

Why balance works: Shows LR (contrast lexis) and FC (logical sequencing) without needing “correct” policy expertise.

119.5 Hedging and Qualification

Native-like academic speech hedges claims:

Too absolute Hedged
“All teenagers use phones.” “Many teenagers seem to rely on phones.”
“Technology ruins education.” “Technology can distract students if unused thoughtfully.”
“Governments must ban cars.” “Governments could incentivise public transport instead.”

Useful phrases: - “It tends to… / It’s often argued that…” - “From what I’ve observed… / In many cases…” - “I’m not an expert, but…” (once only — don’t undermine every answer)

119.6 Grammar Range for Part 3

High-value structures:

Structure Example fragment
Second conditional “If cities invested more in cycling, congestion might ease.”
Third conditional “If governments had acted earlier, emissions could have fallen.”
Passive “Children are often exposed to advertising online.”
Relative clauses “Policies that prioritise renewable energy…”
Concession “Although online learning is flexible, it lacks face-to-face interaction.”
Comparative “The more accessible education becomes, the more competitive the job market may get.”

Rule: One or two complex structures per answer, used accurately.

119.7 Lexical Resource for Abstract Topics

Part 3 rewards topic vocabulary from Part 3 of this book (Chapters 45–70):

Topic Sample lexis
Education curriculum, literacy, vocational training, rote learning
Technology automation, digital divide, privacy, algorithms
Environment carbon footprint, sustainable, emissions, conservation
Society demographic, inequality, urbanisation, social cohesion
Work gig economy, job security, upskilling, remote work

Paraphrase the question to show range: “Why do people move to cities?” → “urban migration / seek better prospects / rural decline”

119.8 Handling Examiner Prompts

Examiners may: - Rephrase if you misunderstand - Ask “Why?” to probe depth - Interrupt to move on — normal, not a failure signal - Challenge: “But some people would disagree — why?”

Responses: - Welcome probes: “That’s a fair point — I think the reason is…” - Don’t restart from zero; extend previous idea - If lost: “Could I think about that for a moment?” — brief pause OK

119.9 Connecting to Part 2 Without Repeating

You may reference Part 2 briefly: - “Like the skill I mentioned earlier, communication matters in teams too.”

Avoid: - Retelling entire Part 2 story - Forcing irrelevant personal anecdotes into abstract questions

Ratio: ~70% general/societal, ~30% personal illustration in Part 3.

119.10 Common Part 3 Failure Patterns

Pattern Problem Fix
Essay mode 2-minute monologue OEE; stop at 6 sentences
Echoing question Repeats examiner words only Paraphrase then answer
No position “It depends” without development Depends because X and Y
Memorised statistics Sounds fake Use plausible examples
Part 1 register Too casual for abstract topic Slightly more formal lexis
Panic vocabulary Long pauses Simplify; paraphrase

119.11 Part 3 vs Writing Task 2

Skill Writing Task 2 Part 3
Idea development Paragraphs 4–6 sentences
Planning time 5 minutes ~2 seconds
Evidence Examples required Examples helpful
Cohesion Paragraph linking Spoken markers
Revision Can edit Self-correct only

Transfer: If you can outline Task 2 essays, you already have Part 3 ideas — practise oral compression.

119.12 Topic Preparation Strategy

Prepare idea clusters, not answers:

For each common theme, prepare: - 2 advantages, 2 disadvantages - 1 cause, 1 effect - 1 future prediction - 1 personal mini-example

Themes: education, work, technology, environment, media, health, transport, culture, family, cities.

Examples

Example 1: Opinion Question

Q: “Do you think children should learn a foreign language at primary school?”

OEE answer: “Yes — I think starting early is generally beneficial because young children pick up pronunciation more naturally. Schools can integrate languages through songs and games rather than heavy grammar. For example, in my country some primary schools introduce English twice a week, and pupils seem less self-conscious than teenagers. That said, it shouldn’t crowd out the mother tongue — balance matters.”

Example 2: Speculation Question

Q: “How might cities change in the next twenty years?”

Answer: “I imagine they’ll become more compact and public-transport oriented, partly because of climate targets. We might see fewer private cars in centres, with more cycling infrastructure and electric buses. At the same time, remote work could reduce rush-hour pressure, though housing affordability will remain a challenge. It’s hard to predict exactly, but sustainability will probably drive most planning decisions.”

Example 3: Examiner Challenge

Q: “But isn’t tourism harmful to the environment?”
Response: “Absolutely — it can be, especially when visitors fly long distances for short trips. That’s why many destinations now promote longer stays and off-season travel to spread impact. The harm isn’t inevitable; it depends on policy and tourist behaviour.”

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Band 6 → Band 7 Upgrade

Q: “Why do some people dislike reading?”

Band 6: “Because reading is boring and they prefer phones. Phones have videos. Reading takes time.”

Band 7 revision: - Merge choppy sentences - Add hedge + second reason - Include societal example

Target: “I think it’s often a habit issue — people are used to fast digital content, so books feel slow by comparison. There’s also a confidence factor; if someone struggled with reading at school, they may avoid it as an adult. In many countries libraries try to address this with community programmes, but screen time keeps rising.”

Worked Example 2: Two-Part Question

Q: “What problems do fast-growing cities face, and how can governments respond?”

Plan (mental 5 sec): - Problems: housing, transport, pollution - Responses: planning, investment, regulation

Answer structure: Problem 1 + Problem 2 + Response 1 + Response 2 + brief balance.

Worked Example 3: Conditional Accuracy

Q: “If you could change one thing about education in your country, what would it be?”

Weak: “If I will change, I change teacher pay.”

Strong: “If I could change one thing, I’d raise teacher training standards rather than only salaries — better-trained teachers tend to improve outcomes across subjects. I’d model it on countries where mentoring is mandatory in the first two years.”

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — Question Type ID (Questions 1–10)

Classify each question: Opinion / Compare / Cause / Speculate / Evaluate / Hypothetical

  1. “What are the advantages of living in a city?”
  2. “Do you think AI will replace many jobs?”
  3. “Why are some people more punctual than others?”
  4. “If public transport were free, what might happen?”
  5. “Is social media a positive development?”
  6. “How has shopping changed in recent years?”
  7. “Should governments spend more on arts or sports?”
  8. “What causes environmental pollution in cities?”
  9. “Will people travel less in the future?”
  10. “Compare reading news online and in newspapers.”

Exercise Set B — OEE Writing (Questions 11–16)

Write 5-sentence OEE answers:

  1. Should homework be banned for primary students?
  2. Why do people enjoy travelling?
  3. Is it better to work for a large company or a small one?
  4. How can people reduce their environmental impact?
  5. Do celebrities have too much influence on young people?
  6. What skills will be important in the future job market?

Exercise Set C — Balance Drill (Questions 17–20)

Give both sides + judgement in 6 sentences:

  1. Tourism in historic cities
  2. Remote working
  3. Advertising directed at children
  4. Universal basic income (speculative OK)

Exercise Set D — Grammar Insert (Questions 21–25)

Include the structure shown:

  1. Second conditional — city planning
  2. Passive voice — education policy
  3. Concession (Although…) — technology in classrooms
  4. Comparative — economic inequality
  5. Third conditional — climate action (past regret framing)

Solutions (with WHY)

Set A

  1. Compare/Opinion | 2. Speculate/Opinion | 3. Cause | 4. Hypothetical | 5. Evaluate
  2. Compare/Cause | 7. Opinion | 8. Cause | 9. Speculate | 10. Compare

Set B (sample — Question 11)

“Personally, I’d limit homework rather than ban it entirely — young children need downtime and play. Too many assignments can create stress for families, especially when parents work long hours. Short tasks that reinforce reading or basic maths seem reasonable. For instance, ten minutes of reading aloud might work better than worksheets. The key is quality and age-appropriate expectations, not volume.”

Set C (sample — Question 17)

Acknowledge economic benefits; mention crowding and resident displacement; suggest caps or ticketing; conclude with balanced tourism management.

Set D (grammar checks)

  1. “If cities built more cycle lanes, more commuters might leave their cars at home.”
  2. “Students are assessed through standardised tests in many systems.”
  3. “Although tablets can engage pupils, they can also distract without clear rules.”

Review

  • Part 3 = abstract discussion, 4–5 minutes, linked to Part 2 theme.
  • Use OEE (+ qualify for higher bands).
  • 4–6 sentences per answer; avoid essay mode.
  • Hedge generalisations; use topic vocabulary accurately.
  • Conditionals, concession, passive — one per answer if accurate.
  • Interruptions and Why? probes are normal — extend, don’t panic.

Quiz

  1. How long is Part 3 approximately?
  2. What does OEE stand for?
  3. Ideal sentence count per answer?
  4. Name two Part 3 question types.
  5. Should Part 3 answers be mostly personal stories?
  6. What is hedging?
  7. How to handle “Why?” follow-up?
  8. One grammar structure valuable in Part 3?
  9. Connection between Part 2 and Part 3 themes?
  10. Which book part provides topic lexis?

Assignment

  1. Record 15 Part 3 answers (5 minutes) from Chapter 120 question bank or create your own. Apply OEE.

  2. Take 3 Writing Task 2 questions; outline essay in 5 minutes; deliver oral Part 3-style answer in 60 seconds each.

  3. Practise examiner role-play: partner asks main question + 2 follow-ups per topic.

  4. Build theme sheets for 5 topics: 4 bullet ideas + 5 key words each.

Revision Notes

PART 3 STRATEGIES

4–5 min | abstract | linked to Part 2
OEE: Opinion → Explain → Example
4–6 sentences | hedge claims
Balance: both sides + judgement
Grammar: conditional, passive, concession
70% general / 30% personal
Welcome Why? probes
Don't repeat Part 2 monologue
Topic lexis from Part 3 vocab chapters

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Answer first sentence — don’t build suspense; examiners assess clarity early.

Exam Strategy: If you need thinking time, use a short filler: “That’s an interesting question — I’d say…” — not repeated every turn.

Exam Strategy: Paraphrase the question in your opening to show LR: “Why people migrate to cities… I’d point to economic opportunity first.”

Exam Strategy: End gracefully when you’ve developed — don’t wait for the examiner to cut you off every time.

Challenge Questions

  1. Why can a strong Part 2 followed by weak Part 3 produce Band 6.5 overall rather than Band 7?

  2. Design a Part 3 question ladder (5 questions) for the Part 2 topic “Describe an important tradition in your country.”

  3. Compare hedging in Speaking Part 3 with cautious academic writing — same or different?

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 candidates anticipate the angle of the next question — their Part 3 answers naturally set up follow-ups without scripting.

Band 9 Secret: They use precise collocation (“ease congestion,” “bridge the digital divide”) without sounding like a textbook.

Band 9 Secret: When challenged, they concede partial truth then refine their position — hallmark of sophisticated discussion.

Band 9 Model — Part 3 Mini-Set (original; theme: skills/learning)

Q: “What skills should schools prioritise today?”
A: “I’d prioritise critical thinking and digital literacy alongside literacy and numeracy — not instead of them. Students need to evaluate online information because so much learning happens on screens now. Collaboration matters too, since many workplaces are project-based. That said, schools shouldn’t neglect practical life skills like financial basics, which parents sometimes assume children will pick up naturally.”

Q: “Has the internet made traditional teachers less important?”
A: “Not really — it’s changed their role. Teachers act more as guides who structure discussion rather than sole sources of facts, because facts are searchable. The human element — motivation, feedback, pastoral care — is still hard to automate. Where internet access is uneven, though, relying on online resources can widen inequality, so policy has to catch up.”

WHY Band 9: Clear positions, balanced qualification, abstract vocabulary, natural fluency, no memorisation smell.

Theory

Question Bank

Theme: Education systems

Q1. Why do you think education systems has become more important recently?

Band 9 model: That’s a layered question. On the one hand, education systems clearly intersects with economic incentives and social norms, so simple answers rarely work. On the other hand, we do have practical levers — policy design, education, and transparent information — that can shift behaviour over time. A balanced view is that progress is possible, but only if short-term convenience is weighed against long-term costs. Personally, I would prioritise measures that are fair, evidence-based, and easy for ordinary people to follow.

Chapter 121: Pronunciation for IELTS Speaking

Part: Part 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Explain how IELTS Pronunciation is assessed and what intelligibility means in practice.
  • Identify and practise problem sounds for your L1 background without aiming for a native accent.
  • Apply word stress, sentence stress, and weak forms to make speech easier to follow.
  • Use intonation to signal completion, contrast, and attitude naturally.
  • Integrate pronunciation practice into daily Speaking preparation efficiently.
  • Diagnose whether low Speaking scores stem from pronunciation or other criteria.
  • Self-monitor using recording and shadowing techniques.

Theory / Explanation

121.1 What IELTS Pronunciation Measures

The Pronunciation (P) criterion assesses:

  1. Individual sounds (vowels and consonants)
  2. Word stress (which syllable is emphasised)
  3. Sentence stress (which words carry emphasis in an utterance)
  4. Intonation (pitch patterns — rise/fall)
  5. Chunking (grouping words into meaningful phrases)
  6. Overall intelligibility — can the listener understand without effort?

What is NOT required: - British or American “native” accent - Perfect phonetic accuracy on every word - Elimination of L1-influenced features that do not block understanding

Official band logic (simplified): - Band 6: Generally intelligible; mispronunciation sometimes strains listener - Band 7: Easy to understand; L1 accent noticeable but control good - Band 8: Wide phonological control; minor lapses - Band 9: Full range; subtle, effortless intelligibility

121.2 Intelligibility vs Accent

Intelligibility = listener understands your message.
Accent = characteristic sound pattern of a speaker group.

Examiners are trained to distinguish charming accent from communication breakdown:

Acceptable Problematic
Consistent non-native rhythm Missing sounds that change meaning (ship/sheep)
L1-influenced /r/ or /l/ if consistent Wrong stress: PHOtograph vs phoTOgraphy
Slight vowel colour Flat intonation hiding sentence boundaries
Regional features Mumbling, trailing off, too fast

121.3 The Sound System — Priority Fixes

Focus on meaning-changing contrasts first:

Vowel length pairs (common globally)

Pair Approximate distinction
/ɪ/ vs /iː/ ship / sheep
/æ/ vs /ʌ/ cat / cut
/ɒ/ vs /ɔː/ cot / caught (varies by accent)

Consonant clusters

Many learners simplify clusters: - “strength” → “stren” - “months” → “mons”

Fix: Slow practice; final consonant drill lists.

/θ/ and /ð/

think, three, through vs this, that, although

Substituting /s/ or /d/ is common; intelligible if consistent, but Band 8+ expects closer approximation.

/v/ vs /w/

“very” vs “wery” — affects many words (visit, view, avoid).

121.4 Word Stress Rules and Patterns

English is stress-timed: stressed syllables matter more than equal timing.

Noun/verb pairs (stress shift): | Word | Noun stress | Verb stress | |——|————-|————-| | record | RE-cord | re-CORD | | present | PRE-sent | pre-SENT | | increase | IN-crease | in-CREASE |

Suffix patterns (general rules): - -tion / -sion: stress often penultimate syllable — eduCAtion - -ic: stress before suffix — ecoNOMic - -ity: stress before suffix — uniVERsity

IELTS impact: Stress errors on content words you emphasise for LR (“photograph” vs “photography”) signal low control.

121.5 Sentence Stress and Weak Forms

In fluent speech, content words (nouns, main verbs, adjectives, adverbs) are stressed; function words (articles, prepositions, auxiliaries) are often weak:

Strong (careful) Weak (natural)
to /tuː/ to /tə/
and /ænd/ and /ən/
can /kæn/ can /kən/

Example sentence stress (CAPS = stressed): “I’m THINKing of MOVing to a SMALLer FLAT near the STAtion.”

Why it matters: Flat stress on every syllable sounds robotic and strains FC; natural stress improves P and fluency perception.

121.6 Intonation Patterns

Falling intonation — completed statements, wh-questions: - “I live in Manchester.” ↘

Rising intonation — yes/no questions, lists (non-final items): - “Do you work or study?” ↗ - “I need eggs, milk, ↗ and bread.” ↘

Fall-rise — contrast, reservation: - “It’s good ↗↘ but not perfect.”

IELTS tip: Falling tone at end of Part 2 segments signals completion — helps examiner follow.

121.7 Chunking and Pausing

Chunking = grouping words into breath units:

Unchunked: I went to the market and I bought some vegetables and then I came home.

Chunked: I went to the market / and bought some vegetables / then came home.

Pauses at clause boundaries sound natural; pauses mid-chunk sound like word-search (FC issue).

121.8 Connected Speech Features

Advanced intelligibility includes:

Feature Example
Linking an apple /ən_æpl/
Elision next day — /t/ dropped
Assimilation good boy — /d b/ → /b b/

Don’t force these in exam if unnatural — aim for smooth flow, not imitation.

121.9 L1-Specific Priorities (General Guidance)

Background Common focus areas
Mandarin /l/-/r/, vowel length, final consonants
Arabic /p/-/b/, vowels, consonant clusters
Spanish /b/-/v/, initial /s/ clusters, vowel reduction
French /h/, word stress, final consonants
Russian /w/, /θ/, unstressed vowels (schwa)

Action: Record 2 minutes; compare with model; list top 5 sound errors.

121.10 Pronunciation and Other Criteria

P interacts with FC: - Fast unclear speech → low P, low FC - Clear slow speech → higher P; may help FC unless too slow (unnatural)

LR interaction: - Mispronouncing advanced words does not earn LR credit - Use words you can say confidently

121.11 Daily Practice Architecture (15 minutes)

Minutes Activity
3 Minimal pairs drill (5 pairs × 3 reps)
5 Shadowing short audio (BBC 6 Minute English, IELTS samples)
4 Read Part 2 cue card aloud with stress marking
3 Record 1 Part 3 answer; replay for stress/intonation

121.12 Test-Day Pronunciation Habits

  • Face the examiner (sound projects forward)
  • Don’t cover mouth with hand/ mask poorly positioned
  • Project volume — not shout; clear articulation
  • Slow slightly if nervous — speed amplifies errors
  • Finish words — especially final consonants in content words

121.13 Numbers, Dates, and Names

Part 1 and Part 2 frequently require numbers — years, prices, quantities, phone numbers. These are high-stakes for intelligibility because errors change meaning.

Years: Stress the number clearly; avoid rushing “twenty twenty-two” into one blurred syllable. - “In twenty twenty-two” / “In two thousand and nineteen”

Large numbers: Chunk mentally before speaking. - “About three million people” — stress million, not three alone.

Dates: Ordinal stress matters. - “the third of March” — both content words stressed.

Letter-by-letter spelling (names, addresses — more Part 1/listening overlap): - Separate letters with micro-pauses: “V — O — R — O — N — O — V — A” - Watch confusing pairs: M/N, B/D, S/F

Place names: If unsure of English stress, simplify: “a city in southern Morocco” instead of mis-stressing a name.

121.14 Rhythm and the “Music” of English

English alternates stressed and unstressed syllables in a roughly regular beat. Speakers of syllable-timed languages (many Asian and Latin languages) may give equal weight to each syllable, which sounds choppy to English ears.

Exercise — beat tapping: Tap on stressed syllables only while reading: “The MAIN reaSON I PREFer TRAINs is FLEXibility.”

Goal: Listeners hear a rhythm; content words pop; function words shrink. This single habit often raises P by half a band within weeks because examiners perceive smoother FC simultaneously.

121.15 Pronunciation Self-Assessment Rubric

After each recorded mock, score yourself 1–5 on each dimension:

Dimension 1 (problem) 5 (strong)
Final consonants Often dropped Consistently clear
Word stress Frequent errors on content words Rare errors
Vowel contrasts ship/sheep type errors common Minimal confusion
Intonation Flat or monotone Appropriate rise/fall
Pace Too fast + unclear OR too slow Natural, chunked
Numbers/names Require repetition Clear first time

Action rule: Improve the lowest dimension first for two weeks before adding new focus areas. Scattershot pronunciation study produces slow progress.

Examples

Example 1: Minimal Pair Sentences

  1. I need to ship this package, not sheep.
  2. It’s a cheap chip, not a sheep ship. (practice chain)

Example 2: Word Stress in Context

“I took a PHOtograph of the photoGRAphic exhibition.”

Example 3: Intonation in Part 3

“Do you think cities are becoming more livable ↘?
Well, ↗↘ some are ↘, especially those investing in green space ↘, but affordability remains a problem ↘.”

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Diagnosis from Recording

Candidate transcript (self-reported): Band 6.5 overall; examiner note simulation — “sometimes unclear.”

Playback findings: - Drops final /t/ and /d/ consistently - Flat intonation in Part 2 - Good vocabulary

Prescription: Final consonant drills 5 min/day; mark stress on cue card notes; one shadowing session daily. Not more vocabulary study.

Worked Example 2: Stress Error Correction

Error: “I’m interested in ECOnomy” (should be ecONomy for field of study)

Fix: Learn stress with audio, not spelling — use dictionary phonetics (Cambridge/Oxford online).

Worked Example 3: Balancing Speed and Clarity

Original: 180 words/min, slurred
Target: 140 words/min, chunked

Method: Read same Part 2 script 3 times; each time pause at slashes: “I’d like to talk about / a coastal town / I visited / in twenty twenty-two.”

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — Minimal Pairs (Questions 1–12)

Say each pair twice; record if possible:

  1. ship / sheep
  2. bit / beat
  3. full / fool
  4. cat / cut
  5. live (v) / leave
  6. very / wary
  7. thin / sin
  8. think / sink
  9. right / light (if /r/ is your focus)
  10. work / walk
  11. cheap / jeep
  12. not / note

Exercise Set B — Stress Marking (Questions 13–20)

Mark primary stress; say aloud:

  1. photograph / photography / photographic
  2. economy / economic / economist
  3. record (n) / record (v)
  4. present (n) / present (v)
  5. international / internationality
  6. comfortable
  7. necessary / necessity
  8. develop / development

Exercise Set C — Chunking (Questions 21–25)

Insert slash chunks; read aloud:

  1. When I was a child we used to visit my grandparents every summer.
  2. The main reason I prefer public transport is that I can read during the commute.
  3. Although technology has many benefits it also creates privacy concerns.
  4. If governments invested more in renewable energy emissions might fall faster.
  5. I’d like to describe a quiet café where I sometimes work on weekends.

Exercise Set D — Intonation (Questions 26–30)

Identify ↗ or ↘ for final phrase:

  1. Do you enjoy cooking?
  2. I live in a small apartment near the centre.
  3. What do you like about your hometown?
  4. First I’ll talk about the location, then the atmosphere.
  5. It’s enjoyable, but it can be expensive.

Exercise Set E — Numbers and Dates (Questions 31–38)

Say clearly; record and replay:

  1. 2019
  2. 3,500,000
  3. the 15th of August
  4. £49.99
  5. 07:45 a.m.
  6. Room B-204
  7. 65%
  8. My surname is Nguyen — N-G-U-Y-E-N.

Exercise Set F — Rhythm Drill (Questions 39–42)

Tap stress only; read each line twice:

  1. I PREFer WORKing from HOME two DAYS a WEEK.
  2. The GOVernment SHOULD inVEST more in PUBLIC transport.
  3. It was the MOST memORable TRIP of my LIFE.
  4. TECHnology HAS changed the WAY we COMmunicate.

Solutions (with WHY)

Set B (stress answers)

  1. PHOtograph, phoTOgraphy, photoGRAPHic
  2. eCONomy, ecoNOMic, eCONomist
  3. REcord, reCORD
  4. PREsent, preSENT
  5. interNAtional (simplified; verify with dictionary)
  6. COMfortable
  7. NEcessary, neCESSity
  8. deVELop, deVELopment

WHY: Stress errors on academic words hurt P in Part 3 especially.

Set D

  1. ↗ (yes/no) | 27. ↘ (statement) | 28. ↘ (wh-) | 29. ↘ (listing completion) | 30. fall-rise on enjoyable ↗↘ then ↘ on expensive

Set E (pronunciation notes)

  1. Stress nineTEEN in twenty nineteen — two clear beats.
  2. Chunk: three point five million — stress million.
  3. Ordinal fifTEENTH + month stress AUgust.
  4. Forty-nine ninety-nine — stress pounds value clearly.
  5. Quarter to eight OR seven forty-five — choose one style; be consistent.
  6. Letter B, pause, two oh four — avoid B204 blur.
  7. Sixty-five percent — stress percent.
  8. Spell with pauses; Nguyen often anglicised — consistency matters more than native model.

Set F

Tap on CAPS syllables only; unstress others. If every syllable feels equally loud, slow down and retry.

Review

  • P = intelligibility, not native accent.
  • Priority: meaning contrasts, word stress, sentence stress, intonation.
  • Chunk speech; don’t swallow final consonants.
  • Shadowing + recording > passive listening.
  • Mispronounced rare words hurt more than simple accurate speech.
  • 15 minutes daily beats occasional long sessions.

Quiz

  1. Is British accent required for Band 9?
  2. Name four features under Pronunciation.
  3. ship vs sheep tests what?
  4. What is a weak form?
  5. Falling intonation typically signals what?
  6. What is chunking?
  7. How does P interact with FC?
  8. One L1-independent stress pattern for -tion words?
  9. Best tool for self-diagnosis?
  10. Should you use words you cannot pronounce?

Assignment

  1. Record 5 minutes of Part 1–3 practice. Transcribe 2 minutes. Mark stress and problem sounds.

  2. Complete 10 days of 15-minute pronunciation routine (section 121.11). Log daily focus sound.

  3. Shadow 3 minutes of authentic audio daily for one week (podcast or IELTS sample).

  4. Create a personal problem sound list (top 8) with minimal pairs and example sentences.

Revision Notes

PRONUNCIATION (P)

Goal: intelligibility, not native accent
Sounds: vowel length, clusters, /θ/ /v/ etc.
Word stress: PHOtograph vs phoTOgraphy
Sentence stress: content words strong
Weak forms: to, and, can → /tə, ən, kən/
Intonation: ↘ statements, ↗ yes/no
Chunking + clear finals
Record + shadow daily
Say words you can pronounce

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Slow down 10% on exam day — nerves speed speech and blur consonants.

Exam Strategy: In Part 2, look up at the examiner periodically — projection and clarity improve.

Exam Strategy: If the examiner says “Sorry?” once, repeat clearly with stress on key word — don’t panic and change your entire answer.

Exam Strategy: Learn stress with new vocabulary — never learn “photography” without audio.

Challenge Questions

  1. Why might a candidate score Band 7 in LR but Band 6 in P — and what is the fastest fix path?

  2. Explain how sentence stress errors can cause examiners to perceive low fluency even when grammar is strong.

  3. Design a 4-week pronunciation plan for a speaker who drops all final consonants.

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 speakers use intonation to organise long turns — slight pitch reset before a new bullet sounds effortless.

Band 9 Secret: They pronounce low-frequency words confidently because they learned them with phonetics, not spelling alone.

Band 9 Secret: Accent is consistent — examiners tune in quickly; inconsistency (random stress) strains more than L1 colour.

Band 9 Model — Annotated Excerpt (original)

“I’d like to talk about a COAstal town ↗ I visited ↘ — ESSaouira ↘, in MoROCCo ↘. / What STRUCK me most ↘ / was the CONtrast ↘ / between the BUSY medina ↘ / and the WIDE, WINDY beach ↘.”

Features: clear word stress, chunk slashes, falling tones on completed ideas, unstressed function words (a, the, me).

Previous: Chapter 120 — Part 3 Question Bank | Next: Chapter 122 — Fluency & Coherence

Chapter 122: Fluency & Coherence for IELTS Speaking

Part: Part 8 — Speaking

Estimated study time 45–120 minutes (adjust by level)
Prerequisites Complete earlier chapters in this Part where marked
Difficulty Progressive — core theory first, then Band 8–9 stretch tasks
Key takeaways Finish Review, Quiz, and Exam Tips before advancing

Learning Objectives

By the end of this chapter, you will be able to:

  • Define fluency and coherence as IELTS assesses them — distinct from “speed” or “talking a lot.”
  • Reduce harmful hesitation, repetition, and self-repair while keeping natural thinking pauses.
  • Use discourse markers and cohesive devices appropriately across Parts 1, 2, and 3.
  • Structure extended answers so listeners can follow without confusion.
  • Apply practical drills to increase speakable length under time pressure.
  • Distinguish fluency problems from grammar or vocabulary problems in self-diagnosis.
  • Maintain coherence when you change direction or forget planned content.

Theory / Explanation

122.1 Fluency vs Coherence — Definitions

Fluency (in IELTS FC): Ability to speak at length without undue effort, undue repetition, or long pauses. Includes: - Pace (not necessarily fast) - Smooth delivery - Willingness to extend

Coherence: Logical organisation and clear progression of ideas. Listeners follow why one sentence follows another. Includes: - Sequencing - Referencing (this, that, the former) - Paragraph-like structure in monologues

Critical distinction: A fast speaker can be incoherent; a slow speaker can be highly coherent. Band descriptors reward both.

122.2 What Counts as “Hesitation”

Not all pauses are equal:

Type Effect
Brief content pause (1 sec) Natural; planning next idea
Language search pause + filler loop Hurts fluency
Mid-clause freeze Hurts FC and sometimes P
Repetition (“I think I think”) Band 6 or below signal
False start + clean restart Acceptable if rare

Band 7 descriptor language: “speaks at length without noticeable effort or loss of coherence” — occasional hesitation OK.

Band 5: “cannot respond without noticeable pauses”; “often self-corrects.”

122.3 The Hesitation Hierarchy — Fixes

Level 1 — Fillers (use sparingly) - Acceptable once: “Well,” “Let me think,” “That’s interesting.” - Overuse: “Um, uh, like, you know” every clause — reduce through recording awareness.

Level 2 — Paraphrase instead of freeze - Can’t find ” ubiquitous” → “you see it everywhere” - Fluency > rare word.

Level 3 — Structural escape - Lost in Part 2 → glance at notes, resume: “Another point about…” - Part 3 → answer at simpler level first, then add layer.

Level 4 — Practice automaticity - High-frequency personal topics (Part 1) should need minimal planning pauses.

122.4 Coherence Devices — Overview

Device Function Example
Sequencers Time/order First, Then, After that, Finally
Additive Add idea Moreover, In addition, Also
Contrast Oppose However, On the other hand, Whereas
Cause/effect Explain Therefore, As a result, Because of that
Example Illustrate For instance, Such as, To give you an example
Summary Close Overall, In short, So basically
Reference Link back This experience, That approach, The former

Part-appropriate use:

Part Coherence priority
Part 1 Light sequencers; don’t over-signpost
Part 2 Clear arc; time sequencers; sensory layering
Part 3 Contrast + cause + qualification

122.5 Discourse Marker Pitfalls

Pitfall Problem
Mechanical listing “Firstly… Secondly… Thirdly…” in Part 1 feels robotic
Wrong marker “However” without contrast
Over-signposting More markers than content
Memorised chunks “In this day and age” every answer

Band 8+: Markers are sparse and accurate — listener notices logic, not templates.

122.6 Extending Answers — SPEEL Framework

When answers are too short, extend with SPEEL:

Letter Move Example prompt
S Specify Names, numbers, places
P Personal reaction “I felt… / I was surprised…”
E Example Past incident
E Explain why Reason/cause
L Link forward “Which is why I…”

Works in Part 1 and Part 2; Part 3 uses Explain + Example most.

122.7 Part-Specific Fluency Strategies

Part 1

  • Target automatic 3-sentence answers on 20 common topics.
  • Reduce question echo (“Do I like cooking? Yes…”) — wastes time.

Part 2

  • One-minute rule: If you finish a bullet in 15 seconds, add detail before moving on.
  • Use past narrative flow: background → event → reflection.
  • Closing flag: “So that’s why…” signals completion to examiner.

Part 3

  • Direct answer first — coherence starts with relevance.
  • One idea per sentence — complex ideas split across sentences.
  • Return to question if you drift: “So to answer your question directly…”

122.8 Repetition and Self-Correction

Harmful repetition: - Same word 5× (“good good good”) - Same structure every answer (“I think… I think…”)

Fix: Synonym circle practice; alternate openers.

Self-correction: - Good: “I went there two years — sorry, three years ago.” - Bad: “Sorry sorry sorry, my English is bad, um, I mean…” (confidence collapse)

Rule: One correction, continue.

122.9 Fluency Building Drills

Drill 1 — 4-3-2

Same topic: speak 4 min → 3 min → 2 min with partner. Forces compression and prioritisation.

Drill 2 — Timer extension

Answer with 1 sentence → partner says “more” until 30 seconds reached.

Drill 3 — No-pause read-aloud

Read graded text smoothly; transfer to own stories.

Drill 4 — Random topic cards

Pick topic; speak 90 sec with only 5 sec prep — builds FC under pressure.

Drill 5 — Filler audit

Record 3 minutes; count fillers; reduce by 50% next attempt.

122.10 Coherence Failure Patterns

Pattern Listener experience
Topic drift “What was the question?”
Missing closure Part 2 feels unfinished
Non-sequitur example Example doesn’t prove claim
Tense shift chaos Timeline confused
Stack of unrelated ideas Part 3 essay without glue

Fix: Outline mentally before Part 3 answers; bullet map in Part 2 prep.

122.11 Fluency vs Grammar Trade-Off

Under pressure, candidates choose: - Safe simple sentences → fluent but Band 6 GRA ceiling - Risky complex sentences → errors + pauses → Band 6 FC ceiling

Optimal: Pre-practise safe complex templates: - “Although X, Y.” - “One reason is… Another is…” - “If I hadn’t…, I wouldn’t…”

Automatic templates free cognitive load for content.

122.12 Measuring Progress

Track weekly mocks:

Metric Band 6 target Band 7 target
Part 1 avg answer length 20+ sec 25–40 sec
Part 2 duration 1:15+ 1:45–2:00
Fillers per minute <8 <4
Self-corrections per part <5 2–3
Coherence breaks (partner flags) <3 0–1

122.13 Reference and Ellipsis for Coherence

Advanced coherence uses reference words to link back without repetition:

Device Example
this/that “I tried online courses. That approach suited my schedule.”
such “It was a such a steep learning curve that I nearly quit.”
the former/latter “Tea calms me; coffee energises me. I prefer the former at night.”
one/ones “I’ve visited many coastal towns, but Essaouira is the one I remember most.”
ellipsis “Some prefer cities; others, the countryside.” (ellipsis of prefer)

Part 2 application: After introducing a place, refer to “there” or “the town” instead of repeating the name six times.

Part 3 application: “That policy” / “This trend” assumes the listener tracks your argument — but only if your previous sentence established the referent clearly.

122.14 When Fluency Breaks Down — Recovery Scripts

Memorise three recovery scripts (structure only, not fixed wording):

  1. Word search: “I’m trying to think of the word — I mean, the situation where…” then paraphrase.
  2. Lost thread (Part 2): “Let me go back to the second point on the card…” glance at notes.
  3. Part 3 overload: “There are probably several reasons — the main one is…” then give one reason well.

Recovery executed calmly protects FC; apologising repeatedly damages it.

122.15 FC Integration Across the Full Test

Think of FC as a single arc across 11–14 minutes:

Phase FC priority
Part 1 opening Warm, steady pace — no rush
Part 1 → Part 2 transition Brief pause OK; examiner introduces card
Part 2 Sustained monologue coherence
Part 2 → Part 3 Shift from narrative to analysis — register change
Part 3 late questions Maintain energy; avoid shortening answers from fatigue

Fatigue management: Part 3 answers often shrink after minute 12. Practise full-length mocks so Part 3 quality holds when tired. Hydrate before the test; shallow breathing tightens speech.

Examples

Example 1: Coherent Part 1 Progression

Q: “Do you like reading?”
A: “Yes — I’m quite an avid reader, mostly non-fiction.” (answer)
E: “I find it relaxing before bed, and it helps me learn about topics I wouldn’t study formally.” (extend)
Ex: “Last month I read a book about urban planning, which oddly connected to a podcast I’d heard.” (example + link)

Example 2: Part 2 Sequencing

“First, I’ll mention where this place is — it’s a lake about two hours north of here. Then, in terms of when I went, it was last autumn, when the foliage was at its peak. What impressed me most was how quiet it was compared with coastal resorts. So overall, it’s somewhere I’d return to for a digital detox.”

Example 3: Part 3 Qualification

“I do think remote work offers flexibility; however, it can blur boundaries between home and office. As a result, some people end up working longer hours. For example, colleagues of mine check email late at night. That said, with clear policies, the benefits usually outweigh the drawbacks.”

Worked Examples

Worked Example 1: Reducing Fillers

Before (30 sec): 12 “um” instances.

Process: 1. Transcribe recording 2. Circle fillers 3. Re-record with pause instead of um — silent 0.5 sec OK

After: 4 fillers; same content; Band +0.5 FC typical in practice.

Worked Example 2: Coherence Repair Mid-Part-2

Drift: Started describing a restaurant; talks about unrelated work stress.

Repair: “Sorry — I’m drifting — the main point about the restaurant was its atmosphere, which helped me unwind after stressful weeks at work.”

WHY: Explicit repair shows coherence awareness; better than continuing drift.

Worked Example 3: Extending Band 5 Part 1

Q: “Do you use social media?”

Band 5: “Yes, I use Instagram every day.”

SPEEL pass: - S: Instagram, mainly stories
- P: I enjoy seeing friends’ updates
- E: Yesterday a cousin posted wedding photos
- E: It keeps me connected abroad
- L: So I probably spend too much time scrolling

Result: 4 sentences, coherent, fluent.

Practice Exercises

Exercise Set A — Fluency Timing (Questions 1–8)

Speak 30+ seconds each (record):

  1. A hobby you enjoy
  2. Your favourite season
  3. A piece of technology you use daily
  4. How you relax after work
  5. A place you’d like to visit
  6. Whether you prefer city or countryside
  7. How you learn new things
  8. Your morning routine

Exercise Set B — Coherence Markers (Questions 9–14)

Rewrite adding one appropriate marker each:

  1. (contrast) I like cities. They are noisy.
  2. (example) Many people learn languages. My sister learned Spanish online.
  3. (cause) Public transport is cheap. I use the metro.
  4. (sequence) I packed. I flew. I checked into the hotel.
  5. (summary) The trip was tiring. It was worth it.
  6. (reference) I prefer tea. Coffee keeps me awake.

Exercise Set C — Problem Diagnosis (Questions 15–20)

Label primary issue: FC-fluency / FC-coherence / LR / GRA / P

  1. 3-second pause every 4 words searching vocabulary
  2. Part 2 story jumps between two unrelated events
  3. Says “However” but adds similar idea, not contrast
  4. Mumbles final syllables
  5. Perfect grammar but 45-second Part 2
  6. Repeats “beautiful” six times in one minute

Exercise Set D — 4-3-2 Drill (Questions 21–23)

Choose one topic; deliver at 4, 3, and 2 minutes:

  1. Importance of education
  2. Effects of technology on society
  3. A memorable journey you took

Note what you cut at each stage — coherence priority exercise.

Solutions (with WHY)

Set B (samples)

  1. “I like cities; however, they can be noisy at night.”
  2. “Many people learn languages — for instance, my sister learned Spanish online.”
  3. “Because public transport is cheap, I use the metro most days.”
  4. “First I packed, then I flew, and after that I checked into the hotel.”
  5. “Overall, the trip was tiring but worth it.”
  6. “I prefer tea; the latter keeps me awake less than coffee.” (or: “Tea, not coffee — that keeps me awake.”)

Set C

  1. FC-fluency (+ LR) | 16. FC-coherence | 17. FC-coherence (marker misuse) | 18. P | 19. FC-fluency | 20. LR (+ FC)

Review

  • Fluency ≠ speed; coherence ≠ using many linkers.
  • Brief pauses OK; filler loops and mid-clause freezes hurt.
  • SPEEL extends short answers; OEE structures Part 3 (Chapter 119).
  • Discourse markers must be accurate and sparse.
  • Self-correct once, move on.
  • Record metrics: duration, fillers, coherence breaks.

Quiz

  2. Define coherence.
  3. What is SPEEL?
  4. One acceptable filler?
  5. Ideal Part 2 duration for Band 7+?
  6. What is 4-3-2 drill?
  7. Harmful vs helpful self-correction?
  8. Part 3: answer first or example first?
  9. Name two contrast markers.
  10. Does fast speech guarantee high FC?

Assignment

  1. Filler audit week: Record daily 3-minute monologue; graph filler count.

  2. Complete 4-3-2 on three Part 3 topics with a partner.

  3. Deliver 10 Part 2 cards; log duration — aim for 90%+ over 1:30.

  4. Transcribe one mock; highlight coherence breaks in red; rewrite those segments.

Revision Notes

FLUENCY & COHERENCE (FC)

Fluency: length without undue pause/repair
Coherence: logical progression
Pauses: OK between ideas, not mid-clause
SPEEL: Specify Personal Example Explain Link
Markers: accurate, sparse, part-appropriate
Extend Part 1; structure Part 2; direct Part 3
One self-correction, continue
4-3-2 | timer extension | filler audit
Record metrics weekly

Exam Tips

Exam Strategy: Silence beats “um um um” — examiners prefer brief thinking pause to filler chains.

Exam Strategy: In Part 2, if you run out at 1:10, have a backup layer: feelings + recommendation + comparison.

Exam Strategy: Topic drift hurts more than simple grammar errors — return to question explicitly.

Exam Strategy: Practise same topics until Part 1 answers feel automatic — saves FC for Part 3.

Challenge Questions

  1. Why do examiners sometimes score coherence lower than fluency for candidates who speak quickly?

  2. Design a 2-week FC intervention for someone with Band 5.5 FC and Band 7 LR.

  3. Compare FC in Speaking with Cohesion in Writing — same skill or different?

Band 9 Tips

Band 9 Secret: Band 9 fluency looks effortless because content is organised before speech starts — even Part 3 answers have invisible micro-outlines.

Band 9 Secret: They never panic-fill — if an idea is missing, they simplify the claim and continue.

Band 9 Secret: Coherence comes from logic, not linker density — one “however” at the right moment beats five misplaced transitions.

Band 9 Model — FC Annotated (original Part 3 fragment)

“To answer directly, I don’t think traditional libraries will disappear — rather, their role is shifting. Instead of being the only source of books, they function as community hubs where people study, access wifi, and attend workshops. Take my local branch as an example: half the floor space is now a children’s reading zone. That said, funding is a real issue; without municipal support, smaller branches might close. On balance, though, the social function keeps them relevant.”

FC features: direct opening, contrast, example, qualification, balanced close — markers serve logic.
